News.title: Pilots accused of being drunk as private jet explodes during Libya crash-landing
News.content:
Pilots accused of being drunk as private jet explodes during Libya crash-landing

The Cessna aircraft caught fire after veering off the runway while landing at Misrata Airport in Libya, with its pilots now suspected of being under the influence of alcohol

View 2 Images The aftermath of the crash (Image: Jam Press)

Two pilots are suspected of being drunk when the private jet they were flying crashed during landing.

‌



The incident took place at Misrata Airport in Libya on Monday and all those on board - the two pilots and a flight attendant - were safely rescued by emergency services.

‌



But Libya's public prosecution has now announced it has ordered the arrest of two pilots for allegedly flying the Cessna Citation Latitude while under the influence of alcohol.

‌



While the identities of the pilots have not been disclosed by authorities, Libyan media reports the captain is a German national and his co-pilot Turkish. After veering off the runway at Misrata Airport during landing, the aircraft caught fire.

View 2 Images The pilots have been accused of being drunk

Brit dad-of-two killed alongside two friends as plane crashes near Swiss Alps resort READ MORE :

Private jet carrying singer and 7 others crash-lands in Brazil and bursts into flames READ MORE :

Shocking pictures from the scene show most of the aircraft turned to ash as dark grey smoke kept rising while firefighters were in attendance. Only the cockpit appeared to still be intact.

‌



The private jet, registered as TC-AKF, took off from Istanbul Ataturk Airport at 5:45am local time without any passengers on board. The plane was on its way to Misrata to pick up passengers, according to reports.

Libya's Transportation Ministry said it suspended flights at the airport after the incident.

The Libyan prosecution said investigators found "evidence that (the pilots) had flown the aircraft while drunk" and ordered their pre-trial detention, Arab News reports.

Article continues below

Authorities added that the two individuals "posed a real threat" to the "airport, its users and the safety of the airspace the aircraft traversed before it crashed".

The aircraft belongs to the Turkish conglomerate Akfen Holding, led by Turkish businessman Hamdi Akin. It was operated by BKNJET Aviation Co. and had capacity for nine passengers.

BKNJET disputed the Libyan authorities' claims that the pilots were drunk, New York Post reports. The operator said: "No verified result or document indicating any such finding regarding alcohol has been received by us."

News.title: Earthquake with 3.3 magnitude strikes near Lincolnshire holiday hotspot
News.content:
Earthquake with 3.3 magnitude strikes near Lincolnshire holiday hotspot

The 3.3 magnitude earthquake hit the North Sea off the coast of Lincolnshire, roughly 25km from Skegness, according to the British Geological Survey (BGS)

View 3 Images The earthquake hit off the Lincolnshire coast, near Skegness (file) (Image: Getty)

An earthquake has struck off the coast of Lincolnshire, just miles from one of the UK's most popular seaside resorts.

‌



The 3.3 magnitude tremor hit the North Sea at a depth of 11km at around 1:04pm today, according to the British Geological Survey (BGS).

‌



The quake was unlikely to have caused any major disruption, but weak shaking may have been felt in several coastal communities close to the epicentre.

‌



Earthquake monitoring site VolcanoDiscovery said people in Chapel St Leonards, Ingoldmells, Mablethorpe and Skegness may have experienced "very weak shaking", while the tremor was unlikely to have been felt as far away as Grimsby, Cleethorpes and Boston.

Hunstanton was also among the areas where very weak shaking may have been felt.

View 3 Images The epicentre was just off the coast of Lincolnshire (Image: BSG)

‌



Tenerife rocked by FOUR earthquakes before volcano drills as tourists feel rumble READ MORE :

Skegness, around 25km from the epicentre, was the closest major town where the earthquake may have been felt.

The popular seaside resort is known for its sandy beach, pier, traditional amusements and family attractions.

VolcanoDiscovery recorded the tremor as magnitude 3.4, slightly higher than the 3.3 figure given by the BGS. Earthquake readings can be revised as seismologists analyse the data, it said.

‌



According to the BGS, 309 earthquakes were recorded across the UK last year, with many too small to be felt. Larger magnitude 4 earthquakes happen roughly every three to four years.

View 3 Images Skegness draws in millions of visitors each year (file) (Image: Getty)

The biggest known earthquake in the UK struck the Dogger Bank area of the North Sea on June 7, 1931. The BGS says the magnitude 6.1 tremor was "the largest known earthquake in the UK".

Article continues below

Its epicentre was around 120km north-east of Great Yarmouth, but the quake was felt across much of Britain and parts of northern Europe, with damage reported in 71 places. In Filey, the top of a church spire was rotated, while chimneys and plaster were damaged in several other towns.

The last magnitude 5 earthquake recorded in the UK was in Lincolnshire in 2008. The BGS says Britain typically experiences a magnitude 5 earthquake every 10 to 20 years, although most tremors recorded in the UK are much smaller and cause no damage.

More recently, a magnitude 2.2 earthquake struck near Grimsby on August 25.

News.title: Vehicle 'drives on wrong side' during Cornwall police chase before kebab shop crash
News.content:
Vehicle 'drives on wrong side' during Cornwall police chase before kebab shop crash

A 'suspicious vehicle' was seen being driven at 'excess speed' and on the wrong side of the road in a town in Cornwall, police said, before crashing into a wall

View Image Commercial Street, Camborne (Image: Google Maps)

A man has been arrested after a car was driven at "excess speed" on the wrong side of the road in Cornwall, police said.

The incident took place in Tolvaddon, Camborne, in the early hours of Monday. Devon and Cornwall Police said a "suspicious vehicle failed to stop" before officers followed.

A short time later, the car crashed into a wall outside a kebab shop in the Commercial Street area of the town, Cornwall Live reports.

No one was injured in the incident. A man in his 20s, from Camborne, has been arrested on suspicion of failing to stop for police, dangerous driving, driving with a proportion of a specified controlled drug above the specified limit and possession of cannabis.

He has since been released under investigation pending further enquiries. A statement from Devon and Cornwall Police reads: "A suspicious vehicle failed to stop for police on Tolvaddon, Camborne, at 1.35am on Monday 14 September.

"Officers followed the car which was seen travelling at excess speed and on the wrong side of the road. The suspect vehicle was involved in a low-speed collision with a wall in the Commercial Street area a short time later.

"No-one was injured during the incident and no other vehicles were damaged. A man in his 20s from Camborne was arrested on suspicion of failing to stop for police, dangerous driving, driving with a proportion of a specified controlled drug above the specified limit and possession of cannabis.

"He has been released under investigation pending further enquiries."

A number of wrong-way crashes have occurred across the UK and Ireland in recent weeks. Last month, two Cleveland Police officers - PC Tom Clough and PC Matthew Blades - lost their lives during a head-on crash on the A66 near Middlesbrough.

A Volkswagen Passat that was being driven the wrong way following a pursuit collided with their police vehicle. It was occupied by five people - Jakub Matusiak, 23, Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-old Michael Robert Cahill. They also died in the crash.

Similarly, just a week before, five other young people were killed when they drove the wrong way down the M9 in County Kildare in Ireland, also injuring three adult sisters and a child who were driving on the correct side of the road.

The five teenagers were named as Joe Carthy, Alex McCarthy, Kamil Pustkowski, Jeremy O'Brien and Jack Kennedy.

News.title: 'Princess Diana's brother Earl Spencer has thrown down the gauntlet to King - how he responds will be telling'
News.content:
Does anyone seriously believe King Charles, a man whom countless people have described over the years as being seriously affected by Princess Diana’s death, regardless of their disaster of a marriage, would say such “monstrous” words?

The pointed language used by Earl Spencer is so outlandish and hyperbolic that even the most committed Republicans would struggle to get on board. But this war of words, which is already spiralling wildly out of control, endangers the very fabric of the monarchy.

And all in the week that Prince Harry has turned up to cosplay being a royal, with 48 hours of public engagements as he strives to rehabilitate his own image now he’s parked up in Britain once again.

View 3 Images Earl Spencer insists he is "telling the truth" about explosive claims in his new book (Image: BBC)

‌



Forget the notion of “your truth” - ridiculously peddled by Oprah Winfrey following her interview with Harry and Meghan after their explosive exit from royal life - there is only one truth here. Princess Diana’s brother Earl Spencer has abandoned his self-imposed shackles from publicly talking about his sister’s experiences within the royal family - all in good time to publicise his book and cash in ahead of the 30th anniversary of Diana’s death.

How convenient then that he has suddenly lifted the lid on private conversations with the then Prince Charles, where he allegedly “sounded giddily elated” upon the tragic news of the death of the mother of his children. Spencer knows the framing around it has the potential to inflict the most damage.

Claiming Charles's “pent-up contempt” for his former wife, and adding that the King sounded almost gleeful - comparing his tone to that of “a lottery winner” - at the very moment the nation was collapsing into grief, is simply staggering. Spencer has laid down the gauntlet to the King his own version of "recollections may vary" is anything but a rebuttal of his version of events.

View 3 Images King Charles responded to Earl Spencer's claims in an unprecedented statement (Image: Jonathan Brady/Pool PA via AP)

‌



These aren't simply unflattering anecdotes about a phone call 30 years ago, they are a direct challenge to the version of events the monarchy has quietly relied on for years - that Charles was a grieving father doing his best amid impossible pressure, not a man irritated by his ex-wife's popularity.

If the public believes Spencer over the Palace, it doesn't just tarnish a moment in history; it corrodes the trust that underpins the King's own reign, at a time when Charles is already contending with health concerns and a slimmed-down, ageing monarchy, and how he will respond to his estranged son’s homecoming.

For an institution that survives on the idea of quiet dignity and closing ranks, those days are over. What happens next will be for the King to decide.

News.title: Tourists swallowed by 'quicksand sludge' after ignoring warnings at Italian park
News.content:
Tourists swallowed by 'quicksand sludge' after ignoring warnings at Italian park

The two tourists were left trapped waist-deep in sludge after venturing beyond warning signs at a nature park in Italy to get pictures of a flock of flamingos

Italy: Tourists rescued after becoming stuck in mud on restricted beach

Two tourists chasing pictures of flamingos ended up stuck waist-deep in sludge after ignoring warning signs at a nature park in Italy.

‌



The women became trapped when the ground beneath them gave way, leaving them stuck in a salt-pan trap that acted like quicksand.

‌



Local reports said the pair wanted pictures of the park's flamingos and continued walking even after the ground began to swallow them. The tourists climbed over a barrier and past danger signs to reach the animals.

‌



Footage showed the moment firefighters rushed over and placed ladders across the sludge so that they could reach the women without sinking themselves.

View 2 Images The women were rescued by firefighters

UK weather maps show 30C heat surge with 10 counties at 28C or more – full list READ MORE :

Met Police officer accused of killing pregnant woman in crash – unborn baby died too READ MORE :

The pair were eventually rescued using rope and did not need hospital treatment. They were given water and hosed down on the spot.

‌



The drama unfolded on September 14 at the Molentargius-Saline Natural Park in Quartu Sant’Elena in Sardinia.

According to local reports, the tourists had crossed barriers beside Viale Colombo, on the way to Poetto beach. Passers-by raised the alarm, bringing fire crews, local police and an ambulance to the scene.

Officers also had to hold back a crowd that gathered to watch the rescue effort.

‌



Park bosses said access to the area was "strictly forbidden" and clearly marked with warning signs.

View 2 Images Park bosses said the area was 'strictly forbidden'

"Molentargius is a protected area, and the restrictions are there to stop people harming the birds and the park's delicate ecosystem," they said. "Breaking the rules is subject to sanctions."

‌



Director Marianna Mossa said: "What happened this morning also shows that respecting the restrictions is vital for people's safety."

She added: "The basins are not accessible or walkable. The surface of the sediment can look stable, but it hides extremely treacherous conditions. The risk of sinking can appear suddenly, as unfortunately happened this morning."

Officials said they are waiting for a report from local police before taking further action. The pair could also face fines from the forestry police.

Article continues below

Initial reports suggested the women may have been from Rome. Their names have not been released.

News.title: Earl Spencer hits back at Palace and claims King Charles went 'ballistic' in row after Diana's death
News.content:
Earl Spencer hits back at Palace and claims King Charles went 'ballistic' in row after Diana's death

In a new interview with the BBC, Princess Diana's brother has claimed he is "telling the truth" after Buckingham Palace hit back at claims in his new book that the King said of his former wife after her death "rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough"

Earl Spencer fumes 'I'm telling the truth' in bombshell BBC interview

Princess Diana's brother says he is "telling the truth" about claims King Charles said the royal family would “forget her soon enough" following her tragic death in 1997.

‌



Earl Spencer accused the then-then Prince Charles of launching into a furious tirade against him in a phone call in the days after the princess was killed in a Paris car crash, alongside her lover Dodi Fayed. The Earl said he told the King how he strongly disagreed with the decision made by the royals to have princes William and Harry - aged just 15 and 12 - walk behind their mother’s coffin during her funeral procession.

‌



Buckingham Palace issused a strongly worded rebuke just over an hour after Spencer’s claims emerged in a newspaper serialisation of his new book on Thursday, saying the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

‌



View 3 Images Earl Spencer has insisted he is "telling the truth" after explosive allegations in his new book (Image: BBC)

"I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said," the Earl said, s peaking to the BBC today. Pressed on whether he disagreed with Buckingham Palace disputing his version of events, Spencer hit back saying they had not issued a formal denial of the phone call alleged to have taken place.

“They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary," he said. The late Queen Elizabeth II issued a now famous statement, including the line “recollections may vary”, in the aftermath of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s claims following their exit from the monarchy, that unnamed members of the family “had concerns” over the colour of their unborn son Archie’s skin colour.

‌



Reacting to the rebuttal from the palace, Earl Spencer said: “Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?” Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: “I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

“I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that.”

View 3 Images Princess Diana's brother spoke to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg (Image: BBC)

‌



In further extracts published on Thursday, Spencer also claimed the King “sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner". The Earl told the BBC that while he did not keep contemporaneous notes of the conversations with the King, or keep a diary, he told close family members at the time “because it was so monstrous".

Royal sources today told The Mirror that Spencer’s explosive claims are “utter nonsense”. Well placed palace insiders also reacted with dismay that Diana’s brother has chosen to use the monarch as “a punching bag” to publicise his tell-all memoir on his sister’s life, ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death next year.

One source, who worked for the royal family for a decade said: “(The allegations) couldn't be further from the truth of a man (King Charles) who was deeply affected by Diana’s death.” The source added: “To claim anything other than he was overwhelmingly concerned for the wellbeing of his son’s futures, without their mother, is simply contumelious.”

‌



View 3 Images The King in Scotland earlier this week (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

In a two minute 39 second clip of the upcoming BBC interview with presenter Laura Kuenssberg, Spencer alleged the King “went ballistic” and “ranted for a while”, accusing his family of not having an adequate sense of duty. He added: “And then he stopped and I thought, oh now, now he's gonna pull himself together and say something more appropriate. And then, he said, 'we'll forget her soon enough'.”

Spencer said he couldn't say exactly what went through his mind at that moment as he was “just so stunned”, adding: “I just, after a stunned silence, I said, I cannot believe you just said that. And I hung up on him.”

Article continues below

Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next Tuesday and is expected to be highly critical of the royal family. Buckingham Palace has declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments.

News.title: England squad: Palmer and Trent back as snubbed star's partner takes aim at Thomas Tuchel
News.content:
Thomas Tuchel has announced his latest England squad as the Three Lions all prepare for an extended, revamped three-week international break across late September and early October

Thomas Tuchel has named his 26-man England squad for the upcoming international break. Chelsea's Cole Palmer and Real Madrid's Trent Alexander-Arnold have received recalls.

Palmer has impressed under Xabi Alonso this season, scoring four times and adding two assists in five appearances. He is back in the Three Lions camp after missing the World Cup. Another face returning to the England fold is Alexander-Arnold, despite a difficult start to the season at Real Madrid, where he has been in and out of the XI alongside Denzel Dumfries.

Elsewhere, Bournemouth's Alex Scott and Liverpool's Rio Ngumoha have been selected by Tuchel, who were included in the four-person warm-up group before the World Cup earlier this summer. Lewis Hall also makes it following an excellent start to the season at Newcastle United, while Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite has earned a place as a reward for a solid start to the campaign.

News.title: Mel B's daughter among stars spotted in purple beanie at London Fashion Week
News.content:
Mel B's daughter among stars spotted in purple beanie at London Fashion Week

Phoenix Brown, Heartstopper star Jenny Walser and former Love Islander Jordan Hames were among the celebrities spotted wearing a limited-edition purple Grimace beanie at London Fashion Week

View 7 Images Phoenix Brown showed off her beanie before heading to the H&M&YOU&I event (Image: PinPep)

A host of celebrities have been spotted out and about wearing an unusual fashion accessory as they made their way to a range of shows that mark the beginning of London Fashion Week. Heartstopper actress Jenny Walser, TV presenter Charli Fisher and former Love Islander and model Jordan Hames were pictured n the capital wearing a purple beanie.

Phoenix Brown – daughter of Spice Girl Mel B –was seen at the H&M&YOU&I event wearing the headpiece, which has a pair of cartoon eyes. The quirky, fully reversible purple and yellow hat draws inspiration from Grimace, the iconic McDonald's character who first burst onto the scene in 1971.

View 7 Images Brown oozed cool as she headed inside (Image: PinPep)

Jenny, best known for her roles as Tori Spring in the hit Netflix series and Louise Wrigley in Call The Midwife, were seen wearing the accessory ahead of the Mithridate Show at Space House on Thursday. Meanwhile, Charli modelled the beanie as she turned up for The Art of Belonging show at Asia House in central London.

Jordan, who shot to fame on the 2019 series of Love Island, showed off the eye-catching hat as he made his way to 180 The Strand, while stylist and designer Kyle De'Volle turned heads wearing the beanie as he rocked up at Dover Street Market for the BFC Jewellery Showcase.

The eye-catching beanie has been launched to mark the arrival of McHappy Day , a new fundraising day taking place across the UK with the aim of raising vital funds for Ronald McDonald House UK.

7 View 7 Images Stylist Kyle De’Volle was also spotted wearing the Charity Beanie (Image: PinPep) 7 View 7 Images The hat topped off his all-denim outfit (Image: PinPep)

Ella Joseph, CEO at Ronald McDonald House UK, said: "We are so excited to see the limited-edition Grimace Beanie getting such a warm reaction at London Fashion Week.

"As we head into Autumn, a beanie is a stylish essential, but it also contributes to McDonald's McHappy Day fundraising as all proceeds from every Beanie sold will be donated directly to Ronald McDonald House UK.

"Ronald McDonald House UK offers vital support for families with children in hospital by providing them free accommodation, within walking distance of their ward."

7 View 7 Images Jenny Walser looked great as she stepped out ahead of the Mithridate Show (Image: WILL_IRELAND) 7 View 7 Images Charli Fisher wore the Beanie while heading to The Art of Belonging (Image: PinPep)

View 7 Images Ex-Love Islander Jordan Hames was also seen getting involved (Image: WILL_IRELAND)

She added: "The 14 Ronald McDonald Houses across the UK give families access to community and a place that they can call home, helping to alleviate the practical and financial pressures that come with hospital stays.

"This means that with every purchase of a Grimace Beanie, customers can help make a real difference to families when they need it most."

Scheduled for Saturday 26th September, £1 from every qualifying main meal purchased at selected restaurants will go straight to the charity, bolstering its efforts to support families of seriously ill children throughout the UK.

Priced at just £5, the Grimace Beanie is available now at participating McDonald's restaurants or through the McDonald's App.

It's certainly a surprising addition to London Fashion Week, which will showcase Spring/Summer 2027 collections from some of the most influential names in the fashion industry.

The twice-yearly showcase ranks amongst the fashion industry's elite "Big Four" weeks, sitting alongside Paris, Milan and New York, and plays a crucial role in shaping worldwide style trends each season.

News.title: 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview
News.content:
Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"

Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Buckingham Palace declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments.

The remarks may bring a renewed focus to the war of words between the Palace and the King's former brother-in-law.

News.title: MI5 accepts it gave evidence based on lies in neo-Nazi spy case
News.content:
He said "MI5 accepts without reservation" the findings of a damning report which concluded that it gave evidence based on "lies" about having kept to its core secrecy policy - known as 'neither confirm nor deny' (NCND) - about the agent status of the neo-Nazi informant.

The security service claimed it had maintained NCND and, consequently, the courts allowed it to keep information secret from a woman who was abused by him.

But what MI5 said was untrue. The security service had in fact disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020.

A panel of three senior judges - England and Wales' most senior judge, Lady Chief Justice Baroness Sue Carr, President of the King's Bench Division Dame Victoria Sharp and Mr Justice Chamberlain - is considering what action to take over the false evidence.

In particular, it will decide whether to initiate contempt of court proceedings against certain MI5 officers or MI5 itself. Any such move would be unprecedented.

The report, by then-deputy investigatory powers commissioner Sir John Goldring, found that one senior MI5 spy - known as Officer 2 - lied repeatedly, while another - Officer 3 - misled his own colleagues and lied about what he was told.

He also found there were "serious and systemic failures in MI5's conduct" throughout the case.

Otty said MI5 "fully accepts and acknowledges the gravity of the issues raised" in the report, published in July, and they must never happen again.

He added that MI5 had committed to a major programme of reform under the leadership of director general Sir Ken McCallum.

Otty argued against contempt proceedings being brought, saying it would not be in the public interest given Sir John's detailed investigation, MI5's apologies, and its commitment to a programme of reform.

He said Officer 2 had resigned from the service and that Officer 3 had been suspended and was facing disciplinary proceedings, which could lead to his dismissal.

Lawyers for both officers also argued against launching contempt proceedings.

Matthew Butt KC, for Officer 2, said the officer accepted that his conduct had fallen "below the standard expected of him", for which he apologised and expressed regret.

But he said he denied acting dishonestly or having interfered with the administration of justice, and did not accept the report's findings.

Aaron Watkins apologised on behalf of Officer 3 and accepted his conduct "undoubtably" contributed to the courts and parties involved being misled, but denied it had been the result of dishonesty.

He said the evidence presented by Sir John fell short of the threshold for contempt of court, and said such proceedings would not be in the public interest because there had already been a thorough investigation.

Meanwhile, lawyers for the BBC said the corporation considered the threshold had been met and said there was a "very clear public interest" in doing so.

Jude Bunting KC said providing false evidence was "a particularly serious affront to the administration of justice" and noted that while MI5 now offered a sincere apology to the court, its response when the lies were first exposed was "not consistent with transparency or responsibility".

At the conclusion of the hearing, the Lady Chief Justice said it had been a "serious day addressing serious matters".

She said a judgment will be issued at a later date.

News.title: Flight chaos caused by software defect in space of a millisecond, report says
News.content:
An air traffic control failure that sparked widespread travel chaos earlier this month was caused by a "software defect" affecting the system underpinning UK air space management, the national air traffic service Nats has said.

The problem happened "in the space of a millisecond", Nats said, leading to the system producing corrupted data.

The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas.

Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe told the BBC he would not resign, saying the software defect was "very, very obscure."

"You can fly to almost anywhere from almost any airport at almost any time. If that stops, even for a moment, then you get huge disruption.

"My job is to make sure that we have this happen as infrequently as possible," he added.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the disruption "completely unacceptable", while industry body Airlines UK is writing to Nats to demand immediate compensation for costs incurred.

The incident prompted questions over the resilience of Nats' systems, and some airlines questioned the position of Mr Rolfe.

There has also been anger from passengers about how much support they got from airlines, and about the fact that they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation because the regulator judges the situation was extraordinary circumstances.

In an initial report, external, Nats said the software defect meant air traffic controllers had reduced information available, so restrictions were put in place to limit air traffic to maintain safety.

The defect occurred at 10:00am on 8 September, but it did not become apparent this was a serious problem for another two and a half hours.

The system restart did not start until just after 3:15pm, and restrictions on UK airspace were not lifted until 7:30pm.

Flights in and out of the UK's main airports were affected, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.

The disruption took days to completely resolve because of the number of planes and crew left out of place.

Mr Rolfe apologised to those affected by the disruption, saying Nats was "devastated".

"However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question."

Nats has "tested these systems so much," he added.

"We spent so much time making sure they work that anything that does happen of this nature is, by its very nature, going to be incredibly complicated and probably difficult to understand at the time," he said.

Reacting to the Nats report, the transport secretary described the disruption as "completely unacceptable" and "frustrating" for passengers, airlines and airports.

"It's clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos," Alexander said, adding that a Civil Aviation Authority review was underway.

This is the third national air traffic incident in the past three years.

In 2023, a computer shutdown over the August bank holiday weekend caused chaos for 700,000 passengers.

There was another, smaller Nats outage in 2025, which caused 150 cancellations.

Tim Alderslade, chief executive of Airlines UK, said: "Once again, it is passengers who have suffered and airlines who have picked up the pieces - and the tab - of an ATC [Air Traffic Control] system failure, while Nats itself faces no real consequences."

He added that passengers deserved "commitment and proof that the system is being fixed".

Alderslade also said Airlines UK was writing to NATS "to demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience."

News.title: Teen who piloted Channel boat with 165 migrants jailed
News.content:
A teenager who piloted a dinghy carrying a then-record 165 migrants across the English Channel to the UK has been sentenced to two years and three months in prison.

Chan Mathok Atak, 19, from South Sudan, admitted endangering others during a sea crossing on 23 July - the 16th conviction since the new offence was created in January.

Prosecutors at Canterbury Crown Court said Atak created a risk of death or serious personal injury to others on board the boat.

At the time, the so-called "mega dinghy" set a record for the largest number of migrants brought over on a small boat in recent years. That figure has since been surpassed with 230 people on board a vessel in August.

At Canterbury Crown Court on Friday, Judge Sarah Counsell said the offence was so serious "only an immediate custodial sentence can be justified".

She warned Atak that as a foreign national he was liable in principle to automatic deportation once he completed his sentence.

James Harrison, prosecuting, told the court the boat Atak was piloting was 12.8ft (3.9m) wide and 46.9ft (14.3m) long, a similar length to a standard bus.

The boat had travelled between Calais and the UK and was deflating when it was picked up by border force vessels.

News.title: Brother didn't match description of 'Putney pusher', suspect's sisters tell BBC
News.content:
The sisters of the man suspected of being the so-called "Putney pusher" have told the BBC their brother was innocent, and the police showed "no urgency" to clear his name.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Nicholas Brandram's sisters accused the Metropolitan Police of being "negligent and reckless".

Brandram was found dead on Tuesday evening and his family said he "took his own life after months of immense pressure" caused by the investigation.

Brandram's sisters Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker told Today presenter Justin Webb their brother's mental health deteriorated after his arrest and questioned why the police were not able to carry out DNA tests that could have proved his innocence.

News.title: Tenko and Coronation Street actress Stephanie Cole dies aged 84
News.content:
Solihull-born Cole, who trained at Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, after making her stage debut at the age of 17 â playing the 90-year-old medium Madame Arcati in Noel Coward's Blithe Spirit.

She went on to enjoy a lengthy career that spanned TV, radio and film and was perhaps best known for playing Dr Beatrice Mason in the 1980s BBC wartime TV drama Tenko.

The series chronicled the lives of British women in Singapore after the Japanese invasion and their consequent confinement in a Japanese prisoner of war camp.

Cole, in her breakout role, played a doctor who struggled to look after the women's health, opposite Ann Bell and Claire Oberman.

During this same period, Cole also played the moody customer Mrs Delphine Featherstone, aka "The Black Widow" in the Ronnie Barker-starring Open All Hours.

She would go on to win the award for best TV comedy actress for her part as the sharp-tongued photojournalist Diana Trent in Waiting For God.

But she cited her earlier performance as Muriel in Alan Bennett's monologue Soldiering On, as one of her proudest moments. The series also starred Maggie Smith and Julie Walters.

Her stage highlight, by her account, was in a West End production of A Passionate Woman.

News.title: Ryanair boss Michael O'Leary apologises over 'high-fare rapists' remarks
News.content:
Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has said he is "truly sorry" for describing rival airlines as "high-fare rapists".

He had previously refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for the comments.

O'Leary had made the remark earlier this month while talking to journalists ahead of Ryanair's yearly meeting with shareholders.

Following the comments, the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) wrote to him asking for an apology, in a letter seen by the BBC.

O'Leary had originally said that some people were "desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe".

He subsequently defended his choice of words when asked by a reporter from the Press Association whether the language was appropriate.

"British Airways, Lufthansa, and everybody else's high fares, I'll happily offend them on a regular basis," he had added.

Asked whether it would offend sexual assault victims, he said rape was "a terrible crime".

In a video posted on Friday, O'Leary said that, over the last ten days, he had had "conversations with family and friends, both inside and outside Ryanair".

"I have come to realise however that the word that I used so carelessly has caused considerable upset and offence to a wide number of people, especially to victims and survivors.

"I want to apologise, sincerely and unreservedly, to those people, especially to the survivors."

O'Leary described his choice of language as "careless", and said "it won't happen again".

"I will try to learn from this mistake, and do better in future."

Following O'Leary's first comments, the DRCC's chief executive Rachel Morrogh had written to O'Leary accusing him of trying to get a headline with his comments.

She said the DRCC had received calls from rape victims who were "upset and distressed because of what you said".

She offered O'Leary training on the impact of sexual violence and urged him to apologise.

"I can't imagine you would ever use the term so flippantly again if you truly understood [what] it was like to survive rape," she wrote.

In response, O'Leary had said: "I am quite clear that no remarks of mine could possibly trivialise the heinous crime of rape."

He added that as he had not "trivialised the heinous crime of rape" he would "not be issuing any apology or accepting your offer of training".

It was not the first time O'Leary had offended people while talking about his business.

In 2004, he reportedly called the owners of Stansted Airport "a bunch of overcharging rapists", external in a row over airport charges.

He has also previously called some of his own staff "lazy bastards" and once said to passengers looking for a refund "we don't want to hear your sob stories".

In June, he said the airline would "reluctantly" stop charging parents to sit next to children after a watchdog investigation was opened, but insisted its previous policy complied with laws.

News.title: Man in court charged with murder over Armadale shooting
News.content:
A man has appeared in court charged with murdering another man who was shot dead in West Lothian.

Police were called to a property on Harestanes Road in Armadale at about 11:50 on Saturday.

Billy Watson, 35, was found injured and died at the scene.

Frank McCarthy, 57, appeared at Livingston Sheriff Court on Friday, charged with murder and attempting to defeat the ends of justice. He made no plea and was remanded in custody.

A 29-year-old man and 44-year-old man have also been arrested in connection with the incident.

Police Scotland said inquiries were ongoing.

News.title: Nottingham attacks family condemn police promotion
News.content:
The father of a student who was stabbed to death in the Nottingham attacks has criticised a move by Nottinghamshire Police to promote the senior officer who led the investigation.

Grace O'Malley-Kumar, Barnaby Webber and Ian Coates were stabbed on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, leading to a public inquiry.

Rob Griffin, of Nottinghamshire Police, was temporary deputy chief constable from 29 April 2025 and was appointed substantively into the role following a selection process in August, the force said.

Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's dad, told the BBC on Friday: "I think this is completely wrong."

Police say the process consisted of an application form, a people panel and external advisors.

Griffin has previously been described by Barnaby's mother Emma Webber as having "blood on his hands", following the force's failure to detain Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020, after an arrest warrant was issued in September 2022.

News.title: New sighting of missing Lillia, 13
News.content:
Police have received fresh CCTV of a girl who has been missing from home for a week.

Lillia, 13, from Bolton, was last seen by her family last Friday, but was seen later that evening in Manchester's Picadilly bus station, and at the Trafford Centre the following day.

Officers who have been handing out hundreds of leaflets to try to locate Lillia have now released new footage of her at a McDonald's restaurant in Piccadilly from Sunday at about 20:20 BST.

Greater Manchester Police Ch Spt Int Helen Critchley said: "Officers are making every effort to locate Lillia, and our team have been working through hours of CCTV footage and exploring every avenue to try and find her."

At a press conference on Thursday, Critchley issued an appeal on behalf of Lillia's mother Jessica, saying: "Lillia, if you see this appeal, please know your family love you, miss you and just want to know that you are safe.

"You are not in any trouble, they simply want you to come home."

News.title: Driver who killed woman celebrating 60th jailed
News.content:
The court heard Goulty drank two lagers before he drove his silver Vauxhall Astra at 64mph in a residential 30mph limit area before crashing into 69-year-old Sarwar Mohammad's Peugeot Expert Tepee taxi.

Mohammad, of Willow Brook Road in Leicester, who had been driving the taxi and admitted the same offences, was handed a six-month prison sentence, suspended for two years, and told he must do 100 hours of unpaid work.

Prosecutor Steven Bailey told the court Brighton did not know the Sidsaffs, who had come to Leicester for the Radio 2 in the Park music festival, but they shared a taxi because they were going in the same direction.

Brighton, who was from the city, had been out with her friends celebrating her 60th birthday.

Bailey said the collision happened as a result of the "combined bad driving of Thomas Goulty and Sarwar Mohammad", while the taxi was making a right turn towards Westfield Road across the central reservation of the dual carriageway.

Goulty had been out in the city and sent someone a message minutes before the crash saying he was "just out having a couple of beers", and in a roadside test immediately after the crash tested positive for alcohol in his breath, but later assessments could not conclude that he was over the driving limit.

Bailey said Goulty's speed was "excessive", up to 64mph (102km/h) on approach and 55mph at the point of impact.

"He had left himself little or no calculation time and any braking was far too late," he said.

"He drove too quickly for the road and its conditions, about twice the speed limit, having taken alcohol and in the dark."

News.title: Men lose appeal for harassing BBC journalist over A Very British Cult documentary
News.content:
The men were attempting to overturn their convictions from February, when they were each sentenced to 200 hours of community service and given restraining orders banning them from contacting or approaching Nye or her partner for 10 years.

They were also banned from entering the London borough where the couple live for a decade.

A year after the initial broadcast of the BBC programmes about the organisation, the Lighthouse group began a campaign of peaceful, and legal, protests outside BBC offices in London, against Nye and the BBC.

"While there were elements of peaceful protest and freedom of expression, their conduct, as we have already identified, was not proportionate to the proper exercise of those rights and went beyond what was acceptable and indeed became criminal", the judge said.

After an interaction with Nye in July 2024, Kamra gave evidence that he was "dissatisfied" and that questions he had for Nye were still not answered.

The group decided to visit her home address, which they found using a private investigator and said that they had looked up BBC guidance of doorstepping.

"The appellants therefore appreciated that there was a line which their conduct must not cross", said Pounder.

"What happened descended into bullying and oppressive conduct", he added, deeming that the behaviour of the three men was not reasonable.

During the first visit to Nye's home address on 29 August, the group had distributed leaflets they had printed to Nye's neighbours.

The judge said the contents were "not confined to criticism of journalism".

"They identified her to those living in the immediate neighbourhood and associated her with serious allegations concerning racism, dishonesty and the concealment of child sexual abuse by family members," he explained.

"That is materially different from distributing critical literature outside the headquarters of a public broadcaster."

The court heard Kamra later returned to the property to post a handwritten letter saying "we will be back", which "materially reinforced" Nye's concerns, Pounder said.

Deichler, Kamra and Singh visited her property again a week later, on 5 September, before they were later arrested.

The three men maintained that they were performing citizen journalism and were at her property to obtain a doorstep interview, as part of their own documentary, and that they were acting in the public interest.

Judge Pounder accepted that they saw themselves as citizen journalists, but underlined their behaviour was not reasonable, as he pointed to their "deliberate acquisition of a private address, attendance of home, distribution of inflammatory literature, indication return visit and subsequent return".

Giving evidence for the second time, from behind a curtain, Nye told the court of her fear when the three accused went to her property.

It was "extremely" distressing, Nye said.

Their actions had resulted in Nye installing CCTV, panic alarms, direct lines with the police and carrying rape alarms, the court heard.

The three men had also claimed that their attendance outside Nye's home was an expression of their religious beliefs.

Pounder said there was no doubt that their views were "sincerely held", telling them that it had been concluded that a prayer they said outside her door was "an incidental part of their attendance at the address".

The Bible they wanted to give her, Pounder said could have been posted to her via the BBC.

On top of their original convictions, the judge has ordered the three men to each pay an additional Â£1,000.

News.title: Sisters of 'Putney pusher' suspect say DNA will clear his name
News.content:
The results of a DNA test will clear the name of Nicholas Brandram, the suspect in the "Putney pusher" case, his sisters have told the BBC.

The banker was arrested in June, nine years after a woman was pushed in front of a moving bus by a jogger on Putney Bridge in May 2017. He gave a DNA sample to police two months ago but never received the results, his sisters said.

Brandram was found dead in his west London home on Tuesday. His family have insisted he was innocent and said he "took his own life after months of immense pressure" caused by the Met investigation.

The Met said it recognised the "strain that being subject to a police investigation" could cause, but did not respond to this specific claim.

News.title: Johnny Marr guitars sell for almost £4m at auction
News.content:
Guitars owned by The Smiths musician Johnny Marr have sold for almost Â£4m at auction.

The instruments, which were used during his time with The Smiths and on his forthcoming solo album, went under the hammer as part of Christie's Marr's Guitars: The Johnny Marr Collection sale.

The sale lasted for more than five hours and included buyers from 34 countries, fetching Â£3,649,280 - more than three times its estimated value.

Marr said: "The auction has been a great experience and has exceeded all my expectations. I'd like to thank everyone who made bids and special thanks to Christie's for making it so memorable."

News.title: Met PC denies charge over pregnant woman's death
News.content:
A Metropolitan Police officer accused of causing the death of a pregnant woman by dangerous driving has denied the charge.

Mariam Ahmed, 38, died after her Volkswagen Polo was involved in a high-speed collision on Eltham Road in Eltham, south-east London, on 17 October 2024.

Her unborn child could not be saved.

PC Chris Johnson, 56, pleaded not guilty at the Old Bailey to causing her death by dangerous driving. Former PC Danny Tomkins, 35, denied dangerous driving before the crash took place.

The court heard that both officers, who were on duty in separate vehicles as part of a "pre-planned deployment", drove at more than 70mph in a 30mph zone and overtook traffic on the wrong side of the road for around 130m.

Johnson, who was driving the police vehicle involved in the collision, was allegedly travelling at about 50mph at the point of impact, prosecutor Louise Oakley KC said.

Tomkins, whose vehicle was not involved in the collision, overtook Ahmed at 78mph shortly before the crash, prosecutors say.

News.title: Trump ‘bans’ CNN and other media groups from White House for reporting of ‘FAKE NEWS’
News.content:

President Donald Trump on Friday claimed to have “banned” three of the country’s most prominent news outlets from the White House, taking a page from authoritarian leaders by attempting to limit coverage of his administration by legitimate journalists as his and his party’s popularity continue to crumble as the midterm elections approach.

Writing on Truth Social, the president said he would “effective immediately” be “banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW ... and Politico ... from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he added.

All of the outlets mentioned by the president are legitimate and reputable news organizations with long histories of aggressive and independent reporting under both Republican and Democratic administrations.

It’s unclear what, if anything, specifically led to the president’s outburst, but Trump has had a years-long feud with CNN dating back to his first campaign for the presidency and his first term in the White House.

The president does not actually possess the authority to arbitrarily ban entire outlets from the White House based on the content those outlets publish.

Not only does the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution protect the right of journalists to report without government interference, but a 1977 District of Columbia Circuit Court case, Sherill v. Knight, states that “bona fide journalists” cannot be denied access to White House press facilities except in cases when a journalist seeking a press credential to enter the White House “presents a potential source of physical danger to the President and/or his immediate family so serious as to justify his exclusion.”

That decades-old precedent was upheld during Trump’s first term after he attempted to revoke the credentials of CNN’s then-chief White House correspondent, Jim Acosta, and later a columnist for Playboy, Brian Karem, for behavior the White House considered to be inappropriate.

In both cases, the DC Circuit upheld lower court orders directing the White House to restore both journalists’ White House press passes.

Trump has nonetheless pushed to punish news outlets by restricting their access to the White House during his second term.

Last year, his administration seized control of the press pool that had for decades been organized by the White House Correspondents’ Association in order to punish the Associated Press for refusing to change its’ widely used style guide to reflect his administration’s attempt to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.”

His handpicked Pentagon boss, ex-Fox News presenter turned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, has instituted sweeping restrictions on the Pentagon’s own press corps that led nearly every legitimate media outlet covering the Defense Department to turn in their credentials.

It is not clear whether anyone from the White House has attempted to enforce the president’s purported “ban” on CNN, MSNOW and Politico.

As of Friday afternoon, CNN’s press workspace was fully staffed and multiple camera and sound technicians from the network were present on the White House campus.

Asked how he could justify attempting to ban news outlets when he has taken an oath to uphold the U.S. Constitution, Trump replied: “Because they're fake news, and you get so tired of reading and seeing fake news.”

The president then launched into a lengthy rant in which he repeated a bogus claim that Politico had received a subsidy from the Biden administration — actually subscription revenues from government agencies — and suggested that other outlets could also face similar fates if they do not write positive stories about his administration.

“They purposely write negative news, and they do that because want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said. “And honestly, we've done a fantastic job.”

“Look at the numbers. Look at the economic numbers. We have more money coming into our country today than ever before, we have the highest employment that we've ever had in history ... we have the best poverty rate, the lowest poverty rate in the history of our country, and people are making more money today than they ever had,”

Very little of what the president said was actually accurate. For one, the highest-ever recorded U.S. employment rate was 64.7 percent, 26 years ago in April 2000.

Asked about his prior attempts to ban individual reporters, Trump suggested a different judge would have been more amenable to his authoritarian push to restrict a free press.

“To be honest with you, I don't think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day, I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they're going to write false stories all the time,” he said.

He continued complaining that the coverage of his administration by legitimate news organizations is not fawning in the manner practiced by Breitbart News and other partisan outlets.

When a reporter attempted to ask Sanders — who was actually in the Oval Office for the event in her new role as Governor of Arkansas — whether she agreed with Trump’s push to ban entire news organizations, he interjected and repeated himself.

“I don't think somebody should be allowed to come in and write fake stories, fake news, and that's why they have no credibility,” he said.

“They never write a good story ... it's sick. I mean, there's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories. Now, if they want to write them, that's fine. But I don't have to let them into my — into the people's house.”

Travelling to Europe? You have struck gold, with a wealth of cities to explore, each with a fascinating past and its own distinct culture. But some can also set you back a small fortune after factoring in well-located accommodation, restaurant bookings, and attraction entry fees.

Prices for trips to popular places like Paris, London and Stockholm continue to rise, causing some visitors to pay as much as they would at a high-end beach resort.

The most expensive cities tend to be among some of the most popular, too. Selecting a city that you may not have heard much about doesn’t just make the thrill of discovering new landmarks, people, and cuisine more enticing; stepping off the usual tourist trail also leaves behind large crowds – all the while receiving a culture-packed long weekend away for likely half the price.

Kosovo’s capital Pristina is young and vibrant, Poland’s Łódź is a city with an impressive cinematic history, while Chișinău in Moldova blends urban life with an unusually high amount of green space.

We created our list using Numbeo’s cost of living index, discovered where in Europe is the cheapest to visit and picked out our favourites from the list we believe would make an enriching city break.

While looking at crucial factors such as the price of a beer and the cost of public transport, we also checked Skyscanner’s recommendations for the cheapest month to fly.

As a result, we have rounded up our favourite affordable city breaks in Europe that offer just as much to see and do as some of the biggest capitals on the continent.

1. Pristina, Kosovo

open image in gallery Pristina’s National Library is one of the city’s most impressive buildings ( Getty )

Cost of an inexpensive meal: €5.50 (£4.73)

€5.50 (£4.73) Cost of a beer: €2.50 (£2.15)

€2.50 (£2.15) Cost of a coffee: €1.60 (£1.37)

€1.60 (£1.37) Cost of a one-way ticket on public transport: €0.50 (43p)

Perhaps one of the most overlooked city breaks in Europe, Pristina is the best-kept secret among budget-conscious travellers and its youthful residents who give the Kosovan capital its energetic air. More than half of Kosovars are under 30, meaning nightlife has flourished, with clubs such as Zone and Gate among some of the most well-known. By day, locals opt for trendy spots like Soma Book Station, a restaurant-cum-library where cheese plates, burgers or bowls of pasta can be devoured for under £10 while browsing books. Kafet e Rakisë, a well-known street in Pristina, is where travellers will find people conversing with friends over raki or coffee, depending on the time of day, at traditional bars.

The Newborn Monument, a typographic sculpture near the city centre, commemorates Kosovo’s 2008 declaration of independence from Serbia, becoming Europe’s youngest country. More can be learned about the country’s history and Kosovar culture in preserved Ottoman houses at the free-to-visit Ethnographic Museum. For more sightseeing, the formidable National Library of Kosovo is worth a picture: a series of concrete blocks and domes that look as if it has been caught in a giant metal fishing net. Religious buildings, such as the Imperial Mosque and the Cathedral of Saint Mother Teresa, can also be visited, with the latter allowing visitors up its bell tower for city views for around £1.70.

How to do it

Wizz Air and easyJet currently operate flights out of London Luton airport to Pristina. The cheapest month to fly is November from £53 return.

Short-term rentals are available in Pristina, but if you are seeking a well-known brand name for a reasonably low price, Mercure Pristina City has spacious rooms in the heart of the city within walking distance of most major attractions.

Price: From £68



2. Skopje, North Macedonia

open image in gallery The Old Bazaar should be explored on a trip to Skopje ( Getty Images )

Cost of an inexpensive meal: 500 denari (£6.98)

500 denari (£6.98) Cost of a beer: 170 denari (£2.37)

170 denari (£2.37) Cost of a coffee: 114.84 denari (£1.60)

114.84 denari (£1.60) Cost of a one-way ticket on public transport: 40 denari (56p)

Traces of culture from dozens of historical eras shape what North Macedonia’s capital, Skopje, is today, from Roman remains and Ottoman heritage to socialist-era modernism, making for a city break with endless exploration. The city is split by the Vardar River, separating much of its historical attractions from the modern centre on the southern side. On the eastern bank of the river is where visitors will find the Old Bazaar, one of the oldest and largest marketplaces in the Balkans, selling everything from traditional Turkish coffee to local art and gold jewellery. Near the bazaar are the remains of the sixth-century Kale Fortress, situated on the highest point of the city, which is free to walk around.

The city is home to some poignant museums, which cost very little to visit. The Museum of the City of Skopje occupies an old train station where the fingers of the clock remain frozen in time – 5.17am when a devastating earthquake struck the capital in 1963, killing over 1,000 people. Admission is free, with exhibitions detailing the tragedy around the earthquake and other important events in North Macedonia’s history. Likewise, the Museum of the Macedonian Struggle for Independence, which costs just over £4, tells the story of the national revolutionary period, the establishment of Yugoslavia and the World Wars.

How to do it

Wizz Air is the only UK airline to fly to Skopje, with departures from London Luton airport. The cheapest month for a return flight is currently December from £55.

Nordic Hostel is a highly-rated place to stay, with beds under £30 a night, with a choice of private rooms or dormitories with capsule-style bunks. Some rooms come with a balcony, while all guests have access to its inner courtyard garden with places to relax.

Price: From £23



3. Chișinău, Moldova

open image in gallery Chișinău has plenty of green spaces ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

Cost of an inexpensive meal: 200 lei (£8.55)

200 lei (£8.55) Cost of a beer: 40 lei (£1.71)

40 lei (£1.71) Cost of a coffee: 38.88 lei (£1.66)

38.88 lei (£1.66) Cost of a one-way ticket on public transport: 7 lei (30p)

Some visitors to Moldova may be more attracted to its countryside, where acres of vineyards cultivate local grapes across its wine regions, but the country’s capital, Chișinău, is not to be overlooked. The city may be best known for its Soviet-era architecture built from white limestone rising up between a huge selection of green spaces. In fact, the city is regarded as one of the greenest cities in Europe, with its 23 lakes and popular parks such as Stefan cel Mare Central Park, Valea Morilor and the Stefan cel Mare Public Garden, all of which are free to amble around. There is one park which is ticketed to get in, but for the low price of £1.60 for an adult entrance fee, it is worth a visit to Dendrarium Park to see its impressive collection of botanical plants and rare trees.

Other city highlights include exploring its architecture on foot, including the neoclassical Nativity Cathedral and the almost 200-year-old Triumphal Arch, which was built to celebrate the Russian victory over the Ottoman Empire. Delving deeper into Moldovan culture, a trip to the National Museum of History costs £2 per ticket, while traditional cuisine such as stuffed cabbage leaves and meat platters at popular restaurant La Taifas, with some main dishes coming in at £4.

How to do it

Flights to Chișinău from the UK can be caught from London Luton and London Gatwick airports with Wizz Air. The cheapest time to fly is November for £31 return flights.

There are plenty of well-known international hotel brands in the city, such as ibis, Marriott and Radisson, but for something a little cheaper, it's best to go boutique. Hotel Tulip Residence & Spa sits on the edge of a small forest area in the city and has a small swimming pool, a hammam and a restaurant that serves Thai and European dishes.

Price: From £37



4. Podgorica, Montenegro

open image in gallery The Millennium Bridge in Podgorica ( Getty Images )

Cost of an inexpensive meal: €10 (£8.59)

€10 (£8.59) Cost of a beer: €2.80 (£2.41)

€2.80 (£2.41) Cost of a coffee: €2.25 (£1.93)

€2.25 (£1.93) Cost of a one-way ticket on public transport: €1.50 (£1.29)

The capital of Montenegro, Podgorica, sits on a flat plain encircled by mountains. The country’s coastal resorts, such as the breathtaking Bay of Kotor, are far more popular with tourists, which leaves the inland capital often overlooked and usually not at the top of travel bucket lists. For some, this makes exploration all the more exciting, and a lot cheaper too, as there are no crowds to wade through to the next attraction.

Podgorica’s Old Town is lined with narrow alleys where some of the few remaining Ottoman structures that survived World War II still stand, including mosques and a famous 17th-century clock tower. While there isn’t an abundance of attractions here, visitors can indulge in the slow-paced social ritual of sipping cups of coffee slowly, paying at most £2.50 for the pleasure. Oliva is one of the most popular cafe choices. Many locals also head to the banks of the rivers that flow through the city, with the most favoured picnic spot at the confluence of the two main bodies of water, the Morača and the Ribnica. Niagara Waterfall is also a popular nature spot just outside the city centre, with a nearby restaurant to enjoy views of the river from.

How to do it

Catch a flight with Ryanair from Stansted airport and Wizz Air from Gatwick airport to Podgorica’s aviation hub. The cheapest month to fly right now is November, from £37 return.

The four-star Signum Hotel Podgorica has rooms with balconies and views across Podgorica, elevated on high floors away from any city noise. The hotel also has a rooftop restaurant, a gym, and a sauna.

Price: From £75



5. Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina

open image in gallery Sarajevo is one of the cheapest places to visit in Europe ( Getty/iStock )

Cost of an inexpensive meal: 15KM (£6.59)

15KM (£6.59) Cost of a beer: 5KM (£2.20)

5KM (£2.20) Cost of a coffee: 4KM (£1.76)

4KM (£1.76) Cost of a one-way ticket on public transport: 2.20KM (97p)

Bosnia and Herzegovina’s capital, Sarajevo, is one of Europe’s cheapest destinations to visit, with flights at their lowest during the winter months. The city has a huge coffee scene, with locals starting the day with a hot cup of strong, unfiltered coffee brewed in a copper pot (džezva). The drink here is very cheap, so visitors can sample plenty – start at the cafes in the Baščaršija bazaar. Also found here are staples such as ćevapi kebab and pot stew lonac.

Aside from its coffee culture, visitors can learn more about Sarajevo’s complex history through some of its top attractions, including the Ottoman-era Gazi Husrev-Beg Mosque, which can be visited for £1.30, as well as the Tunnel of Salvation museum (£9), which focuses on the 1990s siege of the city.

The War Childhood Museum (£6.60), which spotlights children’s wartime experiences in Bosnia and around the world, is also highly recommended. More light-hearted activities include a trip into the mountains on the Sarajevo cable car (£9 one way), or observing the streets below at sunset from the Yellow Fortress.

How to do it

Ryanair and Wizz Air have direct flights to Sarajevo from London. November is currently the cheapest month to fly (from £45 return.)

There are plenty of hostels to stay in and apartments that can be let for a weekend in Sarajevo for a low price. If staying in a hotel is preferable, Hotel Aziza is a popular choice that is only a 15-minute walk away from Baščaršija.

Price: From £54



6. Bucharest, Romania

open image in gallery Bucharest is considered an inexpensive place to visit for wellness ( Getty/iStock )

Cost of an inexpensive meal: 65 lei (£10.60)

65 lei (£10.60) Cost of a beer: 18 lei (£2.94)

18 lei (£2.94) Cost of a coffee: 16.37 lei (£2.70)

16.37 lei (£2.70) Cost of a one-way ticket on public transport: 4 lei (65p)

Those looking to book a spa break in Europe but don’t have the budget to book a luxury resort should consider the Romanian capital. Therme Bucharest is one of the city’s most popular wellness centres, featuring mineral pools, saunas, treatment rooms and a series of bars and restaurants. The most expensive package sits at around £35.50, while three-hour sessions can be as little as £12.

But Bucharest has much to offer beyond relaxation. Its lively student population has filled streets with affordable and diverse bars and clubs, ideal for a cheap party weekend away.

While inexpensive drinking or day spas are tempting, visitors should also make time for the city’s historic and cultural offerings. The free Walkabout tour, highly rated among tourists, allows visitors to hit all the main attractions in one go, such as the historical centre, the oldest beer house in town and Revolution Square, a historically significant plaza that is also home to the former Royal Palace and the neoclassical Romanian Athenaeum (£2.45).

How to do it

Ryanair, Wizz Air, British Airways and other major airlines all run flights from the UK to Bucharest. The cheapest time to fly is currently October from £32 return.

Book a room at the boutique Peakture Hotel, an accommodation that is situated near Bucharest’s Old Town, complete with stylish rooms and a wine bistro.

Price: From £70



7. Braga, Portugal

open image in gallery Bom Jesus do Monte Sanctuary in Braga is one of the many top attractions ( Getty/iStock )

Cost of an inexpensive meal: €10 (£8.79)

€10 (£8.79) Cost of a beer: €3 (£2.58)

€3 (£2.58) Cost of a coffee: €1.69 (£1.45)

€1.69 (£1.45) Cost of a one-way ticket on public transport: €1.55 (£1.33)

Often considered the “Rome of Portugal”, this lesser-visited third city is often passed over for Porto and Lisbon, which turns out to be rather beneficial for tourists who do visit, as prices are low and crowds are sparse.

While the city represents over 2,000 years of history, Braga has a large youth culture due to the universities found here, causing a creative scene to thrive, with studios and exhibitions such as the Zet Gallery and Mário Sequeira Gallery, both with free admission.

Wandering the streets offers an abundance of beautiful architecture, from the baroque and Gothic cathedral (£2.60) to the Sanctuary of Bom Jesus do Monte, a large Catholic shrine. Away from the landmarks, buildings are often covered with bright blue traditional Azulejo tiles. Be sure to dive into a café along these streets to pick up a slice of frigideira de Braga meat pie.

How to do it

Ryanair, easyJet, British Airways, TAP Air Portugal and more all run flights to Porto, where travellers can catch a 30-minute train to Braga. Flights are cheapest in September from £34.

For an affordable place to stay, Guest House Vila Santa Cruz is a practical choice found in the centre of the Old Town.

Price: From £25



8. Łódź

open image in gallery Łódź is the ideal city break for cinephiles ( Getty Images )

Cost of an inexpensive meal: 38zł (£7.55)

38zł (£7.55) Cost of a beer: 18zł (£3.60)

18zł (£3.60) Cost of a coffee: 14.14zł (£2.90)

14.14zł (£2.90) Cost of a one-way ticket on public transport: 4.40zł (87p)

When thinking of a Polish city break, popular destinations such as Warsaw and Kraków usually spring to mind, yet Łódź in central Poland has a lot to offer city explorers alongside being cheaper than the rest. The city has a huge textile manufacturing heritage, remnants of which can be seen at places such as a former red brick factory, which has been transformed into a huge mall and leisure complex called Manufaktura. The shopping and cultural centre has over 250 stores, 50 restaurants, an art gallery, museums, and even an outdoor zipwire across the open courtyard outside. The city has also made use of other former industrial buildings, such as a power plant turned science and art centre, EC1 Łódź, which holds a planetarium, kid-friendly interactive science centre and a museum dedicated to Polish cinema.

Most of the city’s urban palaces across the city were owned by rich textile tycoons, but now mostly house museums. More on the “HollyŁódź” film history can be learned about in the Cinema Museum (£5.50), found in one of these 19th century palaces, which features historic film technology, costumes and a deep dive into how this one factory-focused city became an epicentre of the Polish film industry. Another palace is now the home of MS1 gallery, which showcases 20th-century modern art from the post-industrial creativity boom. Łódź’s continuing creativity has also seeped into other areas of city, as sightseers may spot more than 150 murals painted on the sides of buildings.

How to do it

Fly with Ryanair to Łódź from London Stansted airport. The cheapest time to fly is September, from £28.

Hotel Ibis Łódź Centrum is a cheap and cheerful place to set up camp while exploring the city, with a central location only metres away from Piotrkowska Street, the main thoroughfare of the city, 207 rooms and a 24-hour bar and lounge.

Price: From £41



9. Granada

open image in gallery Alhambra fortress at sunset in Granada ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

Cost of an inexpensive meal: €14 (£12)

€14 (£12) Cost of a beer: €3 (£2.60)

€3 (£2.60) Cost of a coffee: €2 (£1.70)

€2 (£1.70) Cost of a one-way ticket on public transport: €1.60 (£1.40)

Barcelona and Madrid step aside; the central city of Granada is proving that it is possible to have a Spanish city break without breaking the bank. While the country’s coastlines are one of its biggest bragging points, with warm weather and soft sand, but Spain’s beaches will not cross your mind once you land in the city tucked in the foothills of the magnificent Sierra Nevada mountains. Granada’s UNESCO-protected medieval neighbourhood, the Albaicín quarter, is found on the mountain slopes, where visitors will find Moorish art, architecture and culture, laced together by winding alleys that are free for all to wander around. Next door is the Alhambra, a palace and fortress which is one of the best-preserved examples of historic Islamic architecture built during the 13th and 14th centuries, which can be visited for just over £19.

Granada also has a rich dance culture, with the Roma tradition of Zambra Flamenco honoured with performances in Sacromonte caves, costing around £21 at María la Canastera. The caves became housing for marginalised people in centuries past, more of which can be learned about at the Museo Cuevas del Sacromonte for just over £5, which exhibits eleven caves and what it would have been like to live in them.

How to do it

Wizz Air sells direct flights to Granada’s small airport from Luton airport, however, there are more frequent flights to nearby Malaga airport with many more airlines costing from £28. The cheapest month to fly is in October.

For a cheap place to stay, book a bed at TOC Hostel right next to Granada’s cathedral. Choose from private rooms to bunks, while guests get to enjoy a full kitchen to use, a bar, a restaurant and a common area.

Price: From £12.90



10. Seville, Spain

open image in gallery Seville is one of the cheapest spots to visit in Spain ( Getty/iStock )

Cost of an inexpensive meal: €12 (£10.30)

€12 (£10.30) Cost of a beer: €2.67 (£2.29)

€2.67 (£2.29) Cost of a coffee: €1.69 (£1.45)

€1.69 (£1.45) Cost of a one-way ticket on public transport: €1.40 (£1.20)

As continental Europe’s warmest city, Seville is easily the best choice for an affordable trip away that also offers hours of sunshine and pleasant, year-round weather. While the heat may be a little unbearable in August for a city as temperatures reach highs of 36C, the winter months still bring balmy walm weather, staying between 16C and 21C.

There are a lot of things to see for free in Seville, including the half-moon-shaped Plaza de España that leads to the large Parque de María Luisa, filled with tiled fountains, ponds, pathways and playgrounds. Be sure to stroll along the Guadalquivir River and into other barrios (neighbourhoods), such as Alfalfa and Arenal, which offer many of the city’s best hotels and bars.

Make the most of Seville’s traditional tapas bars, where small plates of food cost only a few euros. Save the budget for sampling local wines such as Vino de Naranja (orange wine). For more foodie exploration, the fresh food market Mercado de Triana is open everyday but Sunday, where local delicacies are found, such as Iberian jamón (ham), olives and cheese.

How to do it

Vueling, easyJet, Iberia, British Airways and Ryanair offer return flights, with October being the cheapest month to visit (from £34).

For a cheap stay in the city centre, the U-Sense Sevilla Centro hotel is only a few steps away from the cathedral, tapas bars and shopping areas, with cosy rooms to bed down in.

Price: From £157

News.title: ‘Worst guard dog’: Golden retriever pesters home intruder to play during break-in
News.content:
A golden retriever pestered a home intruder to play during a break-in in San Diego, California, security video shows.

Homeowner Dante Rowley said he and his family watched the incident unfold in real-time remotely through their home cameras as they were boarding a flight.

Instead of chasing the man away, the family's dog Nash was keen to make friends, bringing the individual his toys.

When police arrived at the door, the pooch appeared to believe they were there for one reason – playtime.

"Nash is the worst guard dog," Rowley wrote.

Footage from outside the house shows police officers placing the man in handcuffs.

News.content:
