Sports.title: Harry Kane smashes ANOTHER record as Bayern Munich star scores 100th Bundesliga goal - 31 GAMES faster than previous holder
Sports.content:
England captain Harry Kane is continuing to break records – becoming the fastest-ever player to score 100 goals in the German Bundesliga.

Kane's penalty against Union Berlin on Friday night took him to treble figures in the country in 98 games – a staggering 31 games faster than the previous record holder.

German legend Dieter Muller took 129 matches to score 100 for FC Cologne, with his record coming in 1977.

He also recently became the fastest player in Bayern history to net 150 goals for the club, taking 153 games.

Only one player has reached 150 goals for one club quicker – Cristiano Ronaldo with Real Madrid. He took 149 games.

Kane has scored a goal every 78.5 minutes in the Bundesliga, which is a better rate than both Erling Haaland and Robert Lewandowski.

More to follow.

Sports.title: Loved-up newlyweds Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce seen in rare selfie after Kansas City Chiefs' NFL Week 1 win
Sports.content:
Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift posed for a sweet selfie with a fan in the wake of the Kansas City Chiefs' Week 1 win over the Denver Broncos on Monday night.

The loved-up pair haven't been seen much together in the wake of their Madison Square Garden wedding in July, but fans were treated to a new snap this week.

The image, which was posted on social media by Texas A&M insider Billy Liucci to his 10,000 followers, showed Kelce - decked in a green polo shirt - with his arm round the man, while Swift took the photo at the front.

Both of the A-listers beamed for the camera as they gave a glimpse into their new married life - and there was certainly reason to be cheerful after Kansas City's dominant opening-day win.

It is understood that the photo was taken after the game, with Travis having showered and changed before meeting up with his now-wife Swift and their pals.

It is unclear whether it was taken at the stadium, or at an alternative venue such as 1587 Prime - Kelce and Patrick Mahomes' restaurant that the group often frequent after games.

Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift posed for a cozy selfie with a fan after the Chiefs' Week 1 win

In the Chiefs' VIP suite, Swift also took a selfie of herself with Pat McAfee on Monday night

For the win over the Broncos, Swift sat alongside her father and Hollywood A-lister Tom Cruise

The reason for Liucci's presence with the love-birds is also unclear - he is the executive editor of TexAgs and a longtime Texas A&M insider, but there is no obvious connection between him and the couple.

The new photo of Travis and Taylor comes on the same week that the Chiefs tight end used his New Heights podcast to gush over his wife's ever-improving football knowledge.

He had previously admitted that she came into their relationship lacking in the details, once believing that players were 'basically out there boxing each other on the field'.

Now, though, she has dived head first into the nuances of her husband's passion, and is regularly seen wildly cheering at games, be it at Arrowhead or further afield.

Speaking to Tom Cruise on this week's bonus edition of New Heights, Kelce said: 'Now she knows everything. She sees the flags coming in, like, "Oh, that might be a defensive hold." [I'm] like, "What'd you say, sweetie?"

Kelce enjoyed a positive night on the field, helping Kansas City to a big win over Denver

Kelce wore his green polo shirt pregame and then changed into it again after the win

'She's like, "That's encroachment." I'm like, "You know what that is?" She's on it now. She's fully engulfed in it.'

Cruise agreed with the sentiment, claiming that Swift was 'schooling me' as they sat together to watch Travis and his teammates beat the Denver Broncos 31-10.

'Just a beautiful couple, in every way,' he added of the newlyweds.

Kelce and Swift got married back in July at an extravagant ceremony at Madison Square Garden, renting the world's most famous arena out for 1,000 of their nearest and dearest.

Sports.title: I saw a different side to Michael Carrick after Man United's loss to Brighton - and here's why alarm bells should be ringing for United fans, writes CHRIS WHEELER
Sports.content:
I saw a different side to Michael Carrick after Man United's loss to Brighton - and here's why alarm bells should be ringing for United fans, writes CHRIS WHEELER

Michael Carrick's experience of the Old Trafford circus was one of the reasons Manchester United brought him back to the club as head coach in January, and he has put it to good use ever since.

Triumph and adversity have been met with an easy smile and well-chosen comment from a man who, by and large, has seen it all in a United career that began two decades ago. For Carrick, blocking out the external noise is second nature.

But in the wake of a disastrous Carabao Cup defeat by Brighton on Wednesday night, we saw a different side to the 45-year-old. Carrick looked agitated – emotional even – after United were beaten at Old Trafford for the second time in four days.

It wasn’t on the same scale as his predecessor Ruben Amorim’s meltdown when United went out of this competition at Grimsby last season, sitting drenched in the dugout, fiddling with his tactics tray and incapable of watching his team lose on penalties.

Nor was it another flash of anger like the one that led to Carrick snapping at interviewer Jan Aage Fjortoft for his ‘ridiculous’ question about United’s lack of passion in the opening-day defeat at Hull.

But for a man who knows the lie of the land at Old Trafford so well, Carrick seemed genuinely shocked by how quickly this season is unravelling – and how fast he must now put it right – following three defeats in six games from a relatively gentle start.

Michael Carrick looked agitated, shocked – emotional even – after his Manchester United side were beaten at Old Trafford for the second time in four days

United defender Ayden Heaven can't bear to look as United slump to a 3-2 defeat on Wednesday night

Since Everton stunned United with a stoppage-time equaliser 11 days ago, his team have lost the Manchester derby and gone out of the cup to Brighton, either side of a Champions League stroll against Sabah of Azerbaijan.

Even the storm surrounding JJ Gabriel’s decision to quit United barely warranted a mention late on Wednesday night as Carrick faced the TV cameras and written press with the boos of United fans still ringing in his ears.

‘A couple of smallish things end up accumulating and, let’s be honest, it feels bigger. All of a sudden it becomes a greater thing from nowhere,’ he admitted.

‘It’s happened over a period of maybe two or three weeks where there’s a lot of frustration and disappointment around, and we need to flip that and start winning games again.

‘Being here toughens you up. It’s all about what you do next and dealing with the ups and the downs.’

We have seen plenty of managers wilt in the pressure cooker of Manchester United in the 13 years since Sir Alex Ferguson stepped down, among them some hugely experienced coaches like Jose Mourinho, Louis van Gaal, David Moyes and Ralf Rangnick.

The comparison United would most like to avoid with Carrick, of course, is Ole Gunnar Solskjaer.

There is no certainty at all that Carrick’s spell in charge will follow the same path as his old friend and team-mate, but the parallels are unavoidable.

Two ex-United favourites with limited experience of coaching at the highest level who were parachuted into one of the biggest clubs in the world as interim manager and did well enough to earn the job on a full-time basis.

There is no certainty at all that Carrick’s spell in charge will follow the same path as his old friend and team-mate Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, but the parallels are unavoidable

Even the storm surrounding JJ Gabriel’s decision to quit United barely warranted a mention as Carrick faced the Press with the boos of United fans still ringing in his ears

History has been a little unkind to Solskjaer. Yes, he lost six of his next 10 games after signing a three-year contract in March 2019 with Carrick on his first-team staff.

But Solskjaer lasted another two-and-a-half seasons, finishing second and third in the Premier League, and was within a penalty shootout of winning the Europa League.

It’s a record that looks better in retrospect, but the view remains that the decision to hand him the job permanently was the wrong one.

When United sought a quick replacement for Amorim in January, Solskjaer and Carrick were available and immediately pushed to the top of the pile of candidates because director of football Jason Wilcox placed great importance on their ability to fit straight into a unique environment they both know so well.

Ultimately, Solskjaer lost out because it felt like too much of a backward step to United and there was some concern over the lack of discretion coming from his camp during the negotiations.

Carrick was seen as the more progressive choice and it was rewarded with a run of just two defeats in 17 games and Champions League qualification.

In April, a month before he was handed a two-year contract, he dismissed the comparisons with Solskjaer, saying: ‘It’s irrelevant really, it really is. That’s not a negative or a positive, it doesn’t really have any link at all.

‘It’s a different time and a different team now, irrespective of me or who's in charge, so I don't really think comparisons make any difference.’

Even at this early stage of the season, though, the poor start is reminiscent of the dip after Solskjaer’s permanent appointment amid concerns that United have left Carrick without the tools to compete with his rivals in the Premier League and Europe.

Like the Norwegian, Carrick is a dedicated club man and unlikely to rock the boat. Once again on Wednesday night, he declined the opportunity to place any blame on an underwhelming transfer window.

Since Everton stunned United with a stoppage-time equaliser 11 days ago (pictured), the Red Devils have lost the Manchester derby and been dumped out of the cup by Brighton

New No 2 goalkeeper Karl Darlow had an inglorious debut against the Seagulls, letting in three goals

United failed to land their top midfield transfer targets, and the most expensive one – £70million Carlos Baleba – arrived with an injury which means he won’t make his debut until October.

The new No 2 goalkeeper, Karl Darlow, was signed as a free agent and had an inglorious debut against Brighton, letting in three goals.

The forwards recruited last year, Benjamin Sesko, Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha, have made a slow start to their second season at the club.

And next summer’s defensive rebuild cannot come soon enough, judging by the loss to Brighton. Two of United’s young prospects, Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven, looked fragile in central defence, and the decision not to sign cover for Luke Shaw at left back appears increasingly flawed.

Shaw missed his third game in a row and Noussair Mazraoui, the latest player to deputise in his position, was struggling long before he was exposed for the winning goal scored by Maxim De Cuyper.

Carrick has been around United long enough to know not to press the panic button. He will have regained his composure by the time he faces the media again at Carrington on Friday.

Win at Fulham this weekend and he can go into the international break with room to breathe and time to fix the early-season problems without any additional pressure.

Lose again, and it will feel like we’re back in familiar territory.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel claims 99% of England fans don't discuss his Argentina mistakes - as he hands Trent Alexander-Arnold and Cole Palmer recalls
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel claims that ’99.9 per cent’ of the England fans he has met since the World Cup have not even mentioned the crushing semi-final loss to Argentina in Atlanta.

Despite the fact that England went in to retreat after taking the lead against Lionel Messi & Co to lose 2-1, Tuchel says that supporters he meets only want to talk about the positives.

Tuchel was heavily criticised for defensive substitutions in the second half that night but said: ‘I know 99.9 per cent of the fans don't talk to me about substitutions, tactical tweaks or tactical details.

‘They speak about where they watched the Mexico game, and they speak about the second-half energy of the Croatia match.

‘They speak about how nerve-racking it was to watch our match against Congo and where they celebrated.

‘This is the feedback I get. This is what we created, and how it should be.’

Subsequently pressed on the matter, Tuchel admitted he had ‘some bad stuff between the Argentina game and France third place game’ but this is understood to have been a reference to media or social media comments.

Apart from that Tuchel feels he has the support of the country ahead of a Nations League campaign that begins with a home game against World Champions Spain a week today.

Trent Alexander-Arnold was the surprise name in Tuchel’s 27-man squad. The Real Madrid star hasn’t played for England since June 2025 but has been recalled after fellow right-backs Reece James, Djed Spence and Ben White all picked up injuries.

Cole Palmer, meanwhile, is also back after recovering form and fitness at Chelsea.

The England manager said: ‘Their quality is undisputed but they need to show it.’

Tuchel said in his opening England press conference two years ago that the former Liverpool player had to always concentrate on his defending.

Asked last night whether he offered enough defensively, Tuchel said: ‘He has to, he has to. It’s necessary.

‘My conviction is that he will but he has no choice.’ Tuchel said he initially hoped to choose a similar squad to his World Cup one only for injuries to force his hand.

As a result there are also call-ups for Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite and Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott along with Leeds forward Dominic Calvert-Lewin.

One player facing an almost impossible road back is Harry Maguire. The Manchester United defender Tweeted about his exclusion from the World Cup squad before it had even been announced last May while his mother said on social media she was ‘absolutely disgusted’ by the decision.

Asked whether the door was now closed on Maguire, Tuchel said: ‘I will not hold it against him for the rest of his life, because I'm not that type of person.

‘I can forget easily and quickly, but I didn't like it and it doesn't help.’

Sports.title: 'I'm not sure I have the time to coach them to keep the ball': Thomas Tuchel makes astonishing claim about England's DNA after coming under fire for tactics during defeat to Argentina
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel admits it may be too difficult for his England team to play the cultured style of possession football favoured by other top international sides.

The England head coach met the media on Friday for the first time since his team’s semi-final World Cup defeat to Argentina and was taken to task over the failure of his team to control games in America and Mexico in the summer.

Tuchel offered the remarkable claim that just about every England fan he had encountered since the tournament had been positive.

‘I know 99.9 per cent of the fans don't talk about substitutions, tactical tweaks or tactical details,’ said Tuchel.

‘They speak about where they watched the Mexico game, and they speak about the second-half energy of the Croatia match.

‘They speak about how nerve-racking it was to watch our match against Congo and where they celebrated.

‘This is the feedback I get. This is what we created, and how it should be.’

Tuchel offered the remarkable claim that just about every England fan he had encountered since the tournament had been positive

The harsher reality is that, despite coming within ten minutes of reaching the final, England’s football in games against Argentina, Norway and DR Congo was not always impressive.

And, after saying on the day of his unveiling two years ago that he wanted his team to play a fast and furious Premier League game, he admitted on Friday it’s hard to maintain that style throughout a long summer tournament.

‘It’s not economical,’ he said.

However, Tuchel then admitted ahead of a Nations League meeting with World champions Spain next that he thinks the alternative still may be too hard to introduce.

‘I'm just wrestling with this myself because even if a team control matches in the Premier League, how many English players are there in these teams?’ said Tuchel.

‘Is this in our DNA? Do we really value control? Is this something that makes us feel good in a match? Is this something that comes easy to us?

‘Do we even realise: “Oh, we're controlling a midfield, everything is fine?”

‘Or do we go: “Yeah, but we're stuck in midfield. We should go, we should attack?”

‘It's all about how English fans cherish a match.

‘I don't think that an English supporter goes to a Premier League match and wants to see a controlled match and a 1-0 late win.

‘I think deep down in the core, English players - and it's a beautiful thing - and the spectators want to go for it.

‘I'm just wrestling with this myself because even if a team control matches in the Premier League, how many English players are there in these teams?’ asked Tuchel

‘Let's go. Let's play for 6-3, let's play for 4-3. Let’s not play 1-0. Bring this ball into the box. Let's play in the box.

‘I think there is no heritage of control around the middle line. No heritage of: “Oh, let's do a deep build-up and then bring them out”.

‘It's just like: “Okay, come on, let's kick the ball into the opponent's box and fight with them”.

‘And this is what I feel now that I have a tournament as an experience.

‘I feel that this team is ready to fight, is always ready to go and this is the beauty of it, that come high pressure moments, where we can play better football, where we maybe lack even a little bit of courage or this energy.’

In a robust exchange with the media at Wembley on Friday, Tuchel dismissed suggestions that he and the FA viewed the World Cup as a success.

In a robust exchange with the media at Wembley on Friday, Tuchel dismissed suggestions that he and the FA viewed the World Cup as a success

But when it was put to him that it was his job to coach his players how to control the rhythm and direction of games through possession football, he said as a national team coach he doesn’t have enough time on the grass.

‘I should be coaching them to keep the ball?', he asked.

‘That’s my job?

‘I’m not sure that I have the time to coach them to (keep the ball).

‘I should coach them to keep the ball? Ok, I need to think about this.’

Tuchel said that the review of the World Cup by the FA had been thorough and examined everything from travel to training times and even when he made his substitutions.

But he pushed back at suggestions he seemed satisfied with the outcome of the tournament.‘I never said it was a big success,’ he said.

‘I said there were a lot of positives about it.

‘I think Spain relied heavily on some last-minute goals of Mikel Merino.

‘I never said “big success”. I said it’s “unfulfilled”.

‘But why is the expectation so high? When did we last win it? When did we ever win it?

‘Why is the expectation so high that even bringing home a medal cannot be acknowledged?

‘I said today it's ambiguous. I said it is still mixed feelings.

‘I think we can play better. I think you and I are both right.

‘There is an element, which is hard for me even to acknowledge, that it is still the best result in 60 years.

‘So if you want to prove something, the medal is a kind of a proof. If you play good or not good, it's a very vague description.

‘I think in knock-out football, in tournaments, no-one wants to play good and go out.

‘Ideally you play better than we did. I 100 per cent agree.

‘Because it increases your chances to go all the way. I said it publicly after the Norway game.’

Sports.title: Brydon Carse will NOT face charges as police drop investigation into alleged 'sexual assault' in connection with nightclub arrest
Sports.content:
England cricketer Brydon Carse will not be charged after an investigation into an alleged sexual assault was dropped, police revealed tonight.

Fast bowler Carse, 31, was removed from second Test consideration after being arrested then de-arrested following an incident at a Derby nightclub last month.

The Durham player still faces disciplinary action by cricket authorities.

Derbyshire Police said that an ‘investigation into reports of an assault in Derby city centre has been closed’.

A spokesperson told the Daily Mail: 'Officers attended Molly Malones in the Wardwick, Derby, in the early hours of Sunday 23 August.

‘A man was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly and was then de-arrested after his details were taken by officers.

Police have dropped an assault investigation surrounding England cricketer Brydon Carse

'Following the man leaving the area staff from the bar told officers that there had been an allegation that a woman had been touched inappropriately over her clothing.

'The victim had asked for help from bar staff and the man was removed from the venue. However, before officers could speak to the woman she had left the bar.’

The spokesperson continued: 'Enquiries were made to identify the woman who had spoken with bar staff and she was eventually identified and spoken to.

'She confirmed that she did not want to make any complaint and, in line with her wishes, no further action was taken.

'In line with crime recording standards the incident was recorded on the force software as a sexual assault.

'Initial statements from the force referred to an assault as neither party had been spoken to in relation to the incident and therefore, to protect the integrity of any potential investigation, we were not able to confirm the nature of the alleged assault at that time.’

Carse, who was part of England's squad for the first Tests against Pakistan and their leading wicket-taker during the Ashes defeat in Australia, had been out celebrating with Durham team-mates following their win over Derbyshire in the County Championship.

A short video posted on social media showed him surrounded by four police officers outside the club, with fellow Durham stars Ben Stokes and Matthew Potts in the background.

The news came shortly fter England's new Test captain Joe Root abolished the team curfew that had been in place since the Ashes defeat in January, insisting his players should be trusted to behave like 'grown adults.

He declared he was ‘really hacked off’ by the latest drinking drama to engulf his side.

Carse's representatives and the ECB have been approached for comment.

Sports.title: The secrets of West Brom's rise revealed: A new recruitment strategy, James Morrison's extraordinary dedication behind the scenes, the academy conveyor belt and the boardroom rebuild
Sports.content:
Joint top of the Championship with a club legend at the helm and chasing a seventh win this century at the home of their greatest rivals. West Bromwich Albion are on the march again and while these are early days, the turbulence of last season is starting to fade from memory.

On Sunday, West Brom tackle Wolves in one of English football’s great fixtures and Baggies fans head for Molineux feeling positive.

Promising head coach James Morrison has guided Albion to 14 points from seven games, the finances look much healthier and supporters have a team starting to make them proud again.

Most importantly, chairman Shilen Patel and the Bilkul Football group appear to have found their feet, two-and-a-half years into their tenure. There should be no repeat of the chaos of last winter, when Eric Ramsay was sacked after only 44 days in charge.

Albion understand there will be trickier days ahead. Yet nearly two years after their impressive boss Carlos Corberan left for Valencia, they are feeling good about themselves once more. And in Morrison, they might just have found Corberan’s natural successor.

As they prepare for the season’s first Black Country derby, Daily Mail Sport looks at how West Brom are building for the future...

West Brom have made a fine start to the season and sit fourth on 14 points, the same total as league leaders West Ham

Club legend Morrison, who takes his team to rivals Wolves on Sunday, was rewarded with a two-year deal last April after keeping Albion up

A CLEAR PLAN

Even when West Brom were staring at relegation to League One, they already knew which way they would go this season. There were plans for both divisions but the focus was clear – invest in youth.

Finally clear of EFL financial restrictions, Albion paid fees totalling £15million for eight outfield players and of those, only 27-year-old midfielder Felix Horn Myhre was over the age of 23.

Midway through last season, Patel discussed the way forward with director of football Ian Pearce and technical director Dominic Price. The trio concluded that if Albion could stay up, it was the perfect chance to reset.

Karlan Grant had been costing the club £2.5m per season under the terms of his move from Huddersfield in 2020 but this summer, his contract finally expired. Other high earners Jed Wallace, Krystian Bielik and Alex Mowatt departed, along with Daryl Dike and Josh Maja.

Albion know that if summer buys Jimmy-Jay Morgan, Rabby Nzingoula or Kareem Tunde shine this season, they may not be able to keep hold of them. It would also mean selling at a profit – far better than watching a highly-paid player in his late-20s or early-30s drift out of contract.

If money is a player’s motivation, you might as well sign him when he’s young and hungry. The standard pay bracket in the second tier is £10-15,000 a week and West Brom are still striving to lower their wage bill since their parachute payments expired in 2023.

You want a better contract? Perform well and you’ll get one. How about Premier League wages? Attract the attention of those clubs by delivering for Albion. This is surely preferable to signing a wealthy journeyman who, naturally, will have at least one eye on his final ‘big’ contract.

Morrison does not scout the players, but Albion would never sign one he had vetoed. Similarly, his recommendations will be heeded.

Former Manchester United midfielder Toby Collyer was on a list of midfielders presented to Morrison as possible targets. Once Morrison insisted Collyer was the only one he wanted, Albion got the £3m deal done. In the case of Morgan, Nzingoula or Tunde, Morrison was handed the information and gave his approval.

West Brom do not pretend this is a revolutionary strategy. At least it is a strategy, though. Don’t forget that last January, West Brom hired Ramsay on the strength of his interview the previous June. Whatever supporters think of the current offering, at least they understand what the club are trying to achieve.

Jimmy-Jay Morgan, 20, joined the Baggies from Chelsea in the summer and already has five goals to his name in all competitions

Albion paid fees totalling £15million this summer for eight outfield players and of those, only 27-year-old midfielder Felix Horn Myhre (pictured) was over the age of 23

NO MORE 'MOZZA’

Morrison was an Albion hero long before he even thought of management. He played for the club from 2007 to 2019, making 341 appearances.

He immediately started coaching in Albion’s impressive academy and when Sam Allardyce was appointed in December 2020, he promoted Morrison to his own backroom team.

With Albion in freefall last February, Morrison stepped up where others might not have. Since then, he has overseen 21 matches in all competitions, winning nine and losing only four.

Even when Morrison was starting to pull West Brom clear of danger, few at the club genuinely believed he would be the long-term solution. He was still ‘Mozza’ rather than ‘Boss’ or ‘Gaffer’. Indeed, when club staff called him ‘Gaffer’ back then, it was usually in jest.

They would not do that anymore. Morrison was rewarded with a two-year deal last April after keeping Albion up and he made his mark instantly.

When all other football staff departed on holiday at the end of the season, Morrison was at the training ground every day for that first fortnight.

The 40-year-old could not rest until he had finalised his coaching team, now comprising Matt Gill, Gavin Strachan, Tony McMahon and Boaz Myhill, and mapped out exactly what pre-season would look like.

Until that was locked down, Morrison ignored those who urged him to take a break. That appetite for hard work is undimmed: after the 1-1 draw with QPR last Saturday, Morrison granted two days off. While his players and colleagues were recharging, Morrison spent a full day at the training ground on Monday, making plans for Molineux.

When all other football staff departed on holiday at the end of the season, Morrison was at the training ground every day for that first fortnight

Born in Darlington, County Durham and a product of the Middlesbrough academy, Morrison is a pleasing contrast to many modern bosses, with their buzzwords that come straight from a coaching manual.

He is quiet, a good listener, and gives simple messages to players. The basic framework is 4-4-2 but this structure can be tweaked game by game depending on the opponent.

There were some at Albion who believed Morrison may become their manager one day – but many more were unsure. Very few envisaged him managing other clubs after Albion. Perhaps, deep down, Morrison wondered the same.

Now, though, those same observers cannot imagine Morrison in any other role and if he, too, harboured those doubts, they have surely disappeared. The Albion boss certainly isn’t plain old ‘Mozza’ anymore.

ACADEMY BENEFITS

West Brom are close to agreeing a new deal with homegrown midfielder Harry Whitwell, whose contract expires at the end of the season. The 20-year-old has impressed this season and has interest from elsewhere, including Premier League clubs, but Albion officials are very optimistic that he will stay at the Hawthorns.

Even in the tough times, Albion continued to fund their academy and it has delivered. Tom Fellows was sold to Southampton for a possible £10m. Goalkeeper Alex Palmer joined Ipswich in a deal worth up to £4m.

Fans were not happy the club received only £6m when Dara O’Shea moved to Burnley in 2023 but at the time, Albion were probably six months from going into administration.

The respected Training Ground Guru platform recently ranked Albion’s academy – which retains Category One status – the 10th best in the country.

Morgan Rogers is often cited as the one who got away. The England forward is now one of the most expensive players of all time, having joined Chelsea from Aston Villa for £117m last summer. He cost Manchester City only £5m when they took him from Albion's academy aged 17 – yet once a wealthy Premier League club arrive on the scene, youth players are very hard to keep. It is doubtful Albion would have received any more had the matter gone to tribunal.

Under the stewardship of Richard Stevens, who has just completed seven years at the club, the academy is run with care and humility.

Though they lost key staff to Aston Villa during Christian Purslow’s time as CEO at Villa Park, Albion’s academy did not take significant damage. They are confident their methods will send more youngsters to the first team, with Whitwell the latest from the conveyor belt.

Albion have continued to fund their academy and it has delivered with Tom Fellows (right) sold to Southampton for a possible £10m

WHERE NEXT?

It has been a good start – but a start is all it is. It usually takes a little more than that to excite Albion supporters and not even a win over Wolves would have them all betting on promotion.

The most important factor now is that the key people share the same ideas. Mark Miles returned to the club as executive director last February following the departure of Andrew Nestor, who split opinion at the Hawthorns.

Miles has rebuilt the leadership team and the ownership group are prepared to allow their senior staff the space to do their jobs. Revenue was up eight per cent in the last accounts and losses down.

A long way to go, then, but West Brom are definitely heading in the right direction.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
