World.title: Norval Morrisseau masterwork not seen for 40 years unveiled at Thunder Bay Art Gallery
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A massive 22-foot painting by the late Ojibway artist Norval Morrisseau is returning to public view for the first time in decades at the Thunder Bay Art Gallery. Here's a look at the piece and some of the history behind it.

After 40 years in storage, a massive painting by Ojibway artist Norval Morrisseau has been unveiled at the Thunder Bay Art Gallery in northwestern Ontario.

The Morrisseau Masterwork painting, at roughly 6.7 metres long and just over three metres high, hadn't been viewed publicly since 1986.

It's on loan from EA Studios Calgary, which is collaborating with the gallery to mount the rolled, raw canvas from its collection on a stretcher — an auxiliary frame with expandable joints — for conservation.

The large Woodland Style mural depicts a gathering of adults, children, animals, birds and spiritual beings in a scene with natural elements.

“I’m really excited. I have to tell you, the first time I unrolled it with our contractors, it was very overwhelming, but in a positive sense," said Joseph Helmy, director of EA Studios Calgary. "This piece, it’s just very spiritual. It’s very powerful. It’s really hard to describe."

“This piece, I think, is going to really bring a lot of people together...," Helmy said.

“From what I’ve learned through the stories that my father has shared and through the expertise of Mr. Jonathan Manovich, Norval’s paintings were created to tell his stories, but they were also created to bridge Indigenous and non-Indigenous people together — and that’s what I hope that this painting will do.”

This masterwork by Ojibway artist Norval Morrisseau had been in storage for four decades, before it was unveiled at the Thunder Bay Art Gallery on Friday. (Marc Doucette/CBC)

Helmy’s family began their relationship with the artist in 1985 when his father, Galal, was recommended to sponsor Morrisseau’s work by Winnipeg art dealer Robert Checkwitch.

Helmy said the artist called and told his father he dreamt he was painting for him in the Canadian Rockies, where he resided in Jasper, which intrigued him and prompted him to book Morrisseau on a flight to Alberta.

Morrisseau continued to live and paint in a studio above EA Studios Calgary, which operated at the time out of the Maligne Canyon Tea House, during the winters until 1987.

“This piece was actually painted for my father and he actually never had this hung on the wall before,” Helmy said. It was shown only at a couple of Edmonton exhibitions and last shown in 1986, he added.

Displayed ‘where it all started’

The art studio has been working since 2025 with the Thunder Bay Art Gallery to unveil the artwork.

“We really have enjoyed working with them over the last two years to make this event happen,” Helmy said.

Gallery staff mount the artwork and prepare to hang it for public to view in Thunder Bay. (Marc Doucette/CBC)

This piece has returned to the place where Norval was born, Helmy noted. He said he couldn’t think of a “better place to start showing this piece back to the public view again."

Morrisseau, who died in 2007 at age 75, is considered the grandfather of contemporary Indigenous art in Canada. He was from Bingwi Neyaashi Anishinaabek First Nation, also known as Sand Point First Nation, in northwestern Ontario.

“Many people associate Morrisseau with some of the larger works, Androgyny, for instance, at the governor general’s home, and when you see the Order of Canada inducted, that’s a Morrisseau piece behind it and that’s a huge epic canvas as well,” said Matthew Hills, the Thunder Bay gallery’s executive director.

“But … it’s a triptych, meaning there are three components of the canvas, and this is one large piece. So in many ways, we feel like this is the early period of Morrisseau starting to work bigger on more epic, larger canvases and really explore some of his artistic genius.”

It’s an entry point for the gallery to something that hasn’t been talked about in the last 40 years and hasn’t been examined, Hills said.

LISTEN | Mathew Hills: Giant Morriseau Painting : Superior Morning 7:48 Mathew Hills: Giant Morriseau Painting A massive Norval Morrisseau masterpiece is returning to public view right here in Thunder Bay. Hear more about that.

In addition to supporting the piece’s conservation, Hills said, the gallery can explore some of the art’s history. It can also share it in a territory and region associated with Morrisseau, he added.

“We’re really happy to have this opportunity to show it off, and to do some conservation work on it and restore it to its full glory."

Hills said the gallery invites the public to come out and take a look. The Morrisseau Masterwork will be on view until Jan. 3.

World.title: Michigan tourist who posted about wearing 'Lake America' sweatshirts to Halifax says it was AI
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A CEO from Michigan has cut her trip to Halifax short after she says she's received death threats over a viral Facebook photo where she and three family members appear to be wearing "Lake America" sweatshirts.

"Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will," said the Sept. 11 photo originally posted by Jane Smith, the CEO of Saginaw-based Family First Credit Union, followed by "lol lol."

In the photo, which has gone viral, Smith and three family members smile and pose in the airport before boarding a flight to Halifax for what was supposed to be a 10-day trip.

Judging by the reaction online, just a few weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to re-name Lake Ontario "Lake America" amid the trade war between the two countries, Canadians were not lol-ing.

" I'd say you dingdongs have messed with the wrong city," a Haligonian commented on an Instagram post by Breaking News Canada that shared the image, which has since been deleted from Facebook.

"Imagine coming to another country to visit and shop and dine at our businesses while actively disrespecting them and expecting great service and kindness. I wonder how many spit burgers and drinks they consumed," commented another person.

" And on the anniversary of 9/11 when Atlantic Canadians were so kind and welcoming of stranded Americans," commented another person on a Facebook post by Northly Halifax.

A screen grab of an Instagram post by Breaking News Canada from Sept. 13 shows the since-deleted Facebook photo by Jane Smith that went viral. (@breakingnews.ca/Instagram)

CBC News has reached out to Smith and the Family First Credit Union in Saginaw, Mich., and not yet heard back. An automatic email reply from Smith said she was out of office "starting today" until Monday.

But in an interview Thursday with ABC12 News in Michigan, Smith said the image was AI-generated and meant to be a joke.

"We weren't trying to make a political statement," Smith told the news outlet.

"However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun at the fact that you know one of the Great Lakes' names were getting changed."

She further explained that the sweatshirts weren't real, saying she ran a photo of them through ChatGPT to add the "Lake America" gear, then posted it to her private Facebook page with an AI label.

When they arrived in Halifax, it was her sister who then re-posted it publicly, added the comment, and didn't include the AI warning, Smith said.

" We never had actual sweatshirts. We never wore sweatshirts."

WATCH | Trump renamed Lake Ontario to 'provoke Canadians': Trump renamed Lake Ontario to 'provoke Canada,' historian says | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 8:34 Historian Tim Naftali says U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to rename the American side of Lake Ontario was intended to stir nationalist sentiment in the U.S. and provoke Canada.

'I n poor judgment'

There's been ongoing backlash over Trump's proposed name change on both sides of the border. Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canadians will call it Lake Ontario "now and always," while Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said "we're into some real foolishness now."

In the U.S., three members of Congress have introduced a bill aimed at stopping Trump's renaming, titled "Hands off our Great Lakes."

"Americans are struggling to afford groceries, housing and everyday essentials, and yet this president chooses to pick petty fights with our closest ally," Democratic Congressman Tim Kennedy, who represents Buffalo and Niagara Falls, N.Y., said in an Aug. 31 news release.

Smith told ABC12 News her family returned to Michigan early because they were receiving death threats, but didn't elaborate.

CBC News has reached out to the Halifax District RCMP, which said they can't confirm whether any individual or organization is associated with a police investigation unless or until charges are confirmed in court or there's an operational need to do so.

In an earlier statement to ABC12 News, Smith said she would like to "sincerely apologize."

"It was insensitive, distasteful and in poor judgment. It should never have been created or shared. Though the image did not depict a real event, I understand that the image was hurtful and offensive," Smith said.

"I never intended to insult, mock or harm anyone, but I recognize that my intent does not erase the impact. I take full responsibility for creating and sharing the image."

The board of directors at Family First Credit Union told ABC12 it "disapproves and rejects" Smith's post, adding they "support and respect our Canadian neighbours."

World.title: CRA still owed over $5B in COVID-19 benefits sent to ineligible recipients
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ottawa is still owed $5.56 billion of outstanding debt related to COVID-19 benefits sent to those who were later deemed ineligible, according to data the Canada Revenue Agency provided to CBC News.

The updated figure dated July 31 indicates the total debt has been nearly halved from last November, by which point the CRA reported it was owed over $10 billion.

According to the CRA, the agency originally gave out about $14 billion in COVID-related benefits to individuals the agency says weren't eligible because they didn't meet the income requirements.

Most of that sum was provided under the Canada emergency response benefit (CERB) or the similar Canada recovery benefit (CRB) program.

CERB was in place from March to October 2020. Applicants had to have earned at least $5,000 in income in the last 12 months, lost income as a result of the pandemic and not been receiving employment insurance in order to be eligible. They received $2,000 every four weeks.

In 2022, the CRA started informing ineligible recipients a repayment was due. The CRA says that since collections began, approximately $3.671 billion in COVID-19 individual benefit debt had been paid back.

The CRA says it's still owed $2.91 billion on CERB payments and $1.81 billion on CRB, as of July 31. Older data the agency provided CBC News indicated it was owed $5.41 billion on CERB and $3.2 billion on CRB, as of Nov. 30, 2025.

How is the outstanding debt reduced?

Repayments only account for a portion of the debt reduction, according to the CRA. It says the balance fluctuates over time due to multiple factors, which also include changes in eligibility and writeoffs of amounts it deems uncollectable.

According to Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), the CRA can recommend a debt for a writeoff to ESDC if the individual in question is dealing with what it considers permanent financial hardship.

"Changes in the overall receivable balance should not be interpreted solely as debt repayments or writeoffs," the CRA said in a statement. "While some debts may be deemed uncollectable for accounting purposes, the debt itself is not cancelled."

It said "the Crown retains the right to recover the amount owing in the future."

The agency said if it determines a taxpayer's debt remains unpaid even if they have the ability to pay it in full, the CRA may take legal action.

"The CRA takes firm and responsible measures against those who seek to avoid paying outstanding amounts," it said.

To help debtors settle what they owe, the CRA says it's adopting a "flexible collection approach to encourage voluntary payments." That includes, for example, broadening the range of ways people can repay their debts and allowing them extended timelines to do so.

The government allows for interest-free repayment over time.

"If individuals are having difficulty paying their debt, we will make every effort to establish appropriate payment arrangements based on individuals' ability to pay," the CRA said.

"We want to help impacted individuals resolve any issues and our agents will work with them on a case-by-case basis."

World.title: Parents of NHL prospect hospitalized after collapse at team workout say he's a 'fighter'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The parents of an Ontario NHL prospect who is in critical condition after collapsing during a team workout say their son is "a fighter" and that they are not giving up on him.

Twenty-one-year-old Matthew Mayich, of Hamilton, was at an early-morning outdoor workout with the Arizona State University (ASU) hockey team on Aug. 20 when he collapsed.

"We know Matthew's a fighter and we're hoping he pulls through this," said Matthew's father, John. He and Matthew's mother, Christina, spoke to CBC News from Phoenix, Ariz.

Before the workout, Matthew was "perfectly healthy," according to Christina.

Now, their lawyer says, he’s "clinging to his life in a hospital bed."

Matthew Mayich is pictured in a St. Louis Blues jersey in a photo the team shared on Aug. 26. (St. Louis Blues)

The incident has made waves in the sports world, prompting the Professional Hockey Players’ Association to speak up about the lack of protections for young athletes.

"When athletes feel pressure to remain silent about an injury, illness, exhaustion or concern because they fear the consequences of speaking up, the system has failed them," said PHPA executive director Brian Ramsay in a statement on Sept. 10, which does not directly name Mayich.

"Athletes should never have to choose between their health and their careers. Period."

WATCH | Family wants answers: Family demands answers after hockey player collapses from 'military style' workout | Duration closed caption 2:26 The parents of Matthew Mayich, a 21-year-old NHL prospect from Stoney Creek, Ont., speak to CBC News after their son collapsed after 'military style' training at Arizona State University. Mayich is in critical condition and unlikely to recover, says his lawyer.

He loved hockey but ‘he was a lot more than hockey’

Mayich started playing hockey around age five, according to John, and excelled.

He played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020, and then with the Ottawa 67's. In 2023, he was drafted by the NHL's St. Louis Blues. His parents say they were his biggest fans, along with his younger brother and older sister, travelling everywhere to support him.

"He didn't care if he was at a small rink in Hamilton or a big rink in St. Louis with a lot of people — he just loves the game," John said.

"And he wasn't just about hockey. He was a lot more than just hockey."

Mayich’s parents describe him as "a little fireball," someone who people gravitate toward.

"Ever since he was young … he just lights up the room," said John.

Hockey player got heatstroke, lawyer says

When Mayich joined the ASU hockey team, it was the next rung on the ladder while chasing his NHL team.

The recent transfer to ASU was just getting settled into a new apartment, with his family looking forward to watching him play at the university.

A drone shot of Arizona State University campus in Tempe, Ariz., on Sept. 17. (Andrew Hernandez/CBC)

His parents say they spoke with him briefly before the last workout, adding that he was excited and "ready to work."

Christina said one of Mayich’s teammates called her to tell her what happened, and that the family rushed to Phoenix to be by his side. They haven’t left.

"We were devastated," she said. "Heartbroken. Shocked. [It’s] just so hard to believe."

Mayich suffered heatstroke during the workout, according to the family’s Phoenix-based lawyer, Leonard Aragon, who is less optimistic than the parents that the young athlete will survive.

"I'm a lawyer, not a doctor, but I don't believe so," he told CBC News.

Workout designed to 'break the kids,' lawyer alleges

There were roughly 25 other players at the workout, according to John Mayich.

The morning session, which took place in advance of October's season opener, involved push-ups, running and drills where medicine balls were carried from one side of the field to the other, said Aragon.

The lawyer describes the session as "military-style," taking place in "overwhelming" heat and that water was withheld from players.

"[It] was designed to basically break the kids and try to put some sort of toughness or something like that into the kids at the beginning of the year," Aragon said.

He also says safety guidelines at the university were not followed.

"Protocols that ASU itself says should have been followed, such as monitoring people to see if they have heat problems or having a cool-down tub if someone has heatstroke or heat exhaustion — things like that didn't take place," he said. "And it led to this tragedy."

The university declined an interview request, citing an ongoing review.

It did not respond to questions about whether the individual who ran the workout was vetted and contracted by the university and whether there have been any consequences for the leadership team since the incident.

Instead, an ASU spokesperson referred CBC News to a statement issued on Sept. 3, stating the athletics program has "heat-illness guidelines in place" and that the morning workout included a "third party who had previously worked" with the team.

The statement said university police are investigating, "as they would anytime they are called to a serious incident."

Leonard Aragon is a lawyer representing the Mayich family. (Andrew Hernandez/CBC)

Aragon calls the university’s failure to immediately call for an independent third-party investigation "a slap in the face to the family."

John Mayich's thoughts are also with the young athletes who witnessed what happened to his son.

"It was tragic what happened," he said. "I feel for them also. It's not easy to see that."

Is enough being done to protect athletes?

Athletes are highly competitive, seeking limited spots on sports teams, which is why protections for athletes are critical, says Adam Huxley, a hockey development coach based in Wainwright, Alta.

"When there's 30 players and 20 spots, I can see where the mindset of, 'Well, if I'm not feeling great or something's not going right, I don't want to be the one that says something, because then I seem like I'm the weak link,'" Huxley told CBC News.

He says there should be better education for players so they know when they are being pushed beyond their limits. Huxley also says it should be balanced with teams being able to tell their players it's OK to speak up.

Adam Huxley is a hockey development coach and owner of Huxley Hockey Conditioning. (Samuel Martin/CBC)

"If you're in trouble, say something. If you feel like something's not going right or whatever — and that goes for the player that is involved in it, that goes [for] the teammates that are around [them], OK? And that goes for the staff," Huxley said. "Everyone's gonna learn from this."

In the statement issued by the PHPA, Ramsay said there is an obligation to keep pushing for a culture where speaking up about health and wellness is a strength not a weakness.

"That young man, on the cusp of his career in professional hockey, was failed by the system, the system that should have protected him," Ramsay said in the statement.

The National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA), which oversees student athletes in the United States, said a stated goal is to "ensure well-being … for college athletes."

An NCAA spokesperson declined to comment on the incident.

The NHL also did not respond to inquiries from CBC News.

Family waiting for a miracle

For now, Mayich's parents, siblings, grandparents, aunts and uncles are taking shifts at his bedside.

"Most of the kids usually come around him and they'll sing to him. There's Scripture-reading and prayers constantly. And we tell him funny stories, 'cause he was a funny guy, he was a jokester," Christina Mayich said.

"There's definitely a positive vibe in his room. There's something there that we just cannot explain. So much love, so much peace."

She says the family is taking it one day at a time.

"We're just continuing and asking the Lord to give us our miracle."

World.title: Rogue AI swarm used a University of Toronto link-shortening tool to communicate
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents that hijacked a German website in the spring reportedly also used more than 10 other websites for unsanctioned communications earlier this year, including a link-shortening tool at the University of Toronto.

The university disabled the link shortener's use as a message board after learning that OpenAI agents may have used it, the university said in a statement to CBC News on Friday.

"OpenAI subsequently contacted the university about the possible activity by AI agents, which occurred in June," the statement said.

While the university said there was no security breach and no impact on its digital properties, reports of more rogue AI incidents come amid global concerns that OpenAI and other artificial intelligence companies are losing control of their own technology.

Reuters, which first reported the University of Toronto activity, used data from six sets of independent investigators to show that the agents' rogue activity was more widespread than previously disclosed — and, according to the investigators, probably wider still.

"It’s almost certain that there’s more going on here that we just don’t know about," said Andrew Yoon, a researcher with the California nonprofit CivAI. He told Reuters he tallied 18 previously undisclosed sites used by the agents between May and July. Investigators disagreed on the exact number of discovered sites, but all concurred it was more than 10.

WATCH | Tech leaders want an AI slowdown, Trump does not: Trump dismisses AI warnings as industry CEOs urge slowdown | Duration 2:25 U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday likened critics of ‌artificial intelligence (AI) to 'very negative forces' bringing up scenarios that won't happen and said he wants to make sure the U.S. remains the industry leader. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei outlined a three-step framework intended to slow the pace of development, which received endorsements from SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

On Sept. 4, researchers reported that a swarm of OpenAI agents hijacked a German-language wiki site and turned it into an improvised messaging platform for cheating on tests. The researchers told Reuters the agents left similar messages on the other sites, including U of T.

OpenAI has not publicly explained how or why its agents used third-party sites as improvised message boards, but the researchers who first identified the activity said it was likely because OpenAI had tasked the agents with answering a series of demanding research questions while permitting them only to scan the web for answers, not post anything.

Despite those restrictions, the agents still found ways to talk to one another by taking advantage of quirks that allowed users to make edits using non-standard commands, similar to how students forbidden from talking to one another during an exam can still share answers by scrawling notes on a bathroom stall.

Carney has called for international oversight

Mohit Rajhans of Think Start Inc., which advises businesses on AI adoption, told CBC News Network the duty of care lies with the tech companies to "come clean about how malicious some of this tech is."

He applauded Prime Minister Mark Carney's call for a global "technology stability" body to oversee AI safety, comparable to the international Financial Stability Board, though Rajhans said he's worried that any third party will be "bullied out of the conversation" by the half-dozen major players in Silicon Valley.

OpenAI did not directly address questions from Reuters about how many sites its agents used to communicate or say why it kept the activity under wraps for months. The company did not immediately reply to an interview request from CBC News.

The company announced Wednesday it would keep closer watch on "misalignment" — the industry term for when an AI system strays from the user's and developer's intent or fails to follow human values and safety rules. The company also released six previously unreported instances of rogue AI, but none that mentioned the university.



The company says it has not found any instances as serious as the so-called Hugging Face incident. In that case, around 1,200 agents tasked by OpenAI with working on problems built a covert message board where they collaborated to cheat on their tests and then tried to cover their tracks. About 700 of them ultimately hacked into online platform Hugging Face before they were discovered.
