World.title: Officials report 43% drop in Guanajuato homicides: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📉 Guanajuato homicides down 43% this year : At Friday’s mañanera in Irapuato, National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported an average of 3.2 homicides per day in Guanajuato in August, 75% lower than in February 2025, the state’s most violent month under Sheinbaum. The daily average for the first eight months of 2026 was 4, a 43% year-over-year decline. This year is on track to be the state’s least violent since 2017.

: At Friday’s mañanera in Irapuato, National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported an average of 3.2 homicides per day in Guanajuato in August, 75% lower than in February 2025, the state’s most violent month under Sheinbaum. The daily average for the first eight months of 2026 was 4, a 43% year-over-year decline. This year is on track to be the state’s least violent since 2017. 🚔 10,699 arrests in Guanajuato since October 2024 : Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 172 of the people detained through Aug. 31 were “priority targets.” In the same period, authorities also seized more than 6 tonnes of drugs and over 2,000 firearms, and dismantled two methamphetamine labs.

: Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 172 of the people detained through Aug. 31 were “priority targets.” In the same period, authorities also seized more than 6 tonnes of drugs and over 2,000 firearms, and dismantled two methamphetamine labs. ⚖️ Suspect arrested in murder of Spanish student : García Harfuch confirmed that a man known as “El Trompas,” identified as Francisco Javier Meléndez, was detained Thursday in Cuautla, Morelos, in connection with the murder of Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, a 21-year-old Spanish exchange student.

: García Harfuch confirmed that a man known as “El Trompas,” identified as Francisco Javier Meléndez, was detained Thursday in Cuautla, Morelos, in connection with the murder of Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, a 21-year-old Spanish exchange student. 📞 Sheinbaum says her call with Trump was “very good”: Sheinbaum said she spoke to the U.S. president about trade issues on Wednesday. She said differences have not yet been resolved, but that good progress is being made.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Irapuato, a city in Guanajuato, a state that in recent years has been Mexico’s most violent in terms of total homicides.

At the mañanera, federal security officials took the opportunity to outline the progress that has been made in combating violence in the state. Much of the violence in Guanajuato is related to organized crime, and, in particular, a long-running turf war between the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and the Santa Rosa de Lima Cartel.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Security Minister Omar García Harfuch’s confirmation that a man known as “El Trompas” was detained in connection with the murder in Cuautla, Morelos, of Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, a 21-year-old Spanish woman who was studying at the Autonomous University of the State of Morelos on an exchange program.

In addition, Sheinbaum spoke briefly about her trade-focused call on Wednesday with U.S. President Donald Trump. The call came less than two weeks after Trump asserted that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs — apart from “hot tamales” and “tomatoes” — and therefore the U.S. could cease trading with its southern neighbor. In reality, Mexico supplies a wide range of goods to the U.S., and the economies of the two countries are highly integrated.

Homicides down 43% in Guanajuato this year

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported that there was an average of 3.2 homicides per day in Guanajuato in August. Figueroa highlighted that the daily average in August was 75% lower than that in February 2025, the most violent month in Guanajuato since Sheinbaum took office in October 2024.

She reported that there was an average of 4 homicides per day in Guanajuato in the first eight months of 2026, a reduction of 43% compared to 2025. Data presented by Figueroa showed that 2026 is on track to be the least violent year in Guanajuato since 2017.

More than 10,000 arrests in Guanajuato since Sheinbaum took office

García Harfuch reported that more than 10,600 people were arrested in Guanajuato between Oct. 1, 2024 — the date Sheinbaum was sworn in as president — and Aug. 31, 2026.

Of the 10,699 people detained in the state in the period, 172 were “priority targets,” García Harfuch said.

He also reported that over 6 tonnes of drugs and more than 2,000 firearms were seized in Guanajuato between October 2024 and August 2026. In addition, two methamphetamine laboratories were dismantled, García Harfuch said.

Suspect arrested in Morelos femicide case

García Harfuch reported that federal and state security forces detained Francisco Javier “N” on Thursday in connection with the murder of Tacoronte. The suspect has been identified as Francisco Javier Meléndez in media reports. He was detained in Cuautla, a city around 40 kilometers southeast of Cuernavaca, the capital of Morelos.

García Harfuch first reported the arrest in a social media post on Thursday evening.

On Friday morning, he said that “preventing femicides and addressing violence against women” is a “priority” of the federal government.

En #Morelos, autoridades federales y estatales detienen a un hombre por el feminicidio de una joven de nacionalidad española. https://t.co/mLtMcbL8ch pic.twitter.com/jyLFGK6NtE — Secretaría de Seguridad y Protección Ciudadana (@SSPCMexico) September 18, 2026

Sheinbaum discloses ‘very good’ call with Trump

Sheinbaum told reporters that she spoke to Trump on Wednesday.

“It was a scheduled call,” she said, adding that she often speaks to the U.S. president without publicly announcing their discussions.

“Why? Because we’re making progress on trade issues,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that differences over trade have not yet been resolved, but stressed that good progress is being made.

Reuters reported on Sept. 11 that “Mexico and the United States are racing to reach a bilateral trade deal before the U.S. midterm elections,” which will take place on Nov. 3. As part of a bilateral deal, Mexico is seeking the reduction — or ideally the elimination — of U.S. tariffs on Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles.

On July 1, the United States announced that it had declined to renew the USMCA in its “current form,” although the three-way pact remains in effect.

Sheinbaum said her call with Trump was “very good.”

“… The Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco and Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard were with me in the conversation,” she added.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: A mountain, a legend and a dream: Chavela Vargas’ Tepoztlán home
World.content:
The story goes that when Chavela Vargas, the iconic singer of Mexican ranchera music, visited Tepoztlán in the state of Morelos, she was captivated by the mountain known as Chalchitépetl. She was amazed by its beauty, but more importantly, Vargas was struck by the fact that she had dreamed of that exact formation many times, despite never having seen it before. After seeing the mountain, she decided to make the town her home.

“She came, knocked on the door, and asked what she had to do to live here, and that is how she ended up staying,” said Gerardo Ramírez, the manager of Casa Chavela.

How Chavela chose her home

Vargas, who was Costa Rican by birth and famous for her declaration, “We Mexicans are born wherever the hell we want,” arrived in Mexico at age 17 and began her career singing in cantinas. She was later discovered and mentored by the iconic Mexican singer José Alfredo Jiménez. Vargas was a close friend — and perhaps more — to figures like Frida Kahlo, Diego Rivera, Joaquín Sabina and Federico García Lorca, and she became a major icon for the LGBTQ+ movement.

Vargas arrived in Tepoztlán in 2007, by which time she was already a legend whose career was celebrated throughout Latin America and Europe. The house she chose was located on the Tepoztlán-Cuernavaca Federal Highway and belonged to Emma Teresa Ortiz, known as “Monina.” At the time, the property was called Quinta Monina. There were once two other houses on the property, which were also inhabited by artists, including the famous actress María Eugenia Llamas.

When Vargas arrived at Quinta Monina, she requested changes to the house that reflected her strong personality and creativity. Today, the building has become a landmark of Mexican architectural design.

An architectural gem

The initial design of Casa Chavela was straightforward, with a large hallway connecting the kitchen, living room, dining room and two bedrooms, as well as a terrace. This was later transformed at Vargas’ request. Today, the house is a blend of volcanic rock — typical of Tepoztlán construction — and large windows with orange ironwork that bathe the interior in light, reminiscent of functionalist architecture.

“The reason all the ironwork is this orange color is that, when Chavela moved into this house, she asked for the terrace to be enclosed with glass, which has become a distinctive feature of the house,” Ramírez explained.

In 2020, the Romero family — comprising architects, designers and engineers — purchased the property and remodeled it using local materials, inspired by Vargas’ original ideas.

They replaced the tiles, added two rooms and expanded the orange ironwork windows to the bedrooms and dining room, giving the house openness and light. In terms of decoration, the home features ocote pine crafts from the nearby town of Ocotitlán, and Vargas’ iconic jorongos (traditional Mexican woolen garments) hang on the walls. Her famous equipal — a handcrafted, pre-Hispanic-style armchair — lined in bright colors, can also be admired.

A place for art, inspiration and creativity

The surrounding gardens contain more than 60 trees that the owners have added in recent years, while preserving the original vegetation. A Y-shaped pool and numerous totems made from traditional clay from Amayuca, Morelos, add to the house’s unique atmosphere.

A podium in the shape of a kiosk crowns the garden and is used for ceremonies such as weddings. Furthermore, as the land slopes down, an area of old stables appears; these now serve as rooms for artists in residence.

Further down is a huge open living room that serves as a cultural space for concerts, meetings and exhibitions. While Casa Chavela welcomes guests through Airbnb and by renting out rooms like a hotel, it also has a social purpose: It offers free lodging to artists in residence.

Since 2022, five artists have completed residencies of between two and three weeks, donating their work to the house collection. Many of these pieces were inspired by Vargas, though the work can cover any topic.

Vargas spent her final years in this house, from 2007 to 2012. During this time, she found peace and formed a profound relationship with the mountain of her dreams, Chalchitépetl. After a complicated and magnificent life, she found a place of contemplation here, as well as the strength to overcome her struggles. Casa Chavela is undoubtedly imbued with the personal magic and spirit of her personality.

Ana Paula de la Torre is a Mexican journalist and collaborator for various outlets, including Milenio, Animal Político, Vice, Newsweek en Español, Televisa and Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Which neighborhoods in Mexico City have the highest seismic risk?
World.content:
First of all, there is no such thing as Earthquake Month in Mexico City or anywhere in Mexico. One could argue every day is Earthquake Day because of the country’s high seismic activity. Still, residents carry the heavy grief of the coincidences of Sept. 19, the date on which — in completely different years and decades — devastating earthquakes caused the capital to succumb to panic and ruin.

Although scientists know it is practically impossible to predict these seismic events, residents cannot shake the thought that an earthquake might hit Mexico City on Sept. 19.

Beyond the dark humor, the reality is that because Mexico City sits on ancient lakebeds, some areas of the capital are at greater risk during an earthquake.

Colonia Cuauhtémoc

The Cuauhtémoc borough is among the areas most prone to earthquake damage in Mexico City. The neighborhood of the same name, in the heart of the borough, suffered severe damage after the earthquakes of 2017 and 2022. Bordered by Paseo de la Reforma, Juárez and the Historic Center, Colonia Cuauhtémoc remains a hybrid between the business world of tall corporate buildings and residential life.

Besides having some of the tallest buildings in the city, the neighborhood suffers the consequences of poor urban planning. Because it sits primarily in Zone III (Lake Zone) of the city’s seismic microzonation, an area characterized by deep, highly compressible lacustrine clay deposits, it experiences significant wave amplification and has suffered severe damage during historical earthquakes.

Colonia Centro

The Historic Center has layers upon layers of Mexico City’s architectural and archaeological history, sitting directly atop the ruins of Tenochtitlán. For this reason, it is also one of the neighborhoods most affected by strong earthquakes.

Despite being one of the areas with the greatest archaeological and historical wealth in the country, the buildings and temples — some more than 500 years old — bear the scars of earthquakes. A striking example is the Church of Loreto, which tilts noticeably because of seismic tremors.

Colonias Roma Norte and Sur

The streets of Mexico City are known for chaos, and in the Roma Norte and Roma Sur neighborhoods, some of that chaos is visible in the cracks in the pavement. The streets are broken by tree roots pushing through the asphalt, but more often by the shockwaves from major earthquakes.

Efforts by the Cuauhtémoc borough cannot fully patch the scars of past quakes. Among the trendy bars and local cafes lies a stark reminder that this is one of the areas most affected by seismic activity in central Mexico.

Colonia Condesa

The ever-iconic Colonia Condesa, besides being a favorite spot for Sunday strolls, is also sadly one of the areas most affected by earthquakes. The neighborhood rests firmly within Zone III (Lake Zone), which, as noted, is predominantly composed of thick, highly soft clay deposits that dramatically amplify seismic vibrations during major quakes.

For this reason, several older and poorly retrofitted structures collapsed during major events like the 2017 earthquake. Furthermore, due to corruption and a perceived disregard for the safety guidelines required by Mexico City, many fear similar outcomes in the event of future strong earthquakes, as reported by the newspaper Excélsior.

Colonia Juárez

Colonia Juárez does not wait until June to celebrate Pride; popular nightlife venues in the area operate year-round. Despite the area’s lively atmosphere, it is also one of the neighborhoods where earthquakes are felt most intensely.

During low-intensity tremors, business owners and residents often evacuate into the streets even before the seismic alert sounds — a sign of how accustomed locals are to the ground shaking.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: A dog dressed as a taco stand wins Morelia’s pre-Grito Patriotic Pup Contest
World.content:
Pet owners and dog lovers in Michoacán’s state capital kicked off Independence Day festivities early last Sunday, taking part in a Most Patriotic Pup contest.

Morelia’s popular bakery and pastry shop Melón o Sandía sponsored the first-ever “Concurso de Perritos Patrióticos” (Patriotic Puppy Contest) at the city’s Parque Canino 1 on the grounds of the Convention Center in the southern part of the capital.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by MELÓN O SANDÍA (@melonosandia.morelia)

Around 40 dogs participated in the contest, which attracted over 100 onlookers who acted as the voting audience. No entry fee was needed, though owners were required to register their dogs in advance via an online sign-up form.

Dogs of all shapes and sizes showed up in patriotic outfits, ranging from tiny mariachi suits to rebozos and tricolor ribbons, while others were decorated with popular Mexican dishes. A few even were adorned with a food stand theme.

Melón o Sandía hosted the event and offered gift vouchers for the winners, while PetFood Morelia and Maka Recetas — a Mexican pet food company — also supplied prizes for winners and participants.

The top three “best-dressed” dogs won gift vouchers for Melón o Sandía, ranging from 500 pesos (US $29) to 1,000 pesos (US $58) to 1,500 pesos (US $87), and each of the three winners received prize packages from PetFood Morelia worth 1,300 pesos (US $75).

A dog named Maple, who sported an outfit designed to look like a complete taquitos al pastor “Alemán” food stand (a play on words linking the popular “tacos in the style of a shepherd” with the familiar dog breed), was declared “The Most Patriotic Dog.”

Also on offer at Maple’s food stand were “Guaguacoa” (a pun on the sound of a dog bark and barbacoa) and “Suaperro” (a portmanteau between “suadero” — a thin, fatty cut of beef — and the Spanish word for dog).

Second place went to Bebukis, who was adorned with a food tray featuring elotes y lomitos (corn kernels and pork loin) and a tiny cowboy hat, while the third-place prize was awarded to a little pup named Avenita, who carried a bowl of red pozole almost twice its size on its back.

With reports from Mi Morelia and Melón o Sandía

World.title: Fire damages 108 stalls in Acapulco’s Central Market
World.content:
A fire broke out at Acapulco’s Central Market early Wednesday, damaging more than 100 stalls. No serious injuries or fatalities were reported.

The blaze began before 6 a.m. and quickly spread to engulf scores of stalls in the footwear and flowers sections of the market, the largest in Acapulco.

Some 100 firefighters brought the fire under control on Wednesday, but continued working on Thursday to “cool down” three spots from which smoke was still emanating, according to the Acapulco-based newspaper El Sur.

The cause of the blaze hasn’t been officially determined, but a short circuit in the market’s electrical system has been identified as a possible trigger. Raúl Noyola Rocha, Acapulco’s civil protection chief, said Thursday that an investigation by the Guerrero Attorney General’s Office would take up to a week to yield results.

The Acapulco municipal government on Wednesday reported a preliminary toll of 90 stalls damaged — 75 in the market’s footwear section and 15 in the flowers section.

However, Acapulco Mayor Leticia Lozano said Thursday that a total of 108 stalls were in fact damaged.

El Sol de Acapulco reported that cleanup work, including the removal of rubble, was taking place at the market on Thursday. Mexican soldiers and affected shopkeepers were assisting the efforts.

El Sol de Acapulco reported that there was still smoke in the market on Thursday and that “new outbreaks of flames” were occurring. The newspaper also reported the presence of “burnt metallic structures” and “goods reduced to ashes.”

Affected stallholders are set to receive an initial economic support payment from the municipal government on Friday. The government didn’t specify how much each stallholder will get.

Local authorities are also planning to adapt part of the market to accommodate up to 110 temporary stalls while the footwear and flower sections are rebuilt. El Sol de Acapulco reported that a total of 12 fires have now occurred at the Acapulco Central Market, which was built in 1969. A massive blaze in 2023 destroyed around 570 stalls.

With reports from El Sol de Acapulco and El Sur

World.title: Under pressure from Trump on cartels, Sheinbaum turns spotlight on US drug use
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico doesn’t need to be judged “from the outside,” President Claudia Sheinbaum declared Thursday, two days after U.S. President Donald Trump said that “Mexico must take additional action” against drug cartels and arrest “the many corrupt public officials” who have colluded with them.

Responding to a “presidential determination” submitted to the U.S. Congress on Tuesday, Sheinbaum also said she would like to see “a report about what the U.S. government is doing in the United States” to reduce drug use and combat drug trafficking.

La Presidenta @Claudiashein fue contundente: “Podemos cooperar y colaborar, pero las decisiones las toma el pueblo de México y su gobierno, no un país extranjero.

La memoria es el alma de los pueblos y el escudo… Defender nuestra independencia y soberanía es defender a México”. pic.twitter.com/HeNSEpXDwQ — Jesús Ramírez Cuevas (@JesusRCuevas) September 17, 2026

Trump’s remarks on Mexico in the document titled “Presidential Determination on Major Drug Transit or Major Illicit Drug Producing Countries for Fiscal Year 2027” are part of a sustained pressure campaign by the U.S. government aimed at getting the Sheinbaum administration to ramp up the fight against cartels.

Just last week, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio asserted that Mexico isn’t doing “nearly enough” to combat drug cartels, even though he also said, “The Mexicans have done more than they’ve ever done before to go after these groups.”

Rubio suggested that the United States could act unilaterally against such criminal organizations in Mexican territory.

Since Trump began his second term in January 2025, the U.S. government has designated eight Mexican cartels as foreign terrorist organizations. On numerous occasions, the U.S. president has demonstrated his eagerness to combat them with U.S. force, but Sheinbaum is vehemently opposed to any kind of U.S. intervention in Mexico.

Trump urges ‘additional action’ against ‘narcoterrorist organizations that dominate vast areas’ of Mexico

In his presidential determination, Trump identified 23 nations as “major drug transit or major illicit drug producing countries.”

Among those he named were Mexico, China, Colombia, India, Panama and Venezuela.

Trump said that while his administration “has successfully secured our borders from invasion, Canada and Mexico need to do far more to stop the flows of deadly drugs into our country.”

The U.S. president wrote that the United States recognizes the Sheinbaum administration “for seizing greater volumes of drugs, dismantling clandestine laboratories, and deploying additional law enforcement and military resources to our shared border.” He also noted that “United States-Mexican security cooperation has helped eliminate some of the world’s most notorious cartel bosses, including ‘El Mencho.'”

“However,” Trump added, “Mexico must take additional action against the narcoterrorist organizations that dominate vast areas of its territory and continue to threaten the American people.”

Trump also said that “Mexico needs to bolster supply chain integrity by soliciting greater private industry participation and significantly increasing inspections at its ports of entry” — among which are Pacific coast seaports, where Chinese precursor chemicals used to manufacture fentanyl are known to enter the country.

“Canada and Mexico need to do far more to stop the flows of deadly drugs into our country.”https://t.co/4WlUMSoEbM — Gabriela Siller Pagaza (@GabySillerP) September 16, 2026

“Additionally, Mexico’s current investments in its security forces are insufficient to sustain and expand its campaigns against narcoterrorists, their finances, and their criminal networks,” he wrote.

“This includes exposing, arresting, and prosecuting the many corrupt public officials that have aided and abetted the cartels and betrayed their own country’s security and sovereignty.”

Among the officials U.S. authorities would like to see arrested is Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya, who is accused by U.S. prosecutors of drug trafficking in league with the Sinaloa Cartel.

Rocha is on leave as governor, but remains a free man, having thus far avoided arrest and extradition to the United States. Mexican authorities say that U.S. prosecutors have not provided evidence that warrants the arrest of the governor, a representative of the ruling Morena party.

Sheinbaum: ‘We know what Mexico’s problems are’

Asked about Trump’s “presidential determination” at her Thursday morning press conference, Sheinbaum’s initial response was to say that she would like to see “a report about what the U.S. government is doing in the United States” to reduce drug use.

“What’s being done about [drug] use?” she asked.

“… From our point of view, it’s a public health issue,” Sheinbaum said.

She acknowledged that her government has to work to combat the production of drugs in Mexico and their illegal shipment to the United States, but stressed that U.S. authorities also have a responsibility to combat drug use and narcotics distributors in the U.S.

“Where is the effort being made to stop drug cartels and distributors in the United States? What’s going on with money laundering in the United States?” asked Sheinbaum, suggesting that the U.S. government should do more to combat criminal threats in its own territory.

“… In Mexico, we’re acting,” she said.

“… But what’s happening on the other side? … What’s happening with the weapons that come to Mexico from the United States? Yes, there have been arrests, there have been seizures [of firearms], but you couldn’t explain the firepower of organized crime in our country without [talking about] the illegal transit of weapons from the United States to Mexico,” Sheinbaum said.

She went on to say that “we don’t need to be judged from the outside” — a barb directed at Trump and other U.S. officials.

“We know what Mexico’s problems are and we act [against them] every day,” Sheinbaum said.

“… We’re subject to public scrutiny every day and we provide results every day,” she added.

“But what’s happening over there? I would like to see a report from the [U.S.] government itself about the results over there and what they’re doing,” Sheinbaum said.

In February 2025, Trump said he had spoken to Sheinbaum about Mexico’s anti-drugs advertising campaign, which specifically warns against fentanyl use, and pledged that the U.S. government would launch its own anti-drugs campaign “with $100 million and then another $100 million initially.”

An advertising campaign titled “Make America Fentanyl Free” was subsequently launched, but it was funded privately rather than with public money. In late 2025, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration — which often reports on drug seizures and drug-related arrests — launched a separate “Fentanyl Free America” initiative, described as “a comprehensive enforcement initiative and public awareness campaign aimed at reducing both the supply and demand for fentanyl.”

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: As Puerto Vallarta grows, officials weigh crocodile relocation plan
World.content:
Puerto Vallarta’s crocodiles may be headed for a new neighborhood.

Jalisco state officials and Mexico’s Environment Ministry (Semarnat) were scheduled to meet virtually Thursday to review proposals for managing crocodiles and potentially relocating some of them to the Estero El Salado, a protected urban estuary.

The discussion follows weeks of increased sightings in and around Puerto Vallarta, where development has brought homes, roads, hotels and tourists closer to wetlands long occupied by crocs.

In addition to the sightings, there has been at least one death. A 28-year-old man was killed by a crocodile in June on a beach near the Marriott Puerto Vallarta Resort and Spa.

Sergio Ramírez López, director of the Jalisco Civil Protection and Fire Department, said the state proposal is not simply to capture reptiles and release them into their new digs.

“You capture an animal, take it to the El Salado Estuary, it competes with other males, and it ends up going somewhere else,” Ramírez López told UDG TV.

Instead, officials want to first adapt the estuary to accommodate additional animals and reduce territorial competition, he said. There is no timetable and Semarnat would have to validate any plan, he added.

Paola Bauche, Jalisco’s environment secretary, said crocodiles are part of the region’s natural habitat and that authorities do not believe the population is excessive.

An estimated 300 to 350 live in Puerto Vallarta and Banderas Bay, with about 40 measuring more than 2 meters.

Rainy-season flooding and higher water levels allow them to move between the Boca Negra and El Salado estuaries by using the sea. The animals also are in their reproductive period, increasing their mobility and the likelihood of encounters with people.

Bauche said 11 American crocodiles (Crocodylus acutus) — a species under federal protection due to its key role in the ecological balance of estuaries, wetlands and rivers — have died in recent months in the P.V. area.

Although he didn’t specify the causes, at least two of the crocodiles were killed by humans, according to a Mexico News Daily report that also detailed the capture of a 3.7-meter (12-foot) crocodile. One of the dead crocs was found decapitated and another tied up and shot.

Jalisco officials have been working with federal and municipal authorities, hotel owners and specialists on prevention, signage and public outreach that includes a bilingual campaign aimed at ending cruelty toward crocs.

Hotels in Puerto Vallarta and along the Costalegre have been asked to standardize wildlife-warning systems. In Manzanillo, Colima, authorities have installed purple flags on beaches for the first time to warn of crocodile sightings.

For all the concern they can generate, Puerto Vallarta’s crocodiles were recently “honored” at the city’s first Crocodile Festival.

Held on Aug. 22, one day ahead of National Crocodile Day in Mexico, the event at Estero El Salado State Park paired conservation education and estuary tours with practical safety advice on coexisting with the reptiles that continue to fascinate residents of Mexico.

With reports from El Occidental and UDG TV

World.title: Playa del Carmen Sargassum: City Moves to Return Recovered Sand to Beaches as Hotel Building Continues
World.content:
MEXICO · TRAVEL & EXPAT LIFE

Key Facts — The plan Playa del Carmen is seeking a federal permit to return sand that was stripped from beaches during two years of sargassum cleanup back onto eroded stretches of the central coast.

— The season Quintana Roo had collected 127,941 tonnes of sargassum by 11 September 2026 — already above the 92,782 tonnes of all 2025 — with Playa del Carmen carrying roughly a third of the total. Arrivals are now tapering.

— The response A 2 billion Mexican peso (about US$117 million) federal program is shifting collection offshore, with Navy vessels and longer containment barriers.

— The paradox In the same week, the city announced more than US$1.6 billion in new hotel, retail and industrial projects.

— The strain Hotel occupancy fell to 30 percent in Playa del Carmen and 15 percent in Tulum in August, the state tourism minister acknowledged.

After Quintana Roo’s heaviest sargassum season to date, Playa del Carmen wants to give its beaches back the sand that cleanup crews carried away with the seaweed — while investors keep building hotels through the downturn.

A beach-cleaning tractor removes sargassum from the sand in Tulum, Quintana Roo. Mechanized cleanup strips sand along with the seaweed — the sand Playa del Carmen now wants to return to its eroded beaches. (Photo: G.Mannaerts, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Playa del Carmen sargassum cleanup has entered a new phase. The city government confirmed on 18 September 2026 that it is seeking a federal permit to return to its beaches the sand that was removed, mixed with seaweed, during the last two seasons of sargassum collection.

Irving Rafael Lili Madrigal, director of the Federal Maritime Terrestrial Zone (Zofemat), told Reportur that the project has already been filed with Semarnat, Mexico’s federal environment ministry. The city is now working through the requirements the ministry set before granting the permit.

Where the Sand Would Go

The target zones are specific. Lili Madrigal named El Recodo, a beach with visible erosion, the Calle 10 and Calle 12 corridor in the center, and the area near the Xamán-Ha pier on the Playacar side. During cleanup operations in 2025 and 2026, tractors and trucks removed sargassum together with the sand trapped inside it. That sand now sits separated, or partly separated, at collection points.

The municipality plans to automate the separation with a hopper and containers. “We do the separation ourselves; we are automating it with a hopper and containers, which is a bit more engineering, and the separation will be faster,” Lili Madrigal said. What is not yet known: when Semarnat will rule, how much sand can legally be returned, and when the work would start. No date has been announced.

A Record Season, Now Past Its Peak

The sand question exists because the Playa del Carmen sargassum season broke the pattern in 2026. The seaweed began arriving in January, months earlier than the historical April-to-May window. State collection statistics put the total for Quintana Roo at 127,941 tonnes by 11 September — already well above the 92,782 tonnes gathered in all of 2025, itself a record year at the time. Playa del Carmen accounts for the largest municipal share, roughly a third of the statewide volume, and local officials say the season is on track to be the heaviest the state has recorded.

The response has shifted from shovels to ships. On 30 July, President Claudia Sheinbaum announced a 2 billion Mexican peso program (about US$117 million, at roughly 17.15 pesos to the US dollar on 18 September) run through the Navy. A second collection vessel joined the first; the Navy has removed more than 16,000 tonnes at sea this season. Containment barriers now cover nearly 12 kilometres of Quintana Roo coastline, and Playa del Carmen’s own barrier line grew from 2.5 to five kilometres. The stated goal is to raise daily collection capacity from 1,227 tonnes toward 4,000.

The trend is now the visitor’s friend. The Navy lowered its sargassum alert for Quintana Roo from red to yellow on 27 August as arrivals eased. Conditions still vary beach by beach and week to week: the Quintana Roo Sargassum Monitoring Network, directed by hydrobiologist Esteban Amaro Mauricio, tracks around 140 beaches individually — 13 of them in Playa del Carmen. In mid-August its traffic-light map showed 22 northern beaches in red, 17 in orange, 13 in yellow, 45 in green and three free of the algae. Amaro’s network projects arrivals will keep declining through September and largely taper off by October. His caution, worth noting for planners: because 2026 began in January, an early start in January 2027 cannot be ruled out. That is a forecast from the monitoring network, not a certainty.

Building Through the Downturn

The seaweed arrived during a difficult year for the sector. State tourism minister Bernardo Cueto Riestra acknowledged on 14 August that Tulum’s hotel occupancy had fallen to 15 percent — the lowest in its history — while Playa del Carmen stood at 30 percent. He attributed the drop to the atypical sargassum influx and to airlines cutting frequencies to the Mexican Caribbean as fuel costs rose. Some Tulum hotels have closed temporarily; others operate only in high-demand weeks.

Yet the investment pipeline has not paused. On 18 September, Estefanía Hernández, the city’s Secretary of Economic Development and Investment Attraction, announced more than US$1.6 billion in new tourism, residential and commercial projects for Playa del Carmen, Reportur reported. The list includes US$700 million for 900 new hotel rooms, US$400 million for the Plaza La Isla retail project by developer Gicsa, US$300 million in a residential development, and US$200 million for a new Grupo Modelo plant and distribution center. The Mandarin Oriental Kanai Riviera Maya — 120 suites and 49 private residences, estimated to open in 2028 — was named separately, because its investment figure is still being defined.

The global brands are moving the same way. In late August, Marriott confirmed that three Reef resorts in Playa del Carmen — The Reef Playacar (198 rooms), the adults-only Reef 28 (120 suites) and The Reef Coco Beach (198 rooms, expanding to 358 by early 2028) — will join its Tribute Portfolio in 2027, adding 676 rooms to its all-inclusive pipeline. In May, Semarnat authorized a two-hotel complex by Oleum Joint Ventures on the Riviera Maya coast: 286 rooms each, 572 in total, with an investment reported at 800 million Mexican pesos (about US$47 million), according to Riviera Maya News. These are announced figures, not completed construction; the gap between announcement and opening is where downturns usually bite.

What This Means for Travelers and Residents

For anyone planning a trip or living in the city, the practical map is simple. From November through April the beaches are historically largely clear; that remains the most reliable window, though after 2026’s January start the monitoring network cautions that no winter month can be guaranteed. If you are traveling in the coming weeks, treat conditions as changeable: wind direction can move the rafts onshore or away within 48 hours, so check the monitoring network’s live map for your specific beach rather than relying on a general forecast.

Alternatives are unaffected. The cenotes, the ruins inland, and Cozumel’s sheltered west coast see no sargassum. Playa Norte on Isla Mujeres, facing northwest, is among the most reliably clear beaches near Cancún. And the downturn has a flip side for visitors: with occupancy at 30 percent, hotels have cut rates, so autumn stays are cheaper than the same rooms were a year ago. The Rio Times covered the broader season and the new-resort pipeline when it opened in our August report on Cancún and the Riviera Maya, and we track daily costs in our Playa del Carmen cost-of-living guide.

Sargassum is now a structural feature of Caribbean summers, not an anomaly — and Playa del Carmen is learning to manage it as one. The sand permit, the offshore collection, and the continued hotel building all point the same direction: a destination adjusting to a cycle it expects to meet again.

World.title: São Paulo ICMS Mafia: Prosecutors Charge Former No. 3 of State Finance Secretariat — What Changes Now
World.content:
Brazil · Justice

Key Facts — The charge. São Paulo state prosecutors formally charged four men on 18 September 2026 in the “ICMS mafia” tax-credit bribery case. — The names. André Weiss, the former No. 3 of the state finance secretariat; tax auditors Artur Gomes da Silva Neto and Kunio Shimada; and lawyer João André Buttini de Moraes. — The accusations. The case file combines active and passive corruption, money laundering and criminal organisation, in different combinations for each defendant. — The money. The reimbursement requests cited in the complaint exceed R$390 million (about US$76 million); prosecutors traced R$6.3 million (about US$1.2 million) paid in cash. — The dispute. Prosecutors say one charged auditor still works inside the tax authority. The secretariat says he has been suspended without pay since March. — The status. Three defendants are in preventive detention. Prosecutors asked the court to detain the fourth.

Thirteen months after the first raid, São Paulo’s tax-credit corruption investigation has reached the upper ranks of the state finance secretariat — and the formal charges now move from the prosecutors’ office to a judge.

The São Paulo State Court of Justice tower in the city centre. The complaint against the four defendants now goes before a state court specialised in tax crimes. (Photo: Fernanda Grillo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The São Paulo ICMS mafia case entered a new phase on Friday, 18 September 2026. The Ministério Público de São Paulo (MP-SP), the state prosecutor’s office, filed formal charges against four men accused of turning the release of state tax credits into a paid service for large retail companies.

At the top of the list is André Weiss, former head of the tax administration directorate at Sefaz-SP, the state finance secretariat. Brazilian outlets describe him as the former “number three” of the secretariat under Governor Tarcísio de Freitas. Prosecutors say he led the public side of the scheme.

Also charged are tax auditors Artur Gomes da Silva Neto and Kunio Shimada, and tax lawyer João André Buttini de Moraes. The complaint was presented by five prosecutors from GEDEC, the prosecutor’s specialised unit for economic crimes, according to the MP-SP statement.

The Charge and the Charged

The complaint assigns different crimes to different defendants. Weiss faces accusations of passive corruption and criminal organisation; Artur Gomes, of passive corruption; Shimada, of passive corruption and criminal organisation; and Buttini, of active corruption, money laundering and criminal organisation. The alleged conduct runs from 2021 to 2025.

According to the MP-SP’s statement, the group turned administrative acts tied to reimbursement requests for ICMS-ST into an illicit business. ICMS is the state sales tax on goods and services; ICMS-ST, or “substituição tributária”, is a mechanism in which tax is collected earlier in the supply chain, generating credits that companies later claim back.

Those refunds can take years under regular review. Prosecutors say the defendants charged companies a percentage of the credits they wanted released. They identified R$6.3 million (about US$1.2 million) paid in cash, plus invoices for services never rendered that allegedly hid part of the money. The reimbursement requests named in the complaint total more than R$390 million (about US$76 million).

The investigation that led to Weiss’s arrest found that Buttini passed about R$13.6 million (about US$2.6 million) in bribes between mid-2021 and August 2025, money prosecutors say was destined for Weiss. Around R$4.5 million (about US$874,000) was allegedly delivered in cash, in backpacks, at meetings in restaurants and other venues in Pinheiros, a west-side district of the state capital, SBT News reported, citing the MP-SP. The real traded at roughly 5.15 per US dollar on 18 September, mid-market rate.

The proceedings run before the 1st Court for Tax Crimes, Criminal Organisation and Money Laundering of the state capital, according to a statement from Shimada’s defence. The investigation grew out of criminal inquiry No. 18/2025 and drew on a plea-bargain agreement, searches, lifted bank and tax secrecy, phone data and ambient recordings, the MP-SP said.

Three of the four defendants are in preventive detention. Prosecutors asked the court to keep them there and to detain Shimada as well. The MP-SP stressed that the complaint is a formal accusation, not a verdict. A judge must still accept it. The defendants keep the presumption of innocence and the right to a full defence. Maurício Zanoide de Moraes, who represents Buttini, said the defence had not yet received the case files and respects the court-ordered secrecy. The other defences had not commented publicly by Friday afternoon, São Paulo time.

A Case Built in Three Operations

Friday’s charges crown a sequence of operations that has widened for over a year.

It began with Operação Ícaro in August 2025, which targeted fraud involving the pharmacy chain Ultrafarma and the electronics retailer Fast Shop. That phase brought preventive arrests of company executives. Investigators identified Artur Gomes da Silva Neto, then a state auditor, as the scheme’s architect. A bookkeeping firm called Smart Tax, registered in the name of his mother, issued more than R$1 billion (about US$194 million) in invoices that prosecutors say legitimised bribe money, Metrópoles reported.

In March 2026, Operação Fisco Paralelo served 22 search warrants in four cities. It arrested one fiscal agent and targeted auditors with unexplained wealth, including one whose home held a wine cellar valued above R$300,000 (about US$58,000) and gym equipment estimated at R$1 million (about US$194,000). Seizures in that phase included R$725,955 (about US$141,000) in cash. Messages recovered from phones treated bribes in code — words like “coffee” or “vitamins” — with values converted at the dollar exchange rate, G1 reported.

On 3 September, Operação Caldarium ordered the preventive detention of Weiss and Buttini, the phase The Rio Times covered when the São Paulo fraud actions first became public. Retailers Casas Bahia, Assaí and Dia appear in the reporting as companies whose credits benefited from the scheme; none of them is a criminal defendant in this complaint.

The corporate side carries its own bill. Fast Shop, which prosecutors say received R$936.4 million (about US$182 million) in advantages, agreed to pay a fine of R$1.04 billion (about US$202 million) — the largest penalty applied under Brazil’s Anticorruption Law in São Paulo state.

The Auditor Who May Still Be Inside

One detail in Friday’s filing is contested. Prosecutors say Kunio Shimada, a fiscal agent at a São Paulo regional tax office, continues to work in the same function he held during the alleged scheme. Inside the group, investigators say, he was known as “Chief K”. The complaint accuses him of receiving 10 percent of the bribes and of taking part in eight reimbursement requests for Ultrafarma totalling almost R$100 million (about US$19 million), Metrópoles reported.

Sefaz-SP disputes the premise. In a statement, the secretariat said Shimada has been removed from his post, without pay, since 26 March, with his system access blocked, and faces an administrative process that can end in dismissal. His lawyers add that a court ordered those measures in March and that he has complied fully. They call the new detention request unjustified. Which account describes his actual day-to-day status is, for now, a matter of competing claims.

The Institutional Response

The secretariat says the fallout has already changed the institution. Five employees have been dismissed, one exonerated and 23 suspended without pay. Forty-five auditors are under internal investigation by the tax oversight unit. Tax assessments tied to the case have constituted more than R$3 billion (about US$583 million) in credits, including fines and interest.

Sefaz-SP also says it has removed more than 62 percent of products from the substituição tributária regime — the mechanism at the heart of the fraud — and expanded the use of artificial intelligence in its audit filters. That simplifies taxation, but it also narrows the space in which the alleged scheme operated.

What It Means for Foreign Residents and Businesses

For expats and investors, this case is less about one secretariat than about how Brazil’s largest state economy polices itself. São Paulo collects more ICMS than any other state, and the reimbursement queue touches every retailer, importer and manufacturer operating there.

Companies that paid for speed now face assessments, fines and anti-corruption exposure. Companies that waited in line legally absorbed the cost of delay. The correction underway — dismissals, a record state fine, a simpler tax mechanism — points towards cleaner administration, but it will run for years, not weeks.

The longer arc matters too. Brazil’s 2023 tax reform will gradually fold ICMS into a dual value-added tax system, with the transition running to 2033, and is designed to shrink exactly this kind of credit bureaucracy. Cases like this one are part of why that reform gathered support.

What Is Not Known

The court has not yet accepted the complaint, and no trial date exists. Whether the judge has ruled on the fourth detention request was not confirmed by Friday evening. The full defences of Weiss, Artur Gomes and Buttini have not been presented publicly. And because the complaint draws on a plea-bargain agreement, further charges against other officials or companies remain possible. The MP-SP has not given a final total for the scheme’s damage.

The next milestone is procedural and unglamorous: a judge reading the files and deciding whether this becomes a criminal case. That is how accountability inside a tax authority actually advances — one accepted complaint at a time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was charged in the São Paulo ICMS mafia case on 18 September 2026? State prosecutors charged four men: André Weiss, former head of the tax administration directorate at the São Paulo finance secretariat; tax auditors Artur Gomes da Silva Neto and Kunio Shimada; and lawyer João André Buttini de Moraes. The case file combines active and passive corruption, money laundering and criminal organisation, in different combinations per defendant. What was the alleged scheme? Prosecutors say the group charged companies a percentage of the ICMS-ST tax credits they wanted released. They traced R$6.3 million (about US$1.2 million) in cash payments and false invoices, against reimbursement requests exceeding R$390 million (about US$76 million). Is one of the accused still working at the tax authority? That is disputed. Prosecutors say auditor Kunio Shimada remains active in his function. The finance secretariat says he has been suspended without pay since 26 March, and his defence says he has complied with all court-ordered restrictions since then. What happens next in court? A judge must decide whether to accept the complaint and turn it into a criminal case, and whether to order preventive detention for the fourth defendant. Three defendants are already detained. What does the case mean for companies operating in São Paulo? Companies named in the investigation face tax assessments and fines — more than R$3 billion (about US$583 million) in credits have already been constituted, and Fast Shop agreed to a R$1.04 billion (about US$202 million) fine, the largest under the Anticorruption Law in São Paulo state. The secretariat says it has removed 62 percent of products from the tax mechanism at the centre of the fraud.

Sources: SBT News on the formal charges and the MP-SP statement, Metrópoles on the auditor’s disputed status and the defence statements, G1 on Operação Fisco Paralelo, O Globo on the 18 September complaint, Agência Brasil on Operação Caldarium

World.title: Brazil IGP-M Inflation Rises 1.47% in Second September Preview — What It Means for Rents and Contracts
World.content:
BRAZIL · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The number The IGP-M index rose 1.47% in the second preview of September, the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) reported on 18 September 2026.

— The driver Producer prices (IPA), 60% of the index, swung from minus 0.50% in August’s second preview to plus 1.95%.

— The reversal The same reading in August showed a 0.36% decline, and August’s final IGP-M closed at minus 0.22%.

— The context FGV economist André Braz told Valor this was the largest rate since April, when it reached 2.64%.

— The forecast Braz said the preview points to a full-month September result close to 1.5% — a projection, not a final figure. The final number is due on 29 September.

Brazil’s most contract-sensitive inflation gauge has flipped from deflation to its strongest reading since April — a shift that reaches rental contracts, utility tariffs and the central bank’s rate-cut path.

Brazil IGP-M inflation is accelerating again. The General Market Price Index, compiled by the Brazilian Institute of Economics at the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV IBRE), rose 1.47% in the second preview of September, the foundation reported on Friday, 18 September 2026.

The reading marks a clear break with the recent past. In the equivalent August preview, the index fell 0.36%, and August’s final figure closed at minus 0.22%. Friday’s number is also well above the 0.93% recorded in the first September preview on 10 September, which The Rio Times covered when early September gauges first moved higher.

What the Data Show

The IGP-M blends three sub-indices. The IPA, which tracks producer prices and carries 60% of the final weight, jumped from minus 0.50% in August’s second preview to plus 1.95%. The IPC, the consumer-price component with a 30% weight, moved from minus 0.49% to plus 0.47%. Only construction costs cooled: the INCC, 10% of the index, slowed from 0.73% to 0.27%, according to figures released by FGV and reported by Valor and O Povo.

Previews compare like with like. The IGP-M collects prices between the 21st of one month and the 20th of the next, and FGV publishes intermediate readings — the previews — as that window progresses. The full-month figure follows on 29 September, according to FGV’s release calendar.

From Deflation to Acceleration

The swing is large, but it follows a volatile year rather than a straight line. The IGP-M rose 2.73% in April, slowed to 0.84% in May, then posted three negative months: minus 0.50% in June, minus 1.16% in July and minus 0.22% in August, according to FGV’s published series. After August, the index was up 1.85% in 2026 and 2.16% over twelve months — modest readings shaped by the mid-year deflation.

André Braz, the FGV economist who comments on the releases, told Valor that Friday’s result was driven by higher wholesale and retail prices and was the largest rate since April. He said the second preview points to a full-month September figure close to 1.5%. That is a forecast from FGV’s own economist, not a measured result; the final reading on 29 September can still move in either direction.

One external pressure is visible in the background. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, stayed above US$100 a barrel on Friday, Valor reported — feeding wholesale costs much as it did earlier in the month. What the preview does not yet show is how much of the 1.95% producer-price jump came from fuel, food or other items. FGV will publish that breakdown with the final September release.

Why This Index Reaches Further Than Markets

The IGP-M is not Brazil’s official inflation measure — that is the IPCA, calculated by the national statistics agency IBGE. But the IGP-M is written into everyday life. It is the traditional reference for annual rent adjustments in Brazilian lease contracts, and it indexes utility tariffs, school fees and many long-term business contracts, as FGV itself explains.

That is why a single preview matters beyond trading desks. When the IGP-M ran negative through mid-2026, tenants with IGP-M-linked leases saw smaller adjustments — some even faced nominal reductions. A sustained return above 1% a month would reverse that relief over the coming quarters. One preview does not set a trend, and landlords and tenants alike should wait for the final figures before drawing conclusions.

What It Means for Foreign Residents and Investors

For expats renting in Brazil, the practical point is the lease. If your contract uses the IGP-M as its adjustment index, the relevant number is the twelve-month accumulation on your contract’s anniversary date — currently near 2.16%, a historically mild level. A run of stronger monthly readings would push that accumulation up later in the year. Nothing changes today; the correct posture is to know which index your contract names.

For investors, the signal runs through monetary policy. The central bank’s Copom committee cut the Selic, Brazil’s benchmark interest rate, to 13.75% on Wednesday — the fifth consecutive quarter-point cut — hours before the US Federal Reserve moved in the opposite direction, as The Rio Times detailed in Friday’s morning call. Persistent wholesale-price pressure of the kind visible in Friday’s preview is the type of data that can slow an easing cycle, though one preview is not enough to change it.

Cycles turn in both directions. Brazil saw IGP-M deflation as recently as July, and a single strong preview after three negative months is a change of direction to watch — not yet a new regime. The final September reading on 29 September will show how much of Friday’s acceleration holds.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the IGP-M?

The IGP-M (General Market Price Index) is a monthly inflation gauge calculated by FGV IBRE. It combines producer prices (60% weight), consumer prices (30%) and construction costs (10%). It is widely used to adjust rental contracts, utility tariffs and long-term agreements in Brazil.

What did the second September preview show?

The IGP-M rose 1.47% in the second preview of September, released on 18 September 2026, after falling 0.36% in the same reading of August. Producer prices rose 1.95%, consumer prices 0.47%, and construction costs 0.27%. The final September figure is due on 29 September.

Does the IGP-M affect my rent in Brazil?

It can. Many Brazilian leases name the IGP-M as the index for annual rent adjustments. What matters for a tenant is the index’s twelve-month accumulation on the contract’s anniversary date, not a single monthly preview. After August, that twelve-month figure stood at 2.16%.

World.title: USA & Canada Intelligence Brief — Friday, September 18, 2026
World.content:
USA & Canada Intelligence Brief — Friday, September 18, 2026

The Federal Reserve’s Eccles building in Washington, under renovation. The day after the target range rose to between 3.75 and 4.00 per cent, the two-year government borrowing rate fell to 4.67 per cent and the ten-year to 4.94. Photo: G. Edward Johnson, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
