USA & Canada Intelligence Dossier — Friday, 18 September 2026 · Web edition Take it with you. The full dossier is published on the web and updated through the day. Read the web dossier → · Every edition on the dossier page →

United States — Assertive, and quietly disbelieved. Canada — Past anger, into arithmetic.

Washington spent this week issuing instructions, and the people downstream of them spent the week marking those instructions down. The Federal Reserve made money dearer on Wednesday, and by Thursday the lenders who set the real price of borrowing had decided the tightening would not hold.

That is the American temper this autumn, and it is not panic. It is an even-tempered scepticism, in which an announcement is received politely and then discounted by everyone who has to act on it.

The borrowing rates are the evidence. The two-year government rate fell from 4.74 to 4.67 per cent on 17 September and the ten-year from 5.01 to 4.94, on the day the rise took effect.

The same discount is applied inside the government itself. The White House signed a memorandum on Canadian goods with no completion date in it, and three federal judges handed down orders that carried dates.

Congress is half present and already campaigning. The Senate sat on Thursday and confirmed a judge, while the House of Representatives recorded no votes at all on either day.

Canada, for its part, has stopped arguing and started counting. It answered tariffs with tariffs through the summer, and in July its investors quietly sold a record volume of American shares.

Read across the Federal Reserve’s statement and projections, the Treasury’s daily record of government borrowing rates, and the Census Bureau. Then three Statistics Canada releases, the Bank of Canada, the White House, Canada’s finance department, the Senate’s roll-call pages, and Reuters, the Associated Press, Axios, NPR and TIME.

The full USA & Canada Intelligence Dossier is updated daily by the Rio Times Intelligence Desk. It carries the editor’s leader, the deep dive on where a trade war shows up in prices, the country health check and the people who matter. Open the dossier · Browse the archive

The Instruction That Lenders Priced Away

A central bank is obeyed or it is not, and the answer arrives in a day. The Federal Reserve raised its target range to between 3.75 and 4.00 per cent on 16 September, and the money markets spent 17 September moving the other way.

The United States Treasury’s daily curve put the two-year government borrowing rate at 4.67 per cent on 17 September, against 4.74 per cent the day before. The ten-year rate fell from 5.01 to 4.94 per cent and the thirty-year rate from 5.35 to 5.29 per cent.

Lenders for thirty years now ask for six hundredths of a percentage point less than they did on Wednesday. That is not fear of the decision but a quiet judgement that it will not have to be repeated often.

Shareholders took the same view and took it cheerfully. The Associated Press put the Standard and Poor’s 500 index at 7,637.76 at the close on 17 September, up 85.95 points or 1.1 per cent.

It put the Dow Jones industrial average at 51,778.04, up 316.14 points, and the Nasdaq composite at 26,418.30, up 439.87 points or 1.7 per cent. The Russell 2000 index of smaller American companies closed at 2,874.63, up 15.82 points, on the same figures.

The recovery was real but partial, and worth keeping in proportion. The Dow regained 316.14 of the 631.21 points it lost the day before, so Thursday took back about half of Wednesday.

The committee itself sounded anything but hesitant, and its statement of 16 September records that the decision carried by twelve votes to nothing. This desk read that tally on the Federal Reserve’s own page and did not read a list of the names behind it.

The statement says inflation “remains elevated” and that the rise will support “a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal”. Its projections table of the same date puts the median federal funds rate at 4.1 per cent for the end of 2026.

That table records eighteen participants, of whom twelve place the rate at 4.125 per cent for the end of this year, four at 4.375 per cent and two at 3.875 per cent. The midpoint of the new range is 3.875 per cent, so sixteen of the eighteen sit above it — this desk’s reading of the published table, not a Federal Reserve statement.

The week’s other American readings were mixed enough to justify the scepticism on both sides. The Census Bureau put August housing starts at an annual rate of 1,275,000, which it calls 2.6 per cent below July, give or take 12.0 per cent.

That margin is wider than the change it measures, so the Census Bureau’s own release cannot say whether starts rose or fell. Building permits ran at 1,394,000 a year, 2.7 per cent below July and 3.5 per cent above August 2025.

Completions are the firmer number and the more uncomfortable one, at an annual rate of 1,128,000, which the same release puts 27.1 per cent below August 2025. A country finishing far fewer homes than a year ago will feel it in rents before it feels it in prices.

Factories are still busy and paying more to stay that way. The Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia put its factory index at 37.8 for September, down from 47.4 in August and above a forecast of 30.5 that the outlet InvestingLive reported.

Its employment reading fell from 27.9 to 11.8 while its prices-paid reading rose from 40.9 to 48.6. Hiring is cooling while input costs are not, which is the shape of the argument the committee is having with itself.

The labour market gave the committee the better half of that argument. The United States Department of Labor put new claims for unemployment benefit at 196,000 in the week to 12 September, down from 206,000, with a four-week average of 203,250.

Reuters, in a report by Lucia Mutikani datelined Washington, gave the moving holiday as the likely reason for so sharp a fall. A single week around a public holiday is the least reliable week of any quarter.

Energy, which has done most of the damage to prices this year, eased a little. November Brent crude settled at US$104.82 a barrel on 17 September, down US$1.01 or 0.95 per cent, and October West Texas Intermediate settled at US$101.91.

The London bullion market’s afternoon price for gold was US$4,368.10 a troy ounce on the same day, and the dollar index closed at 100.25, flat on the day. A currency that stands still on a rate rise is another way of saying the rise was not believed.

Deadlines The Courts Set, And The One Washington Did Not

An instruction without a date is a threat rather than a decision, and the White House issued one of those this week. Three federal judges, working to no political timetable at all, issued orders that carried dates and consequences.

The presidential memorandum signed on 16 September is titled “Restoring Reciprocity in Government Procurement”. It directs officials to “identify and take all steps permitted by applicable law with respect to Canadian origin items…that can…be removed or made non-available for purchase”.

Its stated reason is that “Canada has unreasonably imposed new barriers to United States companies seeking to access the Canadian government procurement market”. The document names Canada and no other country, and puts the federal purchasing covered by the World Trade Organization’s procurement agreement at “over $280 billion annually”.

It sets no completion date, asking only that the Director of the Office of Management and Budget report progress “from time to time”, while the United States Trade Representative is told to “continue to monitor” Canadian practice. A lever kept in the hand is more useful to a negotiator than a lever pulled.

The one American date that is fixed is 29 September 2026, when import bans on a revised list of Canadian goods take effect. The White House fact sheet of 8 September sets that date and rests the measures on Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, at a rate of 50 per cent.

That same fact sheet records that rock salt and cement came off the list on 15 September and that all-terrain vehicles and further dairy products went on. A list still being edited eleven days before it bites is a negotiating instrument as much as a tariff schedule.

The courts were less provisional. Judge Emmet Sullivan of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia issued a twenty-page order on Wednesday 16 September warning the Attorney General of possible civil contempt, which Axios reported on 17 September.

The case concerns the release and redaction of files on Jeffrey Epstein under a transparency act passed in November 2025. The order says that courts have “the inherent power to enforce compliance with their lawful orders through civil contempt”, which applies where someone violates “an order that is clear and unambiguous”.

Sullivan called a contempt finding premature for now, on the same Axios account, which is a warning rather than a penalty. He required the Justice Department to justify its redaction of emails for private judicial review and to review foreign-language material for relevance.

He rejected the department’s position that such a review was “not practicable”, and held that handwritten notes by the Federal Bureau of Investigation may not be withheld merely because they resemble typewritten reports. The Attorney General named in that order is Todd Blanche, whom the Senate confirmed by 50 votes to 49 on 8 August 2026.

A department confirmed by one vote is now being asked by a judge to show its working. Judge Angel Kelley of the United States District Court in Boston struck down the Education Department’s policy on diversity grants on 17 September.

Reuters reported that the policy had cancelled over US$600 million across 109 grants, forty of them held by institutions in the eight states that brought the case. Kelley held it arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act, the American law that governs how federal agencies must make rules.

Reuters quotes her opinion saying the directive “does not acknowledge the fact that thousands of teachers, as well as teachers in teacher-training pipelines, would be affected, upending the careers of much-needed educators”. A policy struck down as arbitrary is an instruction that was never finished.

Judge Christopher Cooper, also of the District of Columbia court, ordered on 17 September that officials give thirty days’ written notice before any change to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Axios and PBS NewsHour both date that order to Thursday 17 September.

The order covers changes “including but not limited to any demolition” of the main building and requires sworn statements about the closure. The centre had closed to the public the day before, on Wednesday 16 September, for what its management called at least seven days of safety assessment.

The case was brought by Representative Joyce Beatty of Ohio, a trustee of the centre, and PBS NewsHour puts the repair money Congress has allocated at US$257 million. Thirty days is a small number, and this week it was the only firm one an American institution attached to anything.

Key Facts — What lenders did next. They did not believe it, and the ten-year borrowing rate fell to 4.94 per cent on 17 September from 5.01 per cent the day before. — The American share market. Confidence returned within a day, the Standard and Poor’s 500 closing at 7,637.76 on 17 September, up 1.1 per cent on Associated Press figures. — Canadian factories. They are absorbing the war before households feel it, with factory-gate prices up 13.5 per cent on the year in August against consumer prices at 3.0 per cent. — Canadian investors in July. They stopped arguing and started selling, unloading “an unprecedented $31.0 billion of US shares”, Statistics Canada reported on 17 September. — The education grants ruling. A judge set a limit the executive had not, striking down the Education Department’s grant policy on 17 September across over US$600 million and 109 grants. — The two retaliation figures. Neither capital counts the quarrel the same way: Washington says about US$20 billion of American exports, Ottawa says C$27.6 billion of American imports. — Congress this week. The Senate sat and confirmed a district judge by 49 votes to 45 on 17 September, while the House recorded no votes at all. — Brent crude on Thursday. The barrel eased without drama, settling at US$104.82 on 17 September, down 0.95 per cent, with October West Texas Intermediate at US$101.91.

Canada Stops Arguing And Starts Selling

Canada has been loud about this quarrel all summer and is now being quiet about it, which is the more serious phase. The argument is still on the books, but the country has begun settling the matter in its own accounts instead.

The argument first. Canada’s counter-tariffs took effect on 8 September at rates of 15, 25 and 50 per cent, matching the American rates they answer.

They cover steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics, across more than 600 product classifications on the law firm Blakes’ count. Alongside them Ottawa announced C$7.5 billion of new and enhanced support, on top of nearly C$25 billion already committed.

That money includes a C$2 billion Canada Strong Diversification Fund, C$3.5 billion of rapid response support for workers and employers, and a C$1.5 billion regional tariff response initiative. A government that budgets for a dispute has stopped expecting it to end soon.

The two capitals cannot even agree on the size of what they are doing to each other. The White House fact sheet of 8 September puts Canadian retaliatory tariffs at “about $20 billion of U.S. exports”, while Canada’s Department of Finance puts its own counter-tariffs at C$27.6 billion of American imports.

Canada’s figure is stated in Canadian dollars and Washington’s in American dollars, and neither document the desk read shows how it was calculated. Readers should carry both numbers rather than choose between them.

The cost of all this has arrived, and it has not arrived where voters would notice it. Statistics Canada reported on 17 September that its Industrial Product Price Index, or IPPI, which measures what Canadian factories charge at the gate, rose 1.3 per cent in August and 13.5 per cent over the year.

Its Raw Materials Price Index, which measures what those factories pay for inputs, rose 3.1 per cent in the month and 22.8 per cent over the year. Strip out energy and petroleum and the factory-gate index still rose 0.8 per cent in the month.

Strip crude energy out of the raw materials index and it still rose 1.1 per cent in the month and 17.2 per cent over the year. Canada’s consumer price index, by contrast, rose 3.0 per cent over the year to August, on the release Statistics Canada published on 14 September.

Producer prices are therefore rising more than four times as fast as the prices Canadians actually pay. The cost is inside the factory and has not finished walking to the till, which is a squeeze on margins today and a question for households later.

The agency is careful about how much of this it will pin on trade policy. Its release says that “Although the IPPI does not measure the direct effect of tariffs on prices, tariffs may indirectly influence prices measured in the IPPI”.

Metals did the most work, with unwrought gold, silver and platinum group metals and their alloys up 46.3 per cent over the year, the largest single contribution to the annual rise. Refined petroleum rose 4.6 per cent in the month, diesel 9.6 per cent and plastic resins 10.7 per cent.

Prices for crude energy products rose 7.1 per cent in the month, and the release ties that to “The unravelling of the ceasefire agreement between Iran and the United States”. A Canadian price index naming a Middle Eastern ceasefire is a fair measure of how long the thread now is.

Households are feeling the same energy signal, more slowly, with gasoline up 22.8 per cent over the year to August against 25.7 per cent to July. Shelter costs rose 1.5 per cent over the year on the same release, which is what holds the headline rate at 3.0 per cent.

The Bank of Canada left its policy interest rate at 2.25 per cent on 2 September and next decides on 28 October. A central bank facing 3.0 per cent consumer inflation and 13.5 per cent producer inflation is being asked two different questions at once.

Parliament Hill in Ottawa. Canadian factory-gate prices rose 13.5 per cent on the year in August against consumer prices at 3.0 per cent, and Canadian investors sold a record $31.0 billion of American shares in July, on Statistics Canada’s figures.

Then the quiet part, which is the part that matters. A third Statistics Canada release the same morning shows where Canadian savings went while the arguing was going on.

Its sentence reads: “In July, Canadian investors sold an unprecedented $31.0 billion of US shares, after investing $78.1 billion in the first half of 2026”. Those figures are given in dollars the release itself does not label, and Statistics Canada reports them for a Canadian readership.

Total Canadian holdings of foreign securities fell by $30.6 billion over the month. Money moved the other way at the same time, with foreign investors adding $20.7 billion of Canadian securities in July.

Federal government bonds took $22.7 billion of that while foreign investors reduced their Canadian money market holdings by $11.9 billion. The net inflow into the Canadian economy came to $51.3 billion in July on the same release.

Foreign purchases of Government of Canada bonds reached $104.0 billion in the first seven months of 2026, against $13.8 billion in the same period of 2025. The share of outstanding federal government bonds held from outside Canada rose from 40.2 per cent to 46.5 per cent over those seven months.

Canadians are selling American shares and the world is buying Canadian government debt. Selling is a colder thing than protesting, and it is harder to reverse with a speech.

A Prime Minister Shopping For A Second Market

A country that doubts its largest customer goes looking for others, and does it in person. Mark Carney spent two days of this week doing exactly that, in England on Wednesday and in France on Thursday.

He met the British Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the first time on Wednesday 16 September, at Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium in Liverpool. The Associated Press reported that the two men took that first meeting to a football match.

The Associated Press reported that they were expected to discuss “a Canadian-backed proposal to combine competing plans for an international defense bank that could help NATO allies finance increased military spending”. That came from a senior Canadian government official speaking on condition of anonymity, and the same report names “a potentially expanded Canadian role in the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force”.

The same report lists cooperation on drones, artificial intelligence, satellite communications, critical minerals and quantum technology among the expected subjects. A first meeting with a bank and a force on its agenda is not a courtesy call.

Carney went on to Strasbourg the next day and told the European Parliament on 17 September that Canada welcomes the offer Ursula von der Leyen had made to the same chamber on 16 September. The President of the European Commission had proposed that Canada become the European Union’s first associate member.

NPR reports Carney telling the chamber: “Canada and Europe are each strong. Europe and Canada are stronger together”. The same report carries his line that “This alliance is a positive process. That’s my response to the American president”.

His best-known lines ran consecutively: “We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals”, in NPR’s report of the speech. The claim is that Canada stands with Europe in bad weather as well as good, which is the argument compressed into nine words.

TIME also quotes him saying that “Economic integration is now being weaponized, tariffs being used to exert pressure”. On the same TIME account he said he is not proposing a third bloc “in order to become a ‘great power’ rival, only with better manners”.

NPR reports Carney adding that “A stronger, more resilient Canada would be a more effective partner for the United States”. That is an argument addressed to Washington from a chamber in Washington’s absence.

Washington had already answered, and in the register of the week. Donald Trump had responded to the proposal on Wednesday 16 September, the same day Carney was in Liverpool, speaking to reporters on his way to an event in North Carolina.

TIME quotes him saying: “If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things”. He had also called the proposal laughable, on the same TIME account.

Europe was unimpressed by the warning rather than alarmed by it. The French member of the European Parliament Nathalie Loiseau answered that “Democracy is under attack, the geopolitical order is ruined, so we have to team up”, in NPR’s report.

For all the warmth, the offer remains a sentiment rather than an instrument. What associate membership would mean in law has not been set out by any document this desk could open, and NPR reports only that the details still need to be worked out.

Carney also intends to press European states that have not ratified the existing free-trade agreement, on the same NPR account. A second market takes years to build, and the first one closes on 29 September.

One Chamber Sits, The Other Is Away

A legislature that half attends is telling you where its attention has gone. The Senate worked on Thursday and the House of Representatives did not, with the midterm elections of 3 November now the organising fact of the American autumn.

The Senate held three recorded votes on 17 September, read here from the roll-call pages the Senate publishes for each one. Two concerned a single judgeship and the third concerned college sport.

At noon the Senate agreed to take up the Protect College Sports Act by 77 votes to 22, with one senator not voting. The bill is sponsored by Senator Ted Cruz of Texas and Senator Maria Cantwell of Washington, and would set national rules for paying college athletes.

At 12.54 in the afternoon senators voted 49 to 47 to close debate on the nomination of Kasdin Miller Mitchell to a federal district judgeship in northern Texas. At 1.59 they confirmed her by 49 votes to 45, with six senators not voting.

A judge confirmed by four votes on a Thursday afternoon is the quiet half of a week in which three judges ruled against the administration. Both halves are how a federal judiciary gets made and used at the same time.

The college sports bill divided the chamber along lines that were not only partisan. The Deseret News reports that all four Black Democratic senators voted against advancing it, and quotes Senator Cory Booker saying it “jeopardizes college athletes’ health and safety”.

The other chamber was simply not there. The House of Representatives recorded no votes at all on 17 or 18 September, on the Clerk of the House’s own listing.

Its last recorded votes were seven, on 16 September, covering a water resources bill, a ratepayer protection bill and an environmental rule disapproval among others. The Senate itself met only for a formal session at nine in the morning on Friday 18 September, with no votes scheduled.

None of this carries the risk it would in most Septembers, which is the steadying detail in an otherwise thin week. The House passed the Senate’s continuing appropriations measure by 370 votes to 48 on 1 September, funding the government to 11 December 2026.

So the fiscal year ends on 30 September without a funding cliff behind it. A Congress that has already paid for the winter can afford to spend the autumn campaigning.

What This Means From Latin America

Brazil’s benchmark interest rate, known as the Selic, fell to 13.75 per cent with effect from 17 September. The United States raised into the same week, so the gap between borrowing at home and borrowing in dollars narrowed from the Brazilian side and widened from the American one.

What Canada offers this region today is less a policy than a warning about sequence. Producer prices at 13.5 per cent against consumer prices at 3.0 per cent describe a cost firms have paid and households have not, a position familiar across this region.

November Brent at US$104.82 a barrel is the freight cost that moves Brazilian soy, Chilean fruit and Peruvian copper northwards. Statistics Canada’s attribution of August’s crude rise to the Iran ceasefire is a reminder that the price of a Latin American harvest is partly set in the Gulf.

The disagreement between Washington’s US$20 billion and Ottawa’s C$27.6 billion is a small lesson in reading trade statistics. Two governments measuring the same dispute will report it in their own currency, on their own basis, and neither will show the working.

Foreign ownership of Canadian federal government bonds rose from 40.2 to 46.5 per cent in seven months while Canadians sold American shares. Capital looking for somewhere that is neither Washington nor its quarrel is a flow that reaches this region too.

What We Are Watching

The American import bans of 29 September — the White House fact sheet of 8 September bars a revised list of Canadian goods from that date. The measures rest on Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, at 50 per cent. It is the first hard date in the dispute, and it falls eleven days from today.

— the White House fact sheet of 8 September bars a revised list of Canadian goods from that date. The measures rest on Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, at 50 per cent. It is the first hard date in the dispute, and it falls eleven days from today. The United Nations General Assembly high-level week — the United Nations lists the week as 18 to 28 September. The general debate runs from 22 to 28 September, with a climate meeting on 23 September. Several of this dispute’s participants will be in the same building.

— the United Nations lists the week as 18 to 28 September. The general debate runs from 22 to 28 September, with a climate meeting on 23 September. Several of this dispute’s participants will be in the same building. American personal income and outlays for August — the Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes it on 30 September, alongside the third estimate of second-quarter output. It carries the inflation measure the Federal Reserve prefers. It is the first such reading since the rise.

— the Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes it on 30 September, alongside the third estimate of second-quarter output. It carries the inflation measure the Federal Reserve prefers. It is the first such reading since the rise. The Canadian House of Commons sitting week — the chamber’s own calendar lists sitting days from 21 to 25 September. It is the first chance to ask ministers in public what Canada intends to do about 29 September.

— the chamber’s own calendar lists sitting days from 21 to 25 September. It is the first chance to ask ministers in public what Canada intends to do about 29 September. The Bank of Canada decision of 28 October — Governing Council held the policy interest rate at 2.25 per cent on 2 September and publishes a Monetary Policy Report with the next decision. It must weigh consumer inflation at 3.0 per cent against producer inflation at 13.5 per cent.

— Governing Council held the policy interest rate at 2.25 per cent on 2 September and publishes a Monetary Policy Report with the next decision. It must weigh consumer inflation at 3.0 per cent against producer inflation at 13.5 per cent. The Federal Reserve meeting of 27 and 28 October — the committee’s own calendar lists those dates, with no new projections until the meeting of 8 and 9 December. Sixteen of eighteen participants placed the rate above the current midpoint in the September table.

— the committee’s own calendar lists those dates, with no new projections until the meeting of 8 and 9 December. Sixteen of eighteen participants placed the rate above the current midpoint in the September table. The next American consumer price reading — the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes September’s index on 14 October. August’s reading put the headline rate at 3.4 per cent over the year with energy up 16.3 per cent.

Go deeper in the paid web dossier. It carries the deep dive on where a trade war shows up in prices and three ways the next six months can run. It also carries a health check of the continent, the North American calendar and today’s verification notes.

More from the Rio Times Intelligence Desk on 18 September 2026: Africa · Asia · Europe. For how these stories developed, see the USA & Canada Intelligence Brief for 17 September and 16 September.

North American politics and trade policy and their bearing on this hemisphere run through our pillar coverage of The United States & Canada. That section carries the daily record behind this brief.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Federal Reserve do, and how did lenders and shareholders answer?

It raised its target range for the federal funds rate to between 3.75 and 4.00 per cent on 16 September 2026, and the rise took effect on 17 September. The Federal Reserve’s own statement records that the decision carried by twelve votes to nothing. This desk read that tally on the Federal Reserve’s page, and did not read a list of the names behind it. The statement says inflation “remains elevated” and that the increase will support “a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal”. Borrowing costs then fell. The United States Treasury’s daily curve put the two-year government borrowing rate at 4.67 per cent on 17 September, against 4.74 per cent the day before. The ten-year rate fell from 5.01 to 4.94 per cent. The thirty-year rate fell from 5.35 to 5.29 per cent. The Associated Press put the Standard and Poor’s 500 index at 7,637.76 at the close on 17 September, up 85.95 points or 1.1 per cent. It put the Dow Jones industrial average at 51,778.04, up 316.14 points. It put the Nasdaq composite at 26,418.30, up 439.87 points or 1.7 per cent, and the Russell 2000 at 2,874.63, up 15.82 points. The Federal Reserve’s projections table of 16 September puts the median federal funds rate at 4.1 per cent for the end of 2026. It records eighteen participants, of whom twelve place the rate at 4.125 per cent, four at 4.375 per cent and two at 3.875 per cent. The midpoint of the range set that day is 3.875 per cent, so sixteen of the eighteen sit above it; that arithmetic is this desk’s reading of the published distribution and not a statement by the Federal Reserve.

Why are Canadian producer prices rising so much faster than Canadian consumer prices?

Because a tariff war reaches a factory before it reaches a shop. Statistics Canada reported on 17 September on its Industrial Product Price Index, the measure of what Canadian factories charge at the gate. It rose 1.3 per cent in August and 13.5 per cent over the year. Its Raw Materials Price Index, the measure of what those factories pay for inputs, rose 3.1 per cent in the month and 22.8 per cent over the year. Excluding energy and petroleum, the factory-gate index still rose 0.8 per cent in the month. Excluding crude energy, the raw materials index still rose 1.1 per cent in the month and 17.2 per cent over the year. Canadian consumer prices rose 3.0 per cent over the year to August, on the release of 14 September. Statistics Canada is careful about attribution and says that “Although the IPPI does not measure the direct effect of tariffs on prices, tariffs may indirectly influence prices measured in the IPPI”. Energy is the other driver. Prices for crude energy products rose 7.1 per cent in the month, and the release ties that to “The unravelling of the ceasefire agreement between Iran and the United States”. Unwrought gold, silver and platinum group metals and their alloys rose 46.3 per cent over the year, the largest single contribution to the yearly rise. Refined petroleum rose 4.6 per cent in the month, diesel 9.6 per cent and plastic resins 10.7 per cent. For a household the practical reading is that the cost is already inside the system and has not yet finished moving. For the Bank of Canada, which held its policy interest rate at 2.25 per cent on 2 September and decides again on 28 October, it is two questions at once.

What did the three American court rulings decide this week?

They went against the executive branch on three unrelated matters. Judge Emmet Sullivan of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia issued a twenty-page order on 16 September. It warned Attorney General Todd Blanche of possible civil contempt over files on Jeffrey Epstein, and Axios reported it on 17 September. The order says courts have “the inherent power to enforce compliance with their lawful orders through civil contempt”. That applies where someone violates “an order that is clear and unambiguous”, and Sullivan called a contempt finding premature for now. He required the Justice Department to justify email redactions for private judicial review. He told it to review foreign-language material rather than call it “not practicable”, and not to withhold handwritten notes by the Federal Bureau of Investigation merely because they resemble typewritten ones. Blanche was confirmed Attorney General by 50 votes to 49 on 8 August 2026. Judge Angel Kelley of the United States District Court in Boston struck down the Education Department’s policy on diversity grants on 17 September, in a case brought by eight states. Reuters reported that the policy had cancelled over US$600 million across 109 grants, forty of them in the plaintiff states. Kelley held it arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act. Judge Christopher Cooper ordered on 17 September that officials give thirty days’ written notice before changes “including but not limited to any demolition” of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. The case was brought by Representative Joyce Beatty of Ohio, a trustee of the centre. The centre had closed to the public the day before, on Wednesday 16 September, for what management called at least seven days of safety assessment, and PBS NewsHour puts the repair money Congress has allocated at US$257 million.

What changes for Canada’s trade with the United States on 29 September?

American import bans on a revised list of Canadian goods take effect that day. The White House fact sheet of 8 September sets the date and rests the measures on Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, at a rate of 50 per cent. It records that rock salt and cement came off the list on 15 September, while all-terrain vehicles and further dairy products went on. A separate presidential memorandum of 16 September is titled “Restoring Reciprocity in Government Procurement”. It directs officials to “identify and take all steps permitted by applicable law with respect to Canadian origin items…that can…be removed or made non-available for purchase”. Its stated ground is that “Canada has unreasonably imposed new barriers to United States companies seeking to access the Canadian government procurement market”. That memorandum names Canada and no other country. It puts the federal purchasing covered by the World Trade Organization’s procurement agreement at “over $280 billion annually”, and sets no completion date. The two governments describe the retaliation differently. The White House fact sheet of 8 September puts Canadian retaliatory tariffs at “about $20 billion of U.S. exports”. Canada’s Department of Finance puts its own counter-tariffs at C$27.6 billion of American imports, and neither document the desk read shows how its figure was reached. Canada’s counter-tariffs took effect on 8 September at 15, 25 and 50 per cent. They cover steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics, across more than 600 product classifications on the law firm Blakes’ count. Ottawa paired them with C$7.5 billion of new and enhanced support, on top of nearly C$25 billion already committed. That includes a C$2 billion Canada Strong Diversification Fund, C$3.5 billion of rapid response support for workers and employers, and a C$1.5 billion regional tariff response initiative. Where we do not know, we say so, and we correct in the open when we are wrong.

Sources: Federal Reserve, United States Department of the Treasury, United States Census Bureau, United States Bureau of Labor Statistics, Bureau of Economic Analysis. Also Statistics Canada, Bank of Canada, Department of Finance Canada, House of Commons of Canada. Then The White House, United States Senate, Clerk of the House of Representatives, United Nations. And Reuters, Associated Press, Axios, NPR, TIME, PBS NewsHour, Deseret News, Blakes. Reporting window 14–18 September 2026.

World.title: Rencontres de la Photographie Marrakech Opens in Morocco on 7 October 2026
World.content:
MOROCCO · ART

Key Facts — The dates The festival runs from Wednesday 7 to Saturday 10 October 2026.

— The venue It is held at Meydene, on M Avenue in the Guéliz district of Marrakech.

— The edition This is the sixth edition. The festival has existed since 2016.

— The theme The 2026 theme is Deux siècles de lumière, or Two Centuries of Light.

— Who runs it Voix Plurielles of Casablanca and Cultures Nomades Production of Arles organise it.

The Rencontres de la Photographie Marrakech marks photography’s bicentenary. It runs for four days in Guéliz.

Guéliz in Marrakech. The Rencontres de la Photographie is held at Meydene on M Avenue from 7 to 10 October 2026.

What Is Confirmed

The Rencontres de la Photographie Marrakech runs in Morocco from Wednesday 7 to Saturday 10 October 2026. It is the sixth edition.

The venue is Meydene, on M Avenue in Guéliz, the modern district west of the medina.

The theme is Deux siècles de lumière, or Two Centuries of Light, marking two hundred years of photography.

Voix Plurielles, based in Casablanca, and Cultures Nomades Production, based in Arles, organise the festival together.

How the Programme Is Built

The festival runs on exhibitions, screenings, conferences, workshops and professional meetings. It is a working festival rather than a gallery show.

An international call for projects selects part of the programme. Entrants submit documentary, conceptual, intimate or committed work in which light plays a central role.

Twenty laureates each show five works at the Galerie Triptyque in Arles and produce a three-minute video screened in Marrakech.

Thirty finalists receive a two-minute projection and have their full series published on the festival platform.

The Arles connection runs through the whole structure. The Marrakech festival is tied to the French photography circuit rather than standing apart from it.

Where It Sits in Moroccan Culture

Marrakech carries several international festivals, and most of them are built around film or music. A photography festival at this scale is less usual.

The programme has a consistent southward and eastward focus. Previous editions have paired Moroccan photographers with Chinese, African and Mediterranean work.

Guéliz rather than the medina is the deliberate setting. The district is where the city’s contemporary galleries and cultural venues sit.

A bicentenary theme also gives the edition a wider frame than a national one. Two hundred years of photography is a subject no single country owns.

The festival has run since 2016 and positions itself as a platform for contemporary creation rather than a heritage exhibition.

Ten years is long enough for a festival to build a circuit of its own. The Arles partnership is what gives this one reach beyond Morocco.

Marrakech also carries a large seasonal visitor population in October. A festival in that month reaches an audience that is only partly local.

That mix is visible in the programming. Moroccan photographers are shown alongside international work rather than in a national section.

What It Means If You Live in Morocco

For foreign residents in Marrakech, four days of exhibitions and talks in one building is an unusually concentrated cultural programme.

Guéliz is walkable and served by the city’s main avenues. Meydene sits on M Avenue rather than deep in the medina, so access is straightforward.

Early October in Marrakech is warm rather than hot. It is among the better months for spending a day moving between indoor and outdoor spaces.

The professional meetings are aimed at photographers and curators rather than the general public. The exhibitions and screenings are the accessible half.

Four days is also short for a festival of this kind. Anyone intending to see the whole programme should treat it as a full weekend rather than an afternoon.

For anyone working in images in Morocco, the call for projects is the more useful part of the festival than the visit itself.

What Is Not Published

Entry prices, or whether entry is free, had not been published at the time of writing.

Daily opening hours were also unstated, as was the schedule of talks and screenings.

The full list of exhibiting photographers had not been consolidated in one public place.

The dates, the venue, the theme and the organisers are confirmed, and the call for projects is the part with published mechanics.

Whether the festival keeps its October slot in later years is also unsettled. Earlier editions ran in late October rather than at the start of the month.

For visitors planning around it, the four dates are firm and everything built on top of them arrives closer to the week.

The Arles side of the programme runs on its own calendar in July, before the Marrakech dates. The two halves are announced separately.

Anyone submitting work should therefore watch the call for projects rather than the festival dates. The submission deadline is the date that matters for photographers.

World.title: Dakar 2026 Olympic Flame Spends Two Weeks in Senegal’s Capital Until 27 September
World.content:
SENEGAL · SPORT

Key Facts — Where it is The flame is in the Dakar region from 14 to 27 September 2026.

— Where it started The national tour began at Dakar Plateau on 14 September.

— What follows From 29 September to 24 October it visits the country’s 13 other regions.

— Where it ends The relay finishes at the Place de la Nation in Dakar on 30 October.

— The Games The Youth Olympic Games run from 31 October to 13 November across Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly.

The Dakar 2026 Olympic flame is touring Senegal before Africa’s first Olympic event. It is in the capital now.

The steps of the African Renaissance Monument in Dakar. The Youth Olympic flame is in the capital until 27 September 2026.

What Is Confirmed

The Olympic flame for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games is touring Senegal. It is in the Dakar region from 14 to 27 September 2026.

The national tour began at Dakar Plateau on 14 September. The capital therefore gets a full fortnight before the flame leaves.

From 29 September the flame visits the country’s 13 other regions in sequence. They are Thiès, Louga, Saint-Louis, Matam, Diourbel, Fatick, Kaolack, Kaffrine, Tambacounda, Kédougou, Kolda, Sédhiou and Ziguinchor, with stops at Saly and Rufisque.

That leg runs to 24 October. The relay ends at the Place de la Nation in Dakar on 30 October, the day before the Games open.

What the Games Are

The Youth Olympic Games run from 31 October to 13 November 2026. They are the first Olympic event of any kind held in Africa.

About 2,700 athletes are expected, competing in 153 events across 25 sports. The competitors are teenagers rather than senior international athletes.

Three zones host the Games: Dakar itself, the new city of Diamniadio inland, and the coastal resort area of Saly. The opening ceremony is at the Diamniadio Olympic Stadium.

The mascot is Ayo, unveiled at the Grand Théâtre National de Dakar in October 2025. The name means joy in Yoruba.

Senegal was awarded the Games in 2018, and the edition was postponed from 2022. The long run-up is part of why the flame tour is being given a full six weeks.

Why the Relay Is Taking This Long

Six weeks and fourteen regions is an unusually thorough route for a Youth Olympic flame. The intent is to reach the whole country rather than the host city.

Senegal’s population is concentrated on the coast, and the eastern and southern regions rarely host national events. Kédougou and Sédhiou are on the route for that reason.

The flame was lit in Athens earlier in September before travelling to Senegal. That is the standard Olympic sequence.

Relay stages are public occasions rather than ticketed events. They are built around local ceremonies, music and school participation.

Local authorities have been formally asked to prepare receptions for the flame. The tour is as much a civic programme as a sporting one.

What It Means If You Live in Senegal

For residents of the Dakar region, the flame is nearby until 27 September. After that it is a matter of travelling to meet it.

Day-by-day stages within each region are published by the organisers rather than fixed months in advance. The official flame tour pages carry the current schedule.

Relay days bring road closures and crowds in the communes they pass through. That is the practical cost of a stage arriving locally.

For foreign residents, this is the visible part of a two-year build-up that has otherwise been mostly construction and logistics.

The Games themselves will be the larger disruption and the larger opportunity. The flame tour is the announcement that they are close.

Hotel capacity in Dakar and Saly is the constraint most residents will notice first. Two weeks of competition in November will absorb a great deal of it.

What Is Not Fixed

The day-by-day list of communes within the Dakar region changes as the tour runs, and the organisers publish it stage by stage.

Timings for individual stages are also local decisions rather than a single national schedule.

Attendance figures for the relay have not been published, and no organiser estimate exists.

The dates that matter are settled. The Dakar region until 27 September, the regions from 29 September to 24 October, and the Place de la Nation on 30 October.

Ticketing and access arrangements for the Games themselves are a separate matter and were not part of the relay announcements.

For now the flame is the only part of Dakar 2026 that most Senegalese can stand next to. That is the point of sending it to all fourteen regions.

Competition venues and the athlete programme are published separately by the organising committee. The relay is a distinct exercise with its own schedule.

What is fixed is the frame around it. A fortnight in the capital, four weeks in the regions, and a finish in Dakar the day before the Games open.

When are the Games themselves?

From 31 October to 13 November 2026, across Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly. The opening ceremony is at the Diamniadio Olympic Stadium.

How big are the Youth Olympic Games?

World.title: Jazz à Rabat Runs Three Nights in Morocco from 24 September 2026
World.content:
MOROCCO · MUSIC

Key Facts — The dates The festival runs on 24, 25 and 26 September 2026.

— The venue It is held at the amphitheatre of the Parc Hassan II, on Avenue Mohammed VI in Rabat.

— The format Each evening pairs a European ensemble with a Moroccan act, then puts them on stage together.

— Timing Music starts at 7.30 p.m. and the evenings run to around midnight.

— Tickets Entry is listed at MAD 80, roughly US$8 at the rate published on 18 September 2026.

Jazz à Rabat pairs European and Moroccan musicians and then makes them play together. This is the 28th edition.

The Parc Hassan II in Rabat. Its amphitheatre hosts Jazz à Rabat from 24 to 26 September 2026.

What Is Confirmed

Jazz à Rabat runs in Rabat, Morocco on 24, 25 and 26 September 2026. It is the 28th edition of a festival created and supported by the European Union delegation in the country.

The venue is the amphitheatre of the Parc Hassan II, on Avenue Mohammed VI. Music starts at 7.30 p.m. and the evenings run to around midnight.

Six European ensembles are paired with six Moroccan acts, one pairing after another, with a joint set closing each evening.

Entry is listed at MAD 80. At 9.49 dirhams to the dollar, published by open.er-api.com on 18 September 2026, that is about US$8.

The Programme Night by Night

Thursday 24 September opens with the Portuguese Amara Quartet at 7.30 p.m., joined at 8.10 p.m. by the Moroccan percussionist Khalid Kouhen.

The French and German duo Thérapie de Couple follows at 8.50 p.m., then the Moroccan Mohamed El Menjra STVNK Quintet at 9.20 p.m. Both groups play together at 9.50 p.m.

Friday 25 September opens with the Herak and Bulatkin Quartet, working from Balkan traditions, then Hicham Telmoudi joins them. The Belgian group NØ Steam and the Sara Moullablad Quartet follow and close the night together.

Saturday 26 September opens with the Austrian Azure Trio led by Ulrich Drechsler, with the Moroccan Tamzaj Quartet of Younès Fakhar. The Spanish Antonio Lizana Quintet and the Abir El Abed Sextet close the festival.

The pattern is the same every night. Two sets, two collaborations, and a final piece nobody has played before.

Why This Festival Is Unusual

The festival used to be called Jazz au Chellah and was held in the Roman and Islamic ruins of Chellah. It moved to the Parc Hassan II and took a new name.

That change put the festival in the middle of the city rather than at an archaeological site outside it. The audience it reaches is different as a result.

The pairing format is the older tradition and it survived the move. Musicians meet, rehearse and then improvise together for one night.

The European Union delegation runs it with Morocco’s culture ministry and the Rabat-Salé-Kénitra regional authority. It is cultural diplomacy with a house band.

Twenty-eight editions is a long run for any festival. It has outlasted most of the European cultural programmes that started alongside it.

What It Means If You Live in Morocco

At about US$8 an evening, this is among the cheapest live music of its quality anywhere in the country.

The Parc Hassan II is central and walkable from much of Rabat. An outdoor amphitheatre in late September is comfortable rather than cold.

A 7.30 p.m. start and a midnight finish is a full evening. Anyone travelling from Casablanca should check the last train rather than assume one.

For foreign residents, the collaborations are the reason to go rather than the headline names. The joint sets do not exist outside this festival.

Rabat’s cultural calendar is thinner than Casablanca’s or Marrakech’s. An event of this length and price is a fixed point in it.

What Is Not Published

Reduced rates were not detailed in the listings seen at the time of writing, though the seller lists a single MAD 80 entry.

Capacity at the amphitheatre was not stated either. The programme is fixed; the room’s limit is not published.

Whether tickets are sold per evening or as a pass is also unclear from the listing.

The programme itself is unusually complete. Six European groups, six Moroccan acts and a timed running order are all published in advance.

That completeness is the useful part for anyone planning a single evening. The running order tells you exactly which collaboration falls on which night.

Weather is the remaining variable at an open-air venue. Late September in Rabat is mild, and rain at that time of year is uncommon rather than impossible.

Whether the pairings are recorded or broadcast has not been said. Previous editions have circulated mostly through audience recordings rather than official releases.

For a festival built on one-off collaborations, that is a real loss. The joint sets exist for one night and then stop existing.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is Jazz à Rabat 2026?

On 24, 25 and 26 September 2026 at the amphitheatre of the Parc Hassan II, Avenue Mohammed VI, Rabat. Music starts at 7.30 p.m.

How much does it cost?

Entry is listed at MAD 80, roughly US$8 at the rate published by open.er-api.com on 18 September 2026.

Who is playing?

Six European ensembles paired with six Moroccan acts, including Amara Quartet with Khalid Kouhen, NØ Steam with the Sara Moullablad Quartet, and Antonio Lizana Quintet with the Abir El Abed Sextet.

Why is it no longer called Jazz au Chellah?

The festival moved from the Chellah site to the Parc Hassan II in the centre of Rabat and was renamed. The pairing format carried over unchanged.

World.title: Magical Kenya Travel Expo Draws 10,000 Delegates to Nairobi, Kenya on 6 October 2026
World.content:
KENYA · TOURISM

Key Facts — The dates The expo runs from Tuesday 6 to Thursday 8 October 2026.

— The venue It is held at the Uhuru Gardens National Monument and Museum in Nairobi.

— The scale Organisers expect more than 10,000 delegates from 40 countries, up 30% on 2025.

— Who exhibits More than 400 exhibitors and over 250 international buyers are booked.

— The theme This edition is themed on digital transformation and artificial intelligence in tourism.

The Magical Kenya Travel Expo is the country’s main tourism trade fair. The 2026 edition is its largest so far.

Uhuru Gardens in Nairobi, the venue for the Magical Kenya Travel Expo from 6 to 8 October 2026.

What Is Confirmed

The Magical Kenya Travel Expo runs in Nairobi, Kenya from Tuesday 6 to Thursday 8 October 2026. It is the sixteenth edition.

The venue is the Uhuru Gardens National Monument and Museum, on the western side of the city. The Kenya Tourism Board organises the event.

Organisers expect more than 10,000 delegates from 40 countries. That is roughly 30% above the 7,691 who attended in 2025.

More than 400 exhibitors and over 250 international buyers are booked. The theme is digital transformation and artificial intelligence in tourism.

What the Expo Actually Does

This is a trade fair rather than a consumer show. Its business is putting Kenyan operators in front of buyers who sell holidays in other markets.

The hosted buyer programme is the mechanism. Buyers are selected and brought in, and their meetings with exhibitors are scheduled in advance.

June Chepkemei, the Kenya Tourism Board chief executive, has set out the approach plainly. Every element of the programme, from buyer selection to the seminar agenda, is informed by data and demand intelligence.

That framing is the point of the event. It exists to convert interest into contracted bookings rather than to entertain visitors.

The seminar programme runs alongside the meetings. It is where the theme gets discussed rather than where the business is done.

Uhuru Gardens is a recent choice of venue for the expo. The site was redeveloped as a national monument and museum and now takes large events.

That is a change from the conference-centre settings the expo used before. An open site gives more room for exhibitor stands than a hall does.

The Numbers Behind It

Kenya’s stated goal is five million international visitors by the end of 2027. The expo is one of the instruments for reaching it.

Duncan Muriuki, who chairs the Kenya MICE Association, has described business events as the next frontier for tourism revenue. The argument is about value per visitor rather than visitor count.

Raymond Cheruiyot of the Tour Operators Society of Kenya has called the expo a platform to build partnerships and position the country on the global tourism map.

Those are industry voices making an industry case. The delegate figures are organiser projections rather than audited attendance.

The 30% growth claim rests on comparing a projection for 2026 with a recorded figure for 2025. That is worth noting before repeating it.

What It Means If You Live in Kenya

For foreign residents working in tourism, hospitality or logistics, this is the week the sector’s decision makers are in one place.

Uhuru Gardens sits on Lang’ata Road, between the city centre and the national park. Traffic on that corridor is heavy during business hours.

Registration runs through separate tracks for trade visitors, exhibitors, buyers and media. General visitors are also listed, though the programme is built around trade.

Anyone attending for business should register through the correct track rather than arrive on the day. The meeting schedule is set in advance.

For residents outside the industry, the practical effect is three days of increased hotel occupancy and a busier Lang’ata Road.

What Is Not Published

Entry costs for each registration track were not published on the organiser’s homepage at the time of writing.

Nor was a clear split between trade-only hours and any public access. The programme lists general visitors without defining when they can attend.

Daily opening times are also unstated. The dates are firm; the hours are not.

The delegate and exhibitor figures remain projections until the event runs. They are the organiser’s numbers, not a count.

The 2025 figure of 7,691 delegates is a recorded one, which makes it the more useful benchmark. What matters in October is how close the event comes to it.

None of that changes the dates or the venue, which are confirmed. It changes how much weight to put on the headline number.

Tourism arrival figures for Kenya are published separately by the ministry and the board. Those are the numbers against which the five million target will be judged.

An expo cannot deliver that target on its own. It can make the contracts that feed into it, which is a narrower and more testable claim.

Can the public attend?

The programme is built around trade visitors, hosted buyers, exhibitors and media, with general visitors also listed. Public access hours had not been published at the time of writing.

World.title: British Airways Makes Costa Rica a Year-Round London Route
World.content:
If you have ever tried to book a direct flight between Costa Rica and the United Kingdom in June, you already know the problem. The route has only existed in the European winter, which meant anyone travelling outside the high season connected through Madrid, Miami, Panama City or Atlanta and added most of a day to the trip.

That changes in October as British Airways confirmed today that it will keep its London–San José service running all year, with flights scheduled continuously through September 2027. The route also moves from London Gatwick to London Heathrow, the airline’s main base.

Frequencies split by season so between October 2026 and March 2027 the airline will fly five times a week, up from three. Between April and September 2027, when demand from Europe softens, the schedule drops back to three flights a week — but it no longer stops.

For the winter schedule, the flight leaves Heathrow at 11:10 a.m. and lands at Juan Santamaría International Airport at 4:40 p.m. The return departs San José at 6:40 p.m. and reaches Heathrow at 10:50 a.m. the following morning. The crossing takes roughly 11 hours in each direction.

British Airways will operate the year-round service with a Boeing 787-8 carrying 204 passengers — 31 seats in Club World business class, 37 in World Traveller Plus premium economy and 136 in World Traveller economy.

The airport change matters more than it sounds. Gatwick is a secondary base with limited long-haul connections, while Heathrow feeds more than 130 destinations British Airways serves directly. Someone flying in from Manchester, Edinburgh, Dublin, Frankfurt or Milan can now reach San José on a single ticket with one stop instead of hunting for a self-connection across London.

Heathrow also carries more freight. The Costa Rican Tourism Institute said the terminal switch will improve air cargo capacity between Costa Rica and Europe, which affects exporters shipping perishable goods on passenger aircraft.

Marcos V. Borges, executive president of the Costa Rican Tourism Institute, said the announcement represents a significant increase in seats and frequencies from London. Ricardo Hernández, executive director of AERIS, the company that operates Juan Santamaría, said the route’s year-round permanence resulted from joint work between the airport operator, the tourism institute and the airline. Tourism Minister William Rodríguez said earlier this year that negotiations with British Airways ran for roughly two years.

The United Kingdom is the third-largest European source market for visitors to Costa Rica, according to tourism institute figures. The institute reported 15,741 British arrivals by air during the first two months of 2026, and 319,552 arrivals from Europe overall, an increase of 8.8 percent over the same period a year earlier.

The timing is deliberate as the World Travel Market, one of the largest international tourism trade fairs, opens in London in November, and Costa Rica arrives with a confirmed year-round connection rather than a seasonal one. The tourism institute (ICT) has also been running its first pan-European marketing campaign, built around the tagline “live.life.now.”

Costa Rica is not the only beneficiary of a wider British Airways expansion announced the same day. The airline plans to increase Latin American capacity by 25 percent for the northern summer of 2027, moving London–Buenos Aires to a daily operation with an onward leg to Santiago, and taking Rio de Janeiro to daily service as well.

Fares for the new Heathrow flights are already on sale through the airline’s booking system. Travellers holding reservations on the Gatwick service for dates after the switchover should expect to be reaccommodated on the Heathrow departure, and anyone with tight onward connections at Gatwick will need to rebuild that leg.

What Costa Rica gains is a link that no longer disappears for half the year — steadier seat supply, a European hub with real onward reach, and cargo space on a wide-body aircraft twelve months out of twelve.

World.title: Belize and U.S. launch US$125 million 5-year investment in Education and Energy
World.content:
Belize and U.S. launch US$125 million 5-year investment in Education and Energy

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Government of Belize and the United States Government, through the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC), officially launched implementation of the US$125 million Belize Compact, marking the start of its five-year implementation period.

The launch ceremony, held at the Belize Biltmore Plaza in Belize City, featured remarks from Prime Minister John Briceño, U.S. Ambassador to Belize André Bauer, MCC Acting Vice President of Compact Operations Jason Small and MCA-Belize Executive Director Dr. Marcia Bouloy. Implementation of the compact will now be led by MCA-Belize.

The grant will target two major economic challenges identified in Belize: education and the high cost of electricity.

Through the Education Project, investments will focus on strengthening secondary education, improving learning outcomes, developing teachers and school leaders, and expanding technical and vocational education and training to better prepare young Belizeans for further education and employment.

The Energy Project will seek to improve the efficiency and reliability of Belize’s electricity system while helping to reduce overall costs. A major component will strengthen electricity transmission to Ambergris Caye, reducing reliance on higher-cost localized emergency generation, while additional reforms will support modernization of the country’s energy policy and regulatory framework.

Prime Minister Briceño described the compact as a partnership aimed at long-term development.

“MCC and the Government of Belize designed this compact together in the spirit of true partnership,” he said. “This grant builds upon development priorities in Belize to deliver long-term economic growth for our people.”

The five-year initiative is expected to strengthen human capital, support businesses and communities, and contribute to sustainable economic growth.

World.title: Trial pushed to 2027 for police exhibit keeper accused of improperly disposing of weed gummies that got dozens of school-kids high
World.content:
Trial pushed to 2027 for police exhibit keeper accused of improperly disposing of weed gummies that got dozens of school-kids high

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The trial of Belize Police Department exhibit keeper Mario Bustillos over the infamous 2023 weed gummies incident has been pushed back another six months and will now begin in March 2027.

Bustillos was expected to go on trial before High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim on Wednesday, September 16, on a charge of willful oppression, but the matter could not proceed due to the court’s already packed trial calendar for the remainder of 2026.

Bustillos appeared in the High Court with his attorney, Nazira Myles Espat, where his new trial date was set for March 9, 2027. The Crown is expected to call more than 20 witnesses during the trial.

Bustillos is accused of acting in excess of his authority as a police exhibit keeper on April 21, 2023, when he allegedly improperly disposed of bags containing cannabis-infused gummies being kept as police property.

The edibles had originally been seized after entering Belize and were handed over by the Police Anti-Narcotics Unit for storage. Police said Bustillos allegedly disposed of them without authorization in a garbage trailer at the Queen Street Police Station compound. They were subsequently taken to the Belize City transfer station, where some of the gummies reportedly made their way back into circulation and were eventually sold to members of the public, including schoolchildren.

The incident triggered widespread concern after more than 30 children and several adults were hospitalized after consuming the marijuana-laced sweets. Bustillos was subsequently arraigned on 10 counts of negligent harm involving 10 minors and was granted bail.

Those negligent harm charges were later discontinued, and Bustillos was instead charged with willful oppression. By May 2024, the matter had been committed to the High Court for trial.

On December 10, 2025, Bustillos sought a sentencing indication from the High Court while considering a guilty plea. Justice Pilgrim indicated that he was contemplating a sentence of one year imprisonment if Bustillos pleaded guilty. Bustillos rejected the indication and elected to proceed to trial.

The matter subsequently went to case management in January 2026.

Bustillos, who remains on interdiction from the Police Department, remains free on bail pending his March 2027 trial.

World.title: Magical History Tour makes final stop in Corozal Town
World.content:
Magical History Tour makes final stop in Corozal Town

By Zoila Palma: The Belize @45 Magical History Tour made its final stop in Corozal Town on September 16, concluding a nationwide journey focused on dialogue, critical reflection and deeper engagement with Belize’s history and national identity.

Led by the Institute for Social & Cultural Research (ISCR-NICH) in partnership with historian Dr. Assad Shoman, the tour travelled across the country, encouraging Belizeans to examine the struggle for independence, the experiences that shaped the nation and the continuing process of decolonization.

In Corozal, students from Escuela Secundaria Técnica México, Corozal Community College and Cornerstone Presbyterian High School participated in discussions about Belize’s history and diverse national experiences. Students were encouraged to ask questions, share perspectives and consider how the country’s past continues to influence Belize today.

The tour concluded with a public forum at the Corozal House of Culture, bringing together community leaders and residents to discuss Belize’s shared history and its relevance to the future.

World.title: Belize City Council and NICH revitalize historic landmarks
World.content:
Belize City Council and NICH revitalize historic landmarks

By Zoila Palma: The Belize City Council, in collaboration with the National Institute of Culture and History (NICH), is pleased to highlight the completed restoration and placement of statues and monuments at Battlefield Park in downtown Belize City, as well as the rehabilitation of the George Price Bust and Leaf Monument at the George Price Highway Roundabout.

The Belize City Council noted that the completed works have renewed these important public landmarks, helping to preserve their appearance, significance, and place within Belize’s national heritage.

“As we commemorate the 15th anniversary of the passing of the Father of the Nation, Rt. Hon. George Cadle Price, the restoration of the George Price Bust and Leaf Monument is a fitting tribute to his enduring legacy and his contribution to the development of Belize,” the council said.

The Belize City Council remains committed to maintaining, restoring, and preserving our city’s monuments and heritage spaces for present and future generations

World.title: Minister Musa joins Immigration officers for MIDAS Training workshop
World.content:
Minister Musa joins Immigration officers for MIDAS Training workshop

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Immigration, Governance and Labour Kareem Musa joined immigration officers during one of the sessions of the MIDAS training workshop, taking the opportunity to see firsthand how the training will strengthen the work of officers across Belize’s borders and ports of entry.

Minister Musa’s presence reflects his inclusive approach to leadership and his responsibility to remain engaged with the officers who deliver these vital services every day.

The training strengthens the use of the Migration Information and Data Analysis System, MIDAS, helping officers improve the processing of travellers while supporting effective border management and national security.

The workshop brings together 125 immigration officers from the all the ports across the country.
