World.title: Azerbaijani service members participate in international competition in South Korea (PHOTO)
World.content:
Photo: Ministry of Defense of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 18. A group of service members of the Azerbaijan Army participated in the 4th Korea International Combat Training Competition held in Inje, Gangwon Province, Republic of Korea.

This was reported by the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

The international competition, which brought together military personnel from 11 countries, featured exercises in urban and mountain warfare, reconnaissance, ambush, counter-ambush, and forest operations, as well as defense tasks, patrolling activities, and casualty evacuation.

The main objective of the event was to facilitate the exchange of experience in combat readiness among the participating armed forces and to enhance professional engagement.

The participation of Azerbaijan Army service members in international competitions is of significance in terms of demonstrating the high level of combat readiness, professionalism, and operational capabilities of the personnel across diverse combat environments, as well as fostering the sharing of knowledge and skills.

World.title: Nasimi Gardens complex spans 120 hectares: Combining tourism and culture in Shamakhi
World.content:
SHAMAKHI, Azerbaijan, September 18. The Nasimi Gardens complex covers a total area of 120 hectares and is of significant importance for tourism development, Zahra Tagiyeva, project coordinator of the Nasimi Gardens complex, told reporters, Trend's correspondent reports from Shamakhi.

She added that numerous facilities operate on the site and a number of projects are being implemented.

“Among them is Magic Village, which features the world-famous hobbit houses. Capybara Cafe, designed for children’s entertainment, also operates here. In addition, Capybara Land, the first and only specialized capybara farm in Azerbaijan, is located here. Visitors can see the animals up close, touch and feed them.

“More than 150,000 trees and plants have been planted at Nasimi Gardens. More than 100 works and installations by Azerbaijani and foreign artists and sculptors are on display. A museum has also been established, featuring a rich collection reflecting the ancient and modern history and cultural heritage of Shamakhi,” she said.

Honored artist Rashad Alakbarov, who designed the monument to Imadaddin Nasimi erected in Shamakhi District, said the monument took five years to complete.

Around 30 people were involved in creating the sculpture, he added.

“Five years were spent creating Nasimi’s monument. A professional team of around 30 people worked on the sculpture, which was created in a contemporary style. This is the first sculpture made in such a style,” Alakbarov said.

Sabit Zamanov, co-author of the “Love Despite Everything” floral composition installed at the Nasimi Gardens complex, said the work symbolizes life and the inner world of a person.

According to him, the main idea behind the project is to convey the enduring nature of love.

“Three sculptors worked on this composition. The 11-meter floral composition symbolizes love, life and the inner world of a person. The bud emerging from the rose represents new life and the beginning of the future. Of the two angels depicted on the leaves, one represents love, life and beauty, while the other symbolizes playfulness, a free spirit and contradictions. The main idea of the project is to convey the enduring nature of love,” Zamanov said.

President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva visited the Nasimi Gardens complex in Shamakhi on September 17.

The Nasimi Gardens complex is a newly opened venue in Shamakhi District created for residents and visitors to spend their leisure time.

The complex was developed with the aim of contributing to tourism development in Shamakhi, increasing the region’s tourism potential, preserving the area’s natural features and creating a comfortable environment for family recreation and leisure.

Operating as a multifunctional tourism, cultural and recreational project, the Nasimi Gardens complex features various recreational facilities, family entertainment infrastructure, artworks on different themes and catering facilities.

World.title: Armenian PM thanks President Ilham Aliyev for contribution to peace in South Caucasus
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 18. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan thanked President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev for his contribution to establishing peace in the South Caucasus.

He made the remarks at a ceremony where he received the Hessian Peace Prize.

“I would also like to express my gratitude to Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, who is equally deserving of this award. I also want to express my gratitude to the peoples of Armenia and Azerbaijan. Despite the difficulties, human losses and suffering caused by the conflict, they have accepted and supported peace, realizing that they cannot change the past but can change the present and the future by choosing the prospect of peace, prosperity and cooperation instead of what seemed to be an endless conflict,” Pashinyan said.

World.title: Bathla's books show company was $736m out
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Administrators of the Bathla Group have been given up to another year to run the voluntary administration, as they try to secure longer-term funding and work through a sprawling portfolio of property projects and creditor claims.

The NSW Supreme Court on Friday extended the convening period for the administration until September 13, 2027.

But the order does not mean the administration, or Bathla's construction operations, are funded for another 12 months.

Rather, it gives administrators Teneo more time before they are required to convene the second meeting of creditors, where creditors would ultimately be asked to decide the future of the companies.

Administrators are assessing hundreds of Bathla's individual projects. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Why administrators sought another year

The ABC understands the administrators sought the 12-month period because they considered anything shorter inadequate, given the scale of the task ahead.

That includes assessing hundreds of individual projects, working through the group's financial records and, ultimately, providing creditors with enough information to make decisions about the future of the companies.

“We have taken a cautious approach to the time frame to ensure there is sufficient time to progress and complete projects in an orderly way,” Teneo's head of financial advisory Stephen Longley said.

But the ability to keep construction projects moving remains dependent on funding.

"The extension gives us the time needed to progress projects towards completion but that outcome remains dependent on securing further lender support to maintain critical central functions at Bathla," Mr Longley said.

"Locking in this funding is therefore an immediate priority and discussions are continuing."

Bathla Group is on the rocks. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Longer-term funding still not secured

Teneo has secured $4.7 million in initial funding and is continuing talks with lenders over longer-term support for active construction projects and the shared costs of keeping Bathla's operations running.

Bathla's messy next chapter Bathla has bought itself time, but not a rescue. Its future is increasingly being decided project by project.

Six lenders are currently providing the initial funding, while discussions are ongoing with other financiers that could potentially join the arrangement.

The funding talks come as administrators continue to work out the financial position of the group.

There are about $3.4 billion in currently known consolidated creditor claims.

That includes approximately $3.08 billion claimed by secured lenders and $145 million owed to the Australian Taxation Office.

It is also understood it includes about $48 million to private lenders and $110 million to other unsecured creditors, subject to ongoing reconciliation.

Bathla has been on the brink. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Untangling Bathla's financial records

The ABC understands Teneo's review to date has found the group's bank accounts had not been reconciled for some time, while its records may contain about $736 million in overstated inter-company receivables and payables, subject to reconciliation.

Key planning, design and construction information is also understood to be spread across different systems, staff email accounts, network drives and hard-copy records, rather than held in a single central repository, and reviewing these books could take many months.

A preliminary review has identified about 219 current projects carrying approximately $3.13 billion in debt, against a preliminary total value of about $4.87 billion, with figures subject to ongoing review.

Hundreds of properties face different outcomes

The ABC understands about $400 million worth of completed property is currently for sale or under contract.

It is expected that sale proceeds would initially be applied against secured lending, with any further amounts available to the individual Bathla companies, dependent on the outcome of those sales.

Across projects under construction, about a quarter of the lots are already subject to pre-sale contracts, while three-quarters remain available for sale.

It is understood administrators' preliminary assessment also identified about 167 undeveloped sites forming part of Bathla's land bank.

About 30 per cent are expected to be marketed for sale in their existing condition, while the strategy for the remaining 70 per cent is yet to be determined.

World.title: 'Never too old': 83-year-old footballer still getting a kick
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Robert Johnstone has just two rules when he crosses the white line to enter the football field.

"The first rule is don't fall over, because you're out of the game and you look a fool," the 83-year-old says.

"The second rule is get a kick."

Mr Johnstone, affectionately known by his teammates as "Robbie J", lives in South Australia's Riverland, but has also lived in Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland.

Robert Johnstone says he is always trying to improve and is constantly working on his skills. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

He was a latecomer to Aussie Rules football and only picked up the game in his 70s.

And despite his age, he's not ready to give up the sport he's fallen in love with.

"I'd never tried a group sport. I'd been a loner. I did a lot of fun-run walking and stuff," Mr Johnstone says.

"Now I can't walk past a footy without wanting to kick it.

" It's just magic to be out there with like-minded spirits. "

Still quick off the mark

Mr Johnstone plays for his local team, the Riverland Superdogs, who compete in South Australia's AFL Masters league.

The league only allows players age 35 and up, and has competitions across Australia.

The Riverland Superdogs played in the curtain raiser before the 2024 SANFL Russell Ebert Tribute Match. (Supplied: Robert Johnstone)

Mr Johnstone has the title of oldest player in the competition.

"There's an element of danger to it, and I've still got that little bit of ego; I want to be out there," he says.

" You've just got to accept the fact that everyone's quicker than me, but I do have some little wins. "

Riverland Superdogs president Rob Romeo has played alongside Mr Johnstone for almost 10 years.

He says even in his old age "Robbie J" has grown, becoming a better, more refined player.

He might not be a spring chicken, but Robert Johnstone can still kick the ball "almost 30 metres". (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

"He's usually the first one at trainings," Mr Romeo says.

"Things have slowed down slightly over the years, but there was a time when he would put us to shame.

"He's like a little kid, just trying to get a little bit better at kicking, and we'd just say, 'Don't put too much pressure on yourself. Just come out and enjoy yourself.'"

'No-one keeping score'

While there is no finals series or a premier in the AFL Masters, the competitive spirit and camaraderie has brought players back season after season.

Mr Romeo says the Superdogs don't care how good prospective players ae, as long as they are willing to give it a go.

He encourages anyone over 35 looking for community involvement and exercise to consider it.

"As a kid, you go to footy because your mates go, and this is no different," he says.

Robert Johnstone says finding the AFL Masters competition is one of the best things that's ever happened to him. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

"It opens up your friendship web, whether you come from broken relationships or whatever else that may have happened in your life.

"The exercise also helps with mental health."

Inclusivity the key to success

Former AFL Masters and West Adelaide chief executive Conny Wilson also resides in the Riverland.

She has seen "Robbie J" up close on a number of occasions, and says he embodies inclusivity, which AFL Masters is all about.

"As an aging society, these are great opportunities for people to either reconnect with past teammates or for people looking for friendships to come out and try," Ms Wilson says.

"It's also been exceptionally well received by women, who growing up didn't have the opportunity to play football."

Mr Johnstone's passion for the game also extends to his adopted state, seen in his distinctive mullet, transforming from grey to SA's iconic red, blue and yellow for the annual AFL Masters state carnival, which he will play again this year in the over-65s.

Rob Johnstone's hair is ready for the masters state carnival in Newcastle at the end of September. (Supplied: Robert Johnstone)

While the octogenarian doesn't expect to dominate his competition at the carnival, he is confident he can once again make his mark.

" I rarely get pinged for holding the ball, that's a badge of honour. "

World.title: Holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy trial 'didn't have any doubts' she was guilty
World.content:
The lone juror who wanted to convict Lindsay Clancy of murder for killing her three children said he was certain of her guilt, but that other jurors would not listen to him, according to a statement released by his lawyer Friday in his first public comments on the case.

Warning: This story contains details of a crime that may be distressing for some readers.

Eleven of 12 jurors were ready to clear Ms Clancy of criminal responsibility, with the majority feeling that the Massachusetts mother was in the grip of a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she killed her kids.

But juror Michael Desronvil sided with the prosecutors, who had argued that Ms Clancy knew what she was doing.

"I didn't have any doubts," Mr Desronvil said in a statement released on X by his lawyer, Edward Paltzik.

The jury's foreperson had claimed in an earlier media interview that Mr Desronvil had admitted having "reasonable doubt" about Ms Clancy's guilt, but wanted to convict her anyway. Mr Desronvil said that was not true.

"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented," he wrote.

"Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presented, I thought it was enough proof that she [Ms Clancy] knew exactly what she was doing and planned."

The jury's deadlock forced the judge to declare a mistrial on September 4, leaving the case unresolved.

What happens next in Lindsay Clancy case The six-week criminal trial of Lindsay Clancy has collapsed without a verdict, with the judge declaring a mistrial.

The Plymouth County district attorney has yet to say whether he will seek to put Ms Clancy on trial again.

Neither side disputed that Ms Clancy killed her children, Cora, Dawson and Callan, in the family's home in 2023 before trying to end her own life. But her attorney said she was a loving mother experiencing deep delusions and other mental health problems, for which she had been getting treatment.

Since the trial ended, Mr Desronvil has been both publicly praised and scorned for his actions, and his personal life and past financial and legal problems have become the subject of scrutiny by the news media and amateur sleuths.

Among the public revelations: He had a restraining order against him at the time of jury selection and was facing eviction from his apartment due to more than $US12,000 ($16,800) in unpaid rent. He was also accused of domestic violence in 2021, a charge that was later dismissed.

Some of the opinion has fallen along political lines, with Mr Desronvil being praised by some conservative pundits as a hero.

Mr Paltzik, whose past clients have included US President Donald Trump and Martin Shkreli, said on X that Mr Desronvil was in "an undisclosed secure location" in a rural part of northern New England and would not be giving interviews.

"As a devoted father and man of God, he will not be defeated or shattered by the wicked who wish harm upon him," Mr Paltzik wrote.

A fundraiser to cover what organisers say are costs of "security, lawyers, and lost work" for Mr Desronvil has raised over $US289,000 ($405,000).

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has rolled out the welcome mat for him, saying that if he is being harassed, "Florida will provide asylum."

"I'm sure he'd be welcomed and appreciated," Mr DeSantis wrote on X.

AP

World.title: The rice industry is the 'backbone' of this small town, but it's struggling
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

It's just over a month since Australia's largest rice processor, SunRice, laid off nearly 80 workers in southern NSW, and already some people are struggling to pay rent.

Deniliquin has a population of 7,500 and the loss of 68 jobs at the town's rice mill has hit the community hard.

The SunRice mill in Deniliquin is the largest in the southern hemisphere. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

Vinnies Services manager Meghan Fisher said affordable housing was already in short supply in Deniliquin, making it difficult for people who were out of work.

" Not only are they dealing with [not] being able to pay the rent while they're looking for another job or waiting for government allowance … they won't be able to find one that's going to be more affordable. "

The ABC has heard of cases where one family member might have retained their job at the rice mill, while another has been made redundant.

"Even for people who might not have lost their job yet, their understanding is that redundancies will still sort of keep happening over time, that's really hard on a lot of families," Ms Fisher said.

Edward River Mayor Ashley Hall says rice is a key economic driver. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

Edward River Council Mayor Ashley Hall said one in five jobs in the region is directly linked to the rice industry.

"It's a backbone of this community, our retail sector, our health precinct, our education systems, rely on that rice industry," he said.

He fears for the long-term future of rice processing without a change in government water policy.

Downstream businesses, such as Downes Rice Hulls, are also feeling the pinch.

A by-product of milling, the hulls are the hard outer shell around the rice grain and are used for bedding for intensive animal industries.

Keith and Jenny Downes have seen the highs and lows of rice production over 30 years processing the hulls. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

Jenny Downes said the shortage of rice meant they have to mix in straw to produce the bedding, costing her business hundreds of thousands of dollars.

"We've had to put some staff off already," she said. "That's why we bring in the top straw to try and keep our people employed, gives us something to put on the trucks and deliver to the client."

Fears more job losses to come

Deniliquin's SunRice mill is the largest in the southern hemisphere but is operating at a fraction of capacity.

Last year's harvest of 180 thousand tonnes was the smallest in six years.

Almost 70 jobs have been cut at the Deniliquin rice mill. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

The company shed 68 jobs at Deniliquin and another 10 at its milling operations in Leeton in August, while another 13 employees were re-deployed.

SunRice CEO Paul Serra said the low crop production was due to dry seasonal conditions and government policy of buying water entitlements for the environment in the Murray Darling Basin.

"One in every three litres of water that was available for irrigation over a decade ago is now no longer available and that pushes the [water] prices up, which makes it less economical for … crops such as rice," he said.

SunRice CEO Paul Serra says the future of the rice industry depends on water policy. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

With a 22 per cent fall in rice production predicted this summer, the industry and local One Nation MP David Farley have been calling for Commonwealth environmental water to be unlocked for agriculture.

"We think the government can do that very quickly and the funds from that can be used to help fix the river, which enables a working river to also be an environmentally sustainable river," Mr Serra said.

He said he hoped there would be no more cuts to rice processing but wasn't prepared to rule it out.

" We're waiting to see what the season brings for us, we're really hopeful that the government can release water in a timely manner … for growers. "

Adding value to safeguard future

SunRice says more than 90 per cent of its product is value-added. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

SunRice has a $70 million plan to modernise its 50-year-old infrastructure and increase value-adding, like rice cakes, high-protein rice and snack products.

"The more profit we make from selling high-valued rice around the world, the more we can afford to pay for rice in Australia," Mr Serra said.

SunRice is focused on value-adding its products to attract premiums for growers. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

A statement from the federal government said an application from SunRice for co-investment in a rice cake facility is being considered, as is help for affected workers.

"We have been working for some time with the NSW government, industry, the United Workers Union and the community to come up with ways to support workers who were recently laid off by SunRice or whose jobs are uncertain into the future," the statement said.

Watch ABC TV's Landline at 12:30pm (AEST) on Sunday or stream any time on ABC iview.

World.title: How Jack Gunston became an unlikely key to Hawthorn's flag hopes
World.content:
There are a lot of things that get better with age. Fine wine, cheese and even a good pair of jeans can improve as the clock winds along.

Football players aren't meant to be in this class. They start to break down as they get old. The mind is often willing, but the flesh is weak. The physical game takes its toll, with years of hits adding up.

Players like Jack Gunston, however, are determined to prove this wrong. Turning 35 next month, Gunston has preserved himself but actively gotten better. His last two years have been his most fruitful in front of the big sticks, and his value to Hawthorn never more important.

Gunston failed to top 60 season goals in the first 15 years of his AFL career. Since turning 33, he has done it twice.

Gunston's longevity has already seen him kick more than 35 per cent of his goals since turning 30, the sixth-highest rate among AFL-era players with over 500 goals. By the end of his career he may be on the podium.

Gunston sits at the vanguard of a revival of a slice of old-school footy. The era of the stay-at-home lead-up forward was recently thought to have gone the way of the dodo, but its revival has been largely implemented by a rising young crop, alongside Gunston that is. That's thanks to a somewhat hidden rule change.

In his fourth stint, at a third club, Gunston is set to lead a Hawthorn forward line into a shot at its first grand final in 11 years. In its way stands his old club.

Gunston's fourth coming

It's a well-worn cliche that nobody knows what a player will become when their name is first read out on draft night. While pundits will be quick to offer a comparison to a current player, each develops on their own, at their own pace.

Gunston was tabbed by Adelaide on potential, more than what he had shown to date in junior football. One of the youngest in the 2009 draft class, Gunston was green, slight and seen as a work in progress.

But as would eventually be the story for the rest of his career, Gunston quickly exceeded expectations at West Lakes. While the skinny frame and blond tips make him seem like a completely different player, Gunston's first goal — beating his defender for pace on the end of a full field rebound — bore a striking resemblance to his final evolution.

Gunston has been blessed to never carry his burdens alone. His whole career has been spent forming multi-pronged partnerships with multiple All-Australian quality forwards.

Most famous was his key role as one of five career All Australians in Hawthorn's legendary 2010s dynasty forward line, but before that he cut his teeth with Taylor Walker and Patrick Dangerfield. Most recently, he has partnered dangerous smalls, including current foils Nick Watson and Dylan Moore.

Gunston's stint in Adelaide wasn't long, but was fruitful. As the young Victorian was trialled all over the ground and worked on building fitness, there were more than just hints at the electric nature of his career to come.

Most know what happened next at the Hawks: three premierships and plenty of acclaim.

But the good times didn't last forever, and that boom period was followed by a fallow one. Injuries, and a short-lived move to Brisbane, left Gunston's career at the precipice.

His move back to the Hawks, and a shift in the way footy is played, has more than revived his career.

The connection is made

Over the past two years, Gunston has effectively become a player reborn.

Instead of the high-roaming beast pushing away from his match-up, the veteran now stays anchored closer to goal. Gunston often sits in space light years from the play, wastelands usually ignored by forwards in years past.

Gunston has forged a fast connection with the Hawks' contingent of skilful young midfielders such as Jai Newcombe, Connor Macdonald and Josh Ward. In some ways it resembles past great Jason Dunstall's bond with Platten and Jarman.

Hawthorn's set-up usually preserves this open space for Gunston to operate in. With this amount of grass, the 300 gamer gets the chance to deploy all the time-honoured tricks in his arsenal.

Gunston feigns, feints and baulks his opponent into submission. He'll lead to one side before darting back. Without support, direct defenders can be trapped in the blender of his athleticism. The connection between Gunston and his teammates is such that they know where he is going before his last decisive move.

Gunston is also unafraid to use the pockets. The instinct for most defenders is to hedge towards goal, and to cede the territory towards the boundary line. Over the past two years Gunston has made opposition sides pay for doing so.

Gunston has converted more goals from near the boundary, at a better clip, than anyone in the league in the past two years.

Gunston isn't alone in the depth in which he is deployed. A handful of players and teams across the league are experimenting more with "vertical spacing", or making the once-compressed ground long again.

Intriguingly, many of the other stay-at-home forwards are on the younger side of the league's key position forwards. Part of this influence may be down to the introduction of anti-density rules in junior footy, and the flow-on effects when those players have entered the league.

Marks inside 50 have steadily increased since the introduction of the rule in junior footy that requires a certain number of forwards to stay within the forward half and 50 at resets. This may have influenced younger players to be more patient with movement patterns, and shown coaches the value of space in the modern game.

The Brisbane test

Hawthorn faces a fearsome opponent on the way to the grand final: Gunston's old team, Brisbane.

The move of Gunston to Brisbane was designed to help the Lions get over the top. The veteran was meant to help mentor younger Lions forwards in the dark arts of finding space. In reality, early-season injuries, the tragic death of his father, and natural development meant Brisbane found different pathways to premiership glory.

Now it's Hawthorn that is the upcoming challenger.

Six weeks ago the reigning premiers saw off Hawthorn easily. Gunston held up his end of the bargain, kicking three of the Hawks' eight goals, but they were convincingly beaten all over the park. Despite dominating clearances, they completely lost the transition game and were torn to shreds by the furious Lions attack.

In order for Gunston to have a chance to be a difference maker, the Hawks have to be patient in the middle of the ground, and get the ball forward enough to have a chance.

World.title: 'Grumpy' voters in Murray Plains consider party allegiances as election looms
World.content:
Darren Connelly is sitting at his cluttered kitchen table, a 24-hour news channel paused on the TV in the living room.

Aged in his 60s, he's joined a political party for the first time in his life and thrown his support behind One Nation.

"They could put a blue heeler as the candidate, and I'd still vote for them."

Darren Connelly has joined a political party for the first time in his life. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

The earthmoving operator and former president of the local racing club says he typically voted for the Coalition, and once for Shooters, Fishers and Farmers when gun control was on the agenda.

But he's had enough.

"You've got shiny arse-polish bloody professional politicians. They say one thing and do another," he says.

His hometown of Kerang sits in the Murray Plains electorate, in northern Victoria, which has been a Nationals stronghold since the 1980s.

The local member is retiring at the November state election after 24 years.

There is a mood for change in Kerang. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

The town itself has seen plenty of change in that time.

Jobs in agriculture and food manufacturing have declined in the fallout of federal water reform, and now land once home to family farms hosts solar, wind and battery projects.

Mr Connelly wants to "turn the clock way back" and sees the election as his chance.

"The others need to be taught a lesson," he says.

"Get rid of the bloody bureaucracy."

Kerang is home to nearly 4,000 people. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

The race is on

Kerang is a short drive from the NSW border where earlier this year David Farley became One Nation's first federal MP at the Farrer by-election.

Bright yellow pockets of canola indicate harvest is a few months away, and worn roads crumble in more places than 'rough surface' warnings can alert weary drivers to.

The state seat of Murray Plains stretches more than 200 kilometres along the Murray River from Swan Hill to Echuca and Kyabram.

Canola is a common sight in northern Victoria. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Gannawarra Shire mayor Garner Smith is the candidate One Nation hopes will wrest the seat from the Coalition.

Up until now, he's been linked with the National Party as an electorate officer and ministerial adviser for two Nationals politicians and as a Young Nationals state president.

The ABC approached One Nation to request an interview with Cr Smith but were told only written answers to questions were being provided.

The party did not provide responses to those questions.

Cr Smith told a council meeting this week he would step aside as mayor on September 30 and ask for his council allowance to be suspended, though he will remain a councillor to avoid leaving the council "unacceptably thin".

Garner Smith is running for One Nation in Murray Plains. (Supplied: Gannawarra Shire Council)

At nearby Swan Hill there's tension between the old guard and the new.

John Forrest, former long-serving Nationals MP for the federal seat, is on the committee of the Swan Hill Neighbourhood House.

He's glaring across a table at the party's candidate for Murray Plains, Brett Hosking.

"You'll be battling to hold this seat," Mr Forrest warns.

"There's no such thing as a safe seat, let me assure you. And that's the reason why Hanson's getting so much popularity, because they're really cheesed off; they've been neglected for too long."

Brett Hosking stepped down as president of the Victorian Farmers Federation to run for the Nationals in Murray Plains. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Mr Forrest criticises Mr Hosking for turning up without his "chequebook open" and calls the meeting a "publicity stunt" for the ABC, which has been invited to attend the neighbourhood house for this story.

Neighbourhood houses across Victoria are campaigning for more funding from the state government.

The community spaces provide programs and services such as food relief, transport and social events.

A funding shortfall has forced the Swan Hill Neighbourhood House to close each Friday after years of operating five days a week.

Sarina Kelly says she is disappointed there has been no commitment to increase funding for neighbourhood houses. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Co-manager Sarina Kelly tells Mr Hosking the major parties have failed them.

"There's 400 houses all doing amazing things to support their communities and over half of them are struggling to keep the lights on," she says.

Mr Hosking is a fifth-generation mixed farmer who's recently stepped down as the president of the Victorian Farmers Federation (VFF).

His wife is the chair of the neighbourhood house in their tiny hometown of Quambatook.

Sharon Keady, Denis Gell, Sarina Kelly, Brett Hosking and Lindsay McRae outside Swan Hill Neighbourhood House. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

"Full disclosure, I can't go home at night without fighting for it," he says.

"We have a plan to make sure communities are supported, rural Victoria is supported, and I will fight hard for that."

Mr Hosking says he doesn't see Murray Plains as a safe Nationals seat.

"I see it as something that I've got to earn," he says.

"Every election, every person who lives in our community should make a decision about what's important to them, what their values are and how they want to be represented."

A sign at the entry to Ash and Bec Marshall's farm. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

'Confronting' change

Ash and Bec Marshall are grain growers in Normanville, just south of Kerang.

Their family home is an island among crops as far as the eye can see.

But there are plans for wind turbines the size of skyscrapers here.

Ash and Bec Marshall at their Normanville farm. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

At the kitchen table, Bec points out their farming properties on a printed map.

Highlighted areas show an approved wind farm to the immediate north of their home, and two others proposed to the south and north-west.

Ash draws a line to show roughly where the VNI West transmission line is set to cut through one of their smaller properties, as it carries power between NSW and Victoria.

Normanville falls in one of the state's five renewable energy zones earmarking the "best" places for wind, solar and battery projects.

"It's actually really confronting. It's probably the biggest change since clearing of land for agricultural use," Mr Marshall says.

A map showing the VNI West route. (Supplied: VicGrid)

The family fears how life in their home will be affected by possible noise and light flicker from the turbines.

Both One Nation and the Coalition have pledged to scrap VNI West if elected in November.

The decision has been welcomed by the VFF but criticised by bodies including the Clean Energy Council and Environment Victoria, who say the move risks energy security and will increase power bills.

"We're just looking for people to be honest and commit to the policy they can provide, so we can make a good decision for us," Ms Marshall says.

Another controversial government policy in the bush, a higher tax to fund emergency services, already had Ash Marshall offside.

He was among thousands who rallied against the tax outside parliament in Melbourne last year.

Thousands of CFA volunteers and farmers turned out for the protest in May 2025. (ABC News: Simon Winter)

Now with the thought of being called to fight fires on or started by renewable projects, he's considering hanging up the hose after more than 20 years as a Country Fire Authority volunteer.

"Even in six weeks we've gone from any vote to get away from Labor, to stop the Labor government, but then what?

"So then we start to think what are One Nation going to do? Where are the Coalition at?" he says.

"Country people are good people,"

" They're turning good people into grumpy people and really angry people. "

Apology for comments

Claire Mason has returned to her childhood home in Kerang to be a full-time carer for her dad, who has Parkinson's disease and dementia.

In the time before the next fitness class, she runs out of her shed, she's sitting on the verandah in the morning sun while keeping one eye on a monitor inside the house.

Claire Mason in front of the shed she runs fitness classes from. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

It means the day-to-day dramas of state politics take a back seat.

But comments about women and domestic violence hit close to home.

As a councillor, Garner Smith was forced to apologise by a council arbiter in 2022 for comments he made on his Facebook page.

Responding to an article about a leaked video appearing to show former AFL player Dustin Martin groping a topless woman, Cr Smith wrote; "I'd be more worried if he didn't go in for a feel".

The 2022 comments on Facebook by Garner Smith. (Supplied)

He then replied in the comment thread, saying: "To all you triggered, whingeing, whining, bleating, bitching, offended losers, instead of getting a skinny soy latte with a twist of lemon, head to your local independent hardware store, buy a bag of cement and harden the #@&! up."

Ms Mason says the comments perpetuate misogyny and sexism.

"When people in leadership positions can say things like that, it just gives men more green light to continue that behaviour."

Cr Smith did not respond to the ABC's question about these comments, but was asked if he stood by them on ABC Mildura-Swan Hill breakfast radio in August.

"There's bigger ticket items to deal with. I did not pass any opinion on women," he said.

Either way, Ms Mason says she won't be voting for One Nation in November.

"I always lean towards the Greens, but I'm not right across it. I probably have to wait to see what happens [in the campaign]," she says.

Zoe Cook, a Campaspe Shire councillor, is running for the Greens on a platform of public transport and housing.

While she doesn't support scrapping VNI West, Cr Cook is calling for more consultation before it progresses.

Zoe Cook, Campaspe Shire councillor and Greens candidate for Murray Plains. (Supplied)

She says she understands why people in the electorate are upset.

"They're seeing that they have less control over the infrastructure crumbling around them, and then this is the last straw of not being consulted.

"At the end of the day, the climate crisis is upon us and worsening, and we need to be investing in renewable infrastructure," she says.

Election 'test'

Zareh Ghazarian, associate professor of politics at Monash University, says Victoria's three-cornered contest between Labor, the Coalition and One Nation is shaping as one of the hardest elections to predict.

While local issues can lead to a hunger for change, he says Australians are fatigued by the major parties.

Zareh Ghazarian says Victoria's 2026 election is a test for One Nation. (Supplied)

"Opinion polling suggests voters are being persuaded potentially to vote for One Nation, because they feel that is a party seeking to represent new ideas and new solutions."

Labor is yet to name a candidate to contest the seat of Murray Plains.

But Mr Ghazarian cautioned against using the results of by-elections, such as Farrer, to predict a win for One Nation in Murray Plains.

"I think dynamics will change when it becomes a general election. The debate focuses on all sorts of things, not just local issues.

"This is a test for One Nation — whether it is actually enjoying wide support and whether that support is enough for it to win seats."

World.title: Breaking: Trump bans CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House
World.content:
US President Donald Trump says he has banned three prominent media outlets from the White House, in an extraordinary escalation of his attacks on the American press.

Cable networks CNN and MS NOW and political newsletter Politico have been banned effective immediately, with more to follow, Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social.

He said the ban was "a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

"Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America," he wrote.

But half an hour after his post was published, CNN reported its staff continued working at the White House "like a normal Friday afternoon".

Across his two terms as president, Mr Trump has developed a hostile relationship with journalists and media outlets who report critically on his administration.

However, he regularly invites reporters into the Oval Office for impromptu press conferences, and only in rare cases have reporters or outlets been banned.

Last year, the Associated Press news agency was excluded from some Trump events when it refused to follow his order to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

World.title: History beckons for Fremantle, after best-ever fightback propelled them into Grand Final
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

When Hayden Young went back and kicked a remarkable goal from the boundary after the three-quarter time siren, he couldn't have known it would spark his side's greatest comeback.

Never, in 753 AFL games across more than 30 years, had the Dockers recovered from more than 18 points down at the final change to win.

But against Sydney, after what can only be described as an underwhelming three quarters of football, Fremantle created yet more history in a season that keeps on giving to turn a 21-point deficit into a 12-point win.

The Dockers had never won while trailing by 18 points or more at three-quarter time. (AAP Image: Dan Himbrechts)

Shai Bolton produced a stunning long set shot, before Patrick Voss fended Dane Rampe into next week and curled home a brilliant goal to cut the margin to nine points.

Isaiah Dudley, in just his second AFL season, then booted the goal that sent Fremantle to just its second Grand Final.

"We were down for so much, we were playing so poorly for it felt like large parts of it, but we hung in there," Dockers captain Alex Pearce told Fox Footy.

"I don't want to say it's a sense of relief; it's a sense of joy and pride for my teammates in how we were able to play our best footy in that last quarter when the pressure was at its highest."

Flicking the switch

Fremantle fans would have been forgiven for giving up on the Premiership dream midway through the third quarter.

Sydney, undermanned as they were, had an answer for every challenge the Dockers threw their way.

Fremantle had more of the ball but struggled on the short SCG, kicking over the head of their forwards time and again.

Josh Treacy struggled to have an impact as the Dockers missed targets inside 50 on numerous occasions. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Voss, Jye Amiss and Josh Treacy combined for just eight disposals in the first half, which was emblematic of the Dockers' struggles.

Sydney's pressure was intense, as it appeared the Dockers would crack as they did against Hawthorn two weeks ago.

But after the final change, they showed the resolve that had made them the best second-half side for the season.

"We put a bit of pressure on them [Sydney], and they probably didn't play with the same dare," Dockers coach Justin Longmuir told Fox Footy.

"It was a game of adjustments. I didn't think our intensity was off early; I think our method was off early."

Swans fairytale ends

With all the personnel missing, it seemed inevitable that at some stage the Swans would run out of legs.

And in the face of the Dockers' onslaught, they wilted.

Errol Gulden was immense with 36 disposals and eight tackles, while Brodie Grundy toiled in the ruck in a salivating contest against Luke Jackson.

Luke Jackson won his battle against Brodie Grundy, kicking two crucial goals. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

But ultimately, the Dockers had too much talent across the ground, and somehow found another gear to run over the top of the Swans.

It brings to an end a season that will forever be remembered for the events in mid-August which saw the Swans suspend five first-choice players.

The Swans produced a stunning win over Brisbane in their qualifying final in which they also lost captain Callum Mills to a serious knee injury, but couldn't repeat the dose.

"We were in a really good position for three-and-a-bit quarters, and to their credit, at this time of the year you can't give a team any momentum, and they took it," Swans coach Dean Cox said.

"They've been the best team all year, and it showed you've got to play a full 120 minutes against those teams to get the result you're after."

Sydney will be pondering what could have been, while Fremantle has an eye on history.

World.title: How this team of experts guide 80-metre turbine blades down our roads with just millimetres to spare
World.content:
It is just after midnight on a winter morning when we gather at the Port of Newcastle.

In the background coal ships slink by, in the foreground an almost inconceivably vast wind turbine blade lies along the spine of a truck bed like some sort of alien life form strapped to a gurney in a sci-fi film.

It’s so big that it’s hard to fit it all into the frame of your eye from any reasonable perspective. At its tip it tapers to the length of schoolkid’s ruler. Towards that tapered end it has a jagged edge like a cartoon dragon’s teeth, a shape designed to reduce noise as it slices through the air. Peering up at its midsection, you could be looking at a warship’s prow from the ocean’s surface.

A team of transport specialists are making last-minute preparations to move this beast through the sleeping streets of suburban Newcastle and the coal villages of the Hunter Valley, along the Golden Highway to a hillside outside Wellington on the NSW Central Slopes, where it is to be raised upon a tower as part of a Squadron Energy wind farm that will soon be generating enough electricity for about 220,000 homes.

It seems absurd that this thing can be moved at all, let alone along busy roads, but the man in charge of this circus, Steve Spiller, seems impossibly calm. Jovial, even.

The police and pilots gather before the start of the turbine blade’s trip from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW Photo: Janie Barrett

Form and function

Wind turbine blades, explains engineer Dr Rosemary Barnes, are the largest single-component objects that humans regularly either build or seek to move. Artefacts of the modern world tend to shrink as technology advances, but wind turbines, shaped by both economic and physical forces, keep growing.

Longer turbine blades scoop up more wind and generate more electricity with each rotation, says Barnes, who has spent a career designing, building and repairing turbines and blades around the world and now runs a renewable energy consultancy. A dozen huge turbines need fewer gearboxes, less cable and wiring, less maintenance, less concrete and steel to generate as much electricity as dozens of small ones.

As the turbines grow in length, so do the forces exerted upon them. In extreme conditions, a large blade might bend 10 to 15 metres from a straight line. Imagine, says Barnes, a diving board wilting under the weight of a herd of elephants.

“They have to survive that transfer of force hundreds of millions of times over a life of about 30 years. Every time the blade is in the three o’clock position, gravity is bending it one way, and then when it goes into the nine o’clock position, it’s bending the exact opposite way, and it keeps repeating like that as it spins. It’s just like if you bend a paperclip back and forth repeatedly, you know that small load is not going to break it, but you do it enough times, and you get fatigue loading, it is going to break.”

All this means that not only must a blade be handmade from tough, light composite materials, they are stronger when they are crafted in a single piece, rather than disassembled for transport, which brings us back to Spiller and his crew in Newcastle.

The monster they are about to move is 82 metres long and weighs just over 20 tonnes.

The port

The crew is doing last-minute checks on vehicles and equipment. Craig Carpenter is inspecting the Kenworth truck and the purpose-built trailer he is about to drive. The trailer has a long spine that can be extended to suit its load, and six sets of axles at the rear.

The steerer, Freddie Scheepers, checks the truck prior to the start of the turbine blade’s trip from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

Tonight Carpenter’s load from front grille to blade tip will be 92 metres long. Carpenter picked up the nickname Blade Runner One for his smooth driving while moving blades in Western Australia last year, but just as crucial is Freddie Scheepers, who is “steerer” and will pursue Carpenter in a van close behind the truck.

Scheepers must not only keep his own vehicle on the road, but when necessary will use a remote control to steer the rear axles of the trailer. He keeps in constant contact with Carpenter so at any given moment the two know exactly where the blade tip is in relation to the road and the rest of the rig.

“Those two are very, very close, and they’ve got a really good bond. They know what the other bloke is going to do before he does it.” Steve Spiller, Project Manager

When the front of the rig moves upwards and is forcing the tip towards the ground, Scheepers will also be able to raise and lower the blade itself, the last metres of which rest in a hydraulic jack that sits over the axle sets.

“Those two are very, very close, and they’ve got a really good bond,” says Spiller, watching Carpenter and Scheepers make final preparations. “They know what the other bloke is going to do before he does it.”

Mayfield Macca’s

The convoy pulls out at about 1am. There are two police cars, as required by law when moving a load of this size in NSW. There are four pilot vehicles which help manage traffic around the truck and trailer. Scheepers’ steering van hunts along behind the blade like a sheepdog, and we follow in a four-wheel drive with Spiller, the project manager.

The turbine blade starts its journey from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

Also in tow is a Transport NSW vehicle with a couple of observers, there to see if anything can be learnt or improved for future runs. After this, there are still another 195 blades to go, let alone the turbine hubs, tower sections and generators.

“When you pull back the curtain, this is what building a wind farm looks like – thousands of individual movements, decisions and people are needed to get every component to site,” Squadron Energy’s chief executive Rob Wheals later observes.

Steve Spiller, Ares Group project manager, accompanies the turbine blade on its journey from Newcastle to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

“At 80 metres long and shaped like a banana, each blade is one of the most challenging pieces of infrastructure to ever move.”

From Spiller’s radio we can hear occasional chatter from the pilot vehicles, but he leaves the “Bladerunners” to their own quiet comms channel so they can concentrate. Before we’ve even left the Port precinct the blade tip sweeps out over a cyclone fence, clearing it by what seems like centimetres.

Spiller doesn’t flinch. Every move is rehearsed, every distance measured.

The turbine blade crosses the highway from the wrong side on its journey from the Port of Newcastle to the wind farm. Photo: Janie Barrett

At a McDonald’s on a roundabout on Industrial Drive in the neighbouring suburb of Mayfield, the cop cars and pilot vehicles splay out to halt traffic coming from three directions, and Scheepers climbs out of his van to flick a switch on the rig to remote control. He adjusts the height of the suspension, and then he steers the rear of the rig around the turn.

The turbine blade crosses the highway from the wrong side at the intersection of Industrial Drive and Maitland Road, Mayfield. Photo: Janie Barrett

Speed picks up, at least until the caravan reaches the Hunter Expressway. To make it onto that section, the pilots block traffic on the expressway in both directions while the Bladerunners navigate the rig 80 metres down an off-ramp into what would otherwise be oncoming traffic, then drive a kilometre down the wrong side of the road before crossing back. Spiller seems pleased by how smoothly this dance of traffic and truck is performed.

The remote used for steering the rear of the truck that carried the enormous turbine blade. Photo: Janie Barrett

As we head northwest towards the Golden Highway, Spiller relaxes enough to tell his story. He became an expert in moving big stuff almost by accident. At 19, he took a job with a logistics firm and began moving shipping containers. Half a decade later he was moving wind turbine parts, and the work took him around the world with the global giant GE. He has moved bits and pieces of wind farms by sea and land and even air, at one point chartering the world’s biggest aircraft, an Antonov, to move a wind turbine hub and six generators from Leipzig to Adelaide.

In Germany, near the Polish border, he recalls coaxing blades through tiny villages on a truck that could raise them to near vertical from the base to navigate tight spaces.

Freddie Scheepers changes the steering of the rear of the truck from manual to automatic via an external switch on the truck. Photo: Janie Barrett

In Australia, it’s easier because we have so much space. “I moved 300 blades through Toowoomba without complaint,” he boasts. Today he works for the Ares Group, which was contracted by GE, who built the blade at a factory in China, to shepherd it safely off the ship in Newcastle and on to the Squadron Energy site outside Wellington.

Despite the late hour you can tell the convoy is having an impact along the way. In one hamlet we pass within metres of the old coal miners’ cottages. A man in a dressing gown watches on in the pre-dawn from his veranda. His expression is impossible to read in the revolving lights.

Craig Carpenter, the truck driver who drove the turbine blade from Newcastle to the Uungula wind farm. Photo: Janie Barrett

From the sections of widened road you can see along the way the years of preparation that went into this operation. EnergyCo, the NSW government authority responsible for delivering the state’s five renewable energy zones, has spent $130 million preparing this route.



Inland

There are rules about moving oversized loads in the dark on the Golden Highway, so the convoy pulls over before dawn. A quiet pall descends across the still convoy, except for cheerful noises from Carpenter’s cabin. He hums and sings to himself and taps out a rhythm before drifting into silence.

In bright early light, against the country homes in Denman, the enormity of the blade begins to become more clear. It is longer than whole blocks of the little town. Along the Golden Highway, the convoy at times creeps up to something approaching normal traffic speed, and time passes quickly until we reach the site of the wind farm, headquartered on a sheep and cattle operation on rolling green hills east of Wellington.

As the truck prepares to tackle the narrow dirt roads built for the project we are taken into a sprawling site office for a safety induction. Whiteboards on the walls show the progress in the construction of each of the 69 turbines that will soon be operational here. There are posters boosting the “core values” of Squadron Energy, which is owned by Tattarang, the investment company that in turn owned by Andrew Forrest and Nicola Forrest. The values include “Humility” and “Frugality”.

It is midafternoon on a hilltop I had last seen two years earlier when Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Forrest attended a sod-turning ceremony. Bladerunner One finally steps out of his cabin and offers up a great two-armed stretch to the sky. By now Spiller has left the site on his way back to his head office in Melbourne. Workers on-site scramble over the blade, breaking it free of its harnesses and lowering it into a cradle by a half-built tower. By the time it is operational it will stand 148 metres from base to blade tip.

There’s no getting around the impact the project is having on a beautiful landscape. Construction pads are scraped into the ground by each tower and the new roads hum with the sort of traffic flow you’d expect in a prosperous town.

The turbine blade arrives ar the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW Photo: Janie Barrett

Later I ask farmer John Holland, owner of Uungula, for which the wind farm is named, what he makes of it all. He speaks with a careful, precise manner, aware of the controversy that wind projects attract. Squadron, he says, will clean up after the construction is complete, leaving him with new roads, giving even better access to the property’s ridge lines.

He says he has no fear about the impact of the turbines on his stock. Visiting other wind farms, he has seen sheep “camping” under the towers for shade. He reckons the turbines look majestic, but admits that when he saw renders of what they would look like spread across the land he loves he found it “a little confronting.”

He thinks renewable energy is a part of the solution for Australia’s growing energy demand, but not the only one. Like many farmers, he opposes grid-scale solar plants taking up agricultural land. But he has practical considerations too. The rent Squadron will pay for each turbine will let the family retire a fair chunk of debt, though he won’t say how much. Nor will he say how many turbines his farm will host. “That’s a bit like asking how much money I’ve got in the bank. It’s a bit rude.”

But he is happy to say the income has helped settle the questions of succession that can cause such grief to farming families, and to update equipment and improve fences and dams.

“It’s the confidence to be able to run the property the way it should be run.”

I ask him what Uungula means.

“It’s an Aboriginal word,” he says. “It means wind in the hills.”

Workers unload the turbine blade after its long journey. Photo: Janie Barrett

Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Celebrity accountant Anthony Bell to offload Rose Bay pad after $26m buy
World.content:
Exclusive PropertyNewsTitle Deeds Celebrity accountant Anthony Bell to offload Rose Bay pad after $26m buy Kristy Johnson September 19, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Accountant to the stars Anthony Bell has put his Rose Bay apartment on the market in an expression of interest campaign. Bell, whose clients have included Karl Stefanovic and Michael Clarke, said that while he initially intended to make the Rose Bay unit his principal place of residence, he enjoyed renting at Barangaroo’s Crown Residences so much that he decided to buy there. Money manager Anthony Bell has decided to offload his harbourside Rose Bay apartment in Sydney that he renovated. Records show Bell, chief executive officer and principal of accounting and advisory firm Bell Partners, bought the five-bedroom, four-bathroom Rose Bay apartment for $9,657,000 in 2024 from architect Andre Heyko-Porebski and his wife, Louise. Bell intended to make the unit his principal place of residence.



While renovating the interiors, Bell rented at Crown Residences in Barangaroo, a complex now home to a smorgasbord of corporate heavyweights and rich-listers such as Alex Birkenstock, heir of German cult sandal brand Birkenstock, Luna Park co-owner Bill Gravanis, and Lawrence Myers, chief executive officer of James Packer’s family office Consolidated Press Holdings. Anthony Bell and Annika Martyn For a short time, there was also a tenant at the Rose Bay pad. Bell said that he enjoyed Crown’s proximity to his office at King Street Wharf, a short walk away, so much that he decided to purchase there. Records show Bell bought a four-bedroom apartment at Crown for $26,588,000 in December 2024 that settled in July the following year.



Also in 2024, Bell sold his Dover Heights home for $20.78 million after he bought it for $11.5 million in 2017 from his mate, Channel Seven star Larry Emdur and his wife, Sylvie. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Fruit and veg supplier drops about $9.5m in 24 hours on Crown unit Bell also owns two Queensland properties – a Surfers Paradise home bought with wife Annika Martyn, the founder of wellness brand GG Vitality, for $5.3 million in 2024, and a Noosaville abode purchased with then-wife, former model and TV presenter Kelly Landry, for $10,301,000 in 2017. Bell now has sole ownership of the Noosaville residence. The Rose Bay harbourside pad features a neutral palette with refined marble finishes, a custom bar, private gym/Pilates studio, jacuzzi and a north-east facing terrace. Bill Malouf and David Malouf of Highland Double Bay are the listing agents.



Fashion designer lists Byron Shire home Wayne Cooper, the fashion designer behind the eponymous brand that was stocked in Myer for many years, has put his Byron Shire home on the market with a price guide of $4 million to $4.5 million. Fashion designer Wayne Cooper is selling his Myocum abode in the Byron Shire. Records show Cooper and his ex-wife, model Sarah Marsh, purchased the five-bedroom, five-bathroom, resort-style acreage with a pool in Myocum for $5.09 million in 2022. But when the marriage fell apart, it was listed the following year with a $4.5 million guide. Photos on the walls in the listing show Cooper and his wife, Elizabeth Adams.



When it didn’t sell, it was put to auction, attended by Cooper as one of the bidders and Marsh as an observer. After about two bids, Cooper secured sole ownership of the luxury property for $3,871,000. Wayne and his ex-wife Sarah Marsh Scott Barbour The three-level abode has wraparound balconies, covered entertaining areas, a tennis court that awaits a refresh, and views across the coast to Julian Rocks and Mount Warning. Eagle-eyed buyers may notice photos of Cooper and his current wife, Elizabeth Adams, a former UBS banker whom he wed in 2023, in photos on the walls of the listing. Ku Darroch of Byron Bay Property Sales, who is selling the residence alongside Riley Buckland, said the property was a rare estate that immediately left an impression.



“The combination of its elevated coastal outlook, generous scale, privacy and established grounds is exceptional. There is a wonderful sense of space and freedom here, less than 20 minutes from Byron Bay’s fabulous beaches,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Philanthropist’s Byron Bay home with a zen room has $15m price hopes As previously reported by this masthead, in 2008, Cooper and Marsh went to court after a domestic dispute at their home in Tamarama which they have since sold. Cooper pleaded guilty to a charge of common assault and was placed on a two-year good behaviour bond. Police dropped other charges against Cooper of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and stalking and intimidating Marsh.



Cammeray listing The Cammeray home of architect, developer and former restaurateur Dominic Choy and his wife, Irina, is for sale, with local sources indicating the price guide is in the high $20 million range. A waterfront residence in Sydney’s Cammeray with multiple leisure zones has been offered to the market. The Choys previously listed the six-bedroom, six-bathroom waterfront residence in 2024 through different agencies. Records show they bought the property with its private beach, pontoon and jetty, for $3.78 million in 1997.



There is an incredible home cinema. Dominic has done well since arriving in Australia aged 15. He worked as a kitchen hand to support his studies, graduating from the University of New South Wales with an honours degree in architecture. He founded a chain of restaurants in the 1980s and debuted on the Forbes rich list in 1993. His daughter, Dominique Choy is a former pop princess and model who is now a rapper known as Dizzy Dizzo and married to Taiwanese actor Sunny Wang. The vendors are architect, developer and former restaurateur Dominic Choy and his wife, Irina. The Choys’ home has a cinema and bar, wine cellar, sauna, pool, waterfall and koi pond. Alon Beran and William Tu of Sydney Sotheby’s International Realty Neutral Bay are selling the home but both refused to comment on any aspect of the listing when contacted.

World.title: What the cameras missed after Lloyd Meek copped a spray from his coach
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sam Mitchell charged into Hawthorn’s change rooms at half-time of his team’s round seven clash with Gold Coast, ruckman Lloyd Meek firmly in his sights. An errant backwards handball by Meek in the dying stages of the second quarter had led to a crucial turnover, allowing the Suns to score a goal with four seconds left on the clock. Mitchell, fuming, delivered an animated spray – which amateur lip-readers discerned contained a lot of f---s – that quickly went viral on social media, largely due to the wide-eyed expressions of Meek’s shocked teammates. View post on X “I know that when he’s aggressive and he’s fired up, it’s because of how much he cares, and I’m the same,” Meek told this masthead. “I’m exactly the same. So like, we’re all competitive people. We wouldn’t be here if we weren’t. We all want to win. And sometimes those conversations are just what it takes to get the message across. “At the time, obviously no one likes being yelled out. But I was still so stoked with how we were able to respond and come out of that.”



Hawthorn went on to win the game by 49 points, holding Gold Coast goalless in the final term. Meek points out there’s a lot the broadcast cameras don’t see or show. The ruckman said Mitchell checked in with him before running out for the third quarter, and again after the game, to check he was OK. “He came up to me and said ‘well done, you responded really well’, and we had a good chat, no one sees that,” Meek said. Lloyd Meek says his coach Sam Mitchell embodies the values Hawthorn want to be known for. Eddie JIm “You just see one 30-second snippet and think ‘geez, he’s copped a spray’. But it’s like no, we’ve actually had conversations all day.” Growing up in Mininera in regional Victoria – Meek hails from a prestigious rowing family, with his dad and his siblings all winning Head of the Lake titles. He was selected by Fremantle with pick 69 in the 2017 draft, but did not debut in the AFL until his fourth season at the Dockers. He later moved to Hawthorn during the 2022 trade period to seek more opportunities in the ruck. As an example of Mitchell’s close connection to his players, Meek revealed the coach delivered handwritten letters to each of them before their qualifying final win, on the road, against Fremantle.



“[In the letter] he mentioned that he was glad that I picked Hawthorn and had faith in me, and how we’ve both, I guess, grown over that four-year period,” Meek said. Meek said he found it difficult to fully articulate what Mitchell meant to the playing group, heralding the head coach as someone who “makes every single person feels valuable”. A kiss on the head from Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell to Nick Watson after the qualifying final win over Fremantle. AFL Photos “He [Mitchell] is Hawthorn,” he said. “He’s so pivotal and so important to what we’ve built … not discrediting the[other] people; the board and the football club and the other coaches and staff, but he has built so much of the environment that we get to come in and enjoy every day, and that’s probably been something that I have valued and appreciated since coming to Hawthorn. ” “Everything he spoke about and his vision for us and the club was so aligned with what I wanted in my career.” Meek has endless praise for Mitchell’s coaching abilities, but has some doubts about the coach’s prowess at chess. Mitchell and a few other Hawthorn players regularly play chess online, with the head coach known to have a solid winning streak.



“I don’t know if I’ve ever played [against] him, but I reckon I’d be able to beat him,” Meek joked. “I think he likes to play on chess.com, so I think he’s pretty handy. He probably uses AI to cheat.” Hawthorn’s preliminary final clash with Brisbane on Saturday comes six weeks after the back-to-back reigning premiers took them to the cleaners in round 22, the Lions storming to a 67-point win at the Gabba. Related Article Analysis

Brownlow Medal The big intrigue that’s looming for Brownlow night After the thumping loss Mitchell remarked, “we’re better than that, and we’re going to have to prove it”. When he spoke to this masthead this week, Meek was yet to watch footage of the Lions’ semi-final victory over Adelaide because the game clashed with his 10-year-high school reunion in Ballarat; an event the 28-year-old attended alongside his childhood sweetheart, now wife, Elonie, who he met in Year Nine. Ahead of the prelim, Meek intended to keep things simple.

World.title: Powerhouse Parramatta’s $4.5 million opening festival revealed
World.content:
Breaking CultureArt & designCity life Powerhouse Parramatta’s $4.5 million opening festival revealed Linda Morris September 19, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 23-day festival program featuring 179 events heralding the opening of the billion-dollar Parramatta Powerhouse will be unveiled on Saturday, as the government attempts to look past executive turmoil and build public momentum for western Sydney’s first state-significant cultural institution. The launch will proceed minus the museum’s driving force, Lisa Havilah, who was stood down two weeks ago pending the outcome of a formal misconduct investigation into what Parliament was told were “serious” allegations involving two executives of the Powerhouse Museum. The construction fence has come down on the new Powerhouse Museum. Steven Siewert Havilah is said to be strongly defending her conduct. NSW Government Architect Abbie Galvin is serving as acting chief executive until an inquiry by Sydney-based law firm Lander and Rogers concludes. Despite the leadership crisis, the $4.5 million opening festival, funded by the Department of Creative Industries, runs from November 7 to 29 at the new riverside venue.



The line-up is short on high-cost spectacle such as outdoor concerts or drone shows, focusing instead on immersive works, talks and community events. The state government confirmed 65 per cent of the launch program would be free. Ticketed events will cost from $15 to $50 and will go on sale from midday Saturday September 19. “It’s a great way to ease pressure on the budget as the majority of events are free,” Arts Minister John Graham said. The festival kicks off on opening day, November 7, following a ribbon-cutting ceremony, a plaque unveiling and the previous day’s donor preview and media tour. To manage crowd capacity over the November 7-8 launch weekend, patrons will be required to book timed hourly arrival slots through the Powerhouse website from midday this Saturday. Related Article City life Too big to fund, too big to fail: The pitfalls lying in wait for the Powerhouse Seven weeks out from ribbon cutting, general admission pricing for post-opening visits remains unconfirmed, though the biggest show, Task Eternal, will require paid tickets for visitors over the age of 16 years.



At the same time as it is launching its festival, the Powerhouse is advertising itself as Sydney’s newest event destination on socials. It is also advertising rental of its “flexible, large-scale spaces for events from 20 to 1,000 guests”. During the three weeks and four weekends of the festival, operating hours will run from 10am to 5pm Monday through Wednesday, and 10am to 9pm Thursday through Sunday. Post-festival operating schedules have also not been finalised and, as the Herald has disclosed, they are expected to be wound back to 10am to 5pm permanently as Treasury searches for belated cost savings. Former NASA administrator Charles F. Bolden Jr, who flew on four space shuttle missions, leads the space and technology roster alongside science fiction author Ted Chiang (both November 8), whose short story Tower of Babylon inspired the design of the museum’s Task Eternal. Chiang will discuss the pursuit of immortality. Additional talk panels focus on bio-manufacturing, space technology and AI diagnostics. On the opening weekend, Locomotive 3265 – a 124-year-old steam train from the Powerhouse Collection originally commissioned in 1902 – will run passenger trips between Parramatta and Riverstone stations, accompanied by performances from the NSW Railway Band. Related Article Analysis

City life The inside story of the day that shook Sydney’s museum world



On the Powerhouse terrace, British artist Es Devlin presents Come Home Again, an 11-night installation featuring 244 hand-drawn depictions of endangered NSW species created alongside the Botanic Gardens of Sydney, accompanied by live choral performances from River City Voices, Barayagal and Noqu Vanua. Industrial designer Marc Newson (November 7) reflects on four decades of work, while artist Bharti Kher unveils her public sculpture Tree of Life. Sydney Chamber Opera will perform two newly commissioned works responding to Anton Bruckner’s 1869 Locus Iste and an 1879 Sydney International Exhibition cantata held in the museum’s collection. Opening ceremonies begin with a Welcome to Country by the Jannawi Dance Clan and the presentation of a kahu kuri (dog skin) cloak by artist Keren Ruki, featuring a hand-woven kaupapa base that took 3000 hours to complete.
