World.title: What will happen to your most cherished possessions when you die? You don’t want to know
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsParenting Opinion What will happen to your most cherished possessions when you die? You don’t want to know Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist September 19, 2026 — 5:30am

September 19, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The younger generation doesn’t want our stuff. Sorry, correction. Upon our demise, the children are happy to accept the house, the clapped-out car and the bank account (should there be anything in it) – they are less keen on the furniture, the crockery and the table linen. This is according to a recent report which, while British, rings uncomfortably true. An auctioneer is quoted in the report: “A lot of the things baby boomers collected and treasured aren’t really worth a huge amount at the moment, and [they are] flooding the market at the same time.” That vintage train set’s got a one-way ticket to the tip. Getty Images Jocasta and I are hardly “collectors”. We don’t have a lazy Jackson Pollock in the second bedroom. Jocasta lacks a Louis Vuitton handbag lurking in her top drawer. But surely our stuff is worth something? The bookshelf we inherited from Jocasta’s father is beautiful, all dark wood and skilful inlays. As is the silver bowl we picked up two decades ago on a holiday in Mexico – probably fake silver, but it looks lovely, sitting there atop Max’s bookshelf. Plus, there are our dining table and chairs, built from Sydney blue gum by some bloke in Kempsey, the timbers so big you risk a hernia whenever you offer someone a seat.



Where will these things go when we die? According to the report: to the tip, to charity or sold off cheap. Younger people don’t like old stuff. They like new things, usually with a Swedish name from IKEA. The old stuff is too big and too dark for the smaller spaces they are now required to occupy. They need a sofa called a Spjütlägä, a chair called a Färklängër, and a table made entirely of lingonberries. Perhaps, also, this generation has less interest in the past. I cheer on this idea, then remember my own lack of interest in my mother’s treasures. After her death, it fell to me to empty her home. The stuff was well-made, but not my taste. A sideboard of dark carved wood, topped with white marble. A grandfather clock, ticking away. A giant oil painting, featuring an outback scene of cattle and ringers. Younger people don’t like old stuff. They like new things, usually with a Swedish name from IKEA. I discovered that she’d taken out hefty insurance, as if every item was destined for the Louvre. Well, maybe not the Louvre. But the grandfather clock was, according to her, worth tens of thousands, as was the collection of British model cars collected by her husband. (Not my father. My English teacher. Long story.) As it turned out, the most useful things proved to be her rusty old fridge and her dented washing machine. I dispatched them to my oldest son, then setting up a household in Victoria’s Wimmera. He wringed another 10 years out of them. The rest of the stuff was sold at auction, for amounts that would have reduced my mother to tears. The couch: $100. The treasured painting: not much more. And $300 for the fancy sideboard with the white marble top.



Even worse, from my mother’s point of view, was the complete lack of interest in the British toy car collection – insured, as I remember it, for $10,000. In the absence of an offer, I became the owner. They are now in my home. Being destroyed by my grandchildren. Please yell if you are interested in a 1960s Matchbox car with two missing wheels. Related Article Opinion

Pets Lying in defence of a puppy? I think I’ve made a new friend for life Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist Will this be the fate of my own stuff? I’ve hatched a plan to create a list of all the important items in the house. I’ll take a photo of each item, explain its significance, and then send the file to my offspring. Item: An abnormally large wax penis, which we’ve kept for over 45-years. It was a prop for the Joe Orton play What the Butler Saw, an amateur production of which was produced by Jocasta at the Australian National University. I walked past the theatre one day, popped my head in the door and offered to paint her sets. (Not a euphemism.) Anyway, that’s how the parents of these two children met, and so, when they throw the wax penis on the tip, as they inevitably will, at least they’ll know why we kept it. Item: My dad’s Free French Medal. My father had some imperfections, but he was a gregarious and creative man. As a British Navy guy, he worked with the Free French, helped run a Navy newspaper in the Pacific, then visited Hiroshima just months after the bomb. Just because his ungrateful son wrote a misery memoir about his parents’ faults, doesn’t mean his achievements should be forgotten.



Item: A watercolour of a Papua New Guinean woman, drawn by a friend of my father’s, probably in the early 1950s. It has a wooden frame, and the mount – the area between the frame and the image – consists of reeds, beautifully woven. Here’s the thing: the reeds were woven by her, the woman in the picture. The wooden frame was made from the timbers of a WWII warship sunk in Port Moresby Harbour. My father told me these things, and I’ve told my sons, but it was a long time ago. I’m sure they won’t remember. We all need to make a list. I’ve started mine. If you are of my vintage, maybe you should start yours. Need more Richard Glover in your life? World.title: Once pop’s wiliest genius, Beck sounds in need of a proper sea change
World.content:
CultureMusicReview Once pop’s wiliest genius, Beck sounds in need of a proper sea change Ben Madden Barry Divola and September 19, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beck’s Ride Lonesome: a case of diminishing returns. Beck, Ride Lonesome ★★ Beck has always been at his best when taking sharp turns, veering from warped lo-fi to hip-hop-influenced indie rock to slinky funk. So when the US singer-songwriter released 2002’s Sea Change, a sincere song cycle of genuine heartbreak, it was a revelation from a guy who had previously been pretty wry. He’s returned to that mode since then, on 2014’s less convincing Morning Phase, and now he’s gone there again on his first album in seven years. And, sadly, it’s a case of diminishing returns.



The title track is a pale facsimile of 2002’s The Golden Age, from the reverb-soaked melancholia to the high-plains drifter lyrics. The low-hanging strings of In the Night repeat his past Nick Drake obsessions, while It Ends Right Here, with sugar-sweet strumming and give-me-a-hug lines such as “All these people that you knew, all these cities you walk through, all this time it took to find you” could be from the Coldplay songbook. Beck, pictured with the Sydney Symphony Orchestra in May, retreads old ground on his new album. Daniel Boud He’s assembled the same band from back in the day and worked with a similar musical template, but too many of the songs remain stagnant, replicating the sonics but lacking the soul. “I don’t know where I’m going, but it feels like I’ve been here before,” Beck sings on Bleed. He sure has – and he’s done it better. Barry Divola



Robert Baxter’s PARTYANIMAL: the sweatiest nightclub you can imagine. Robert Baxter, PARTYANIMAL ★★★ From the opening seconds of Robert Baxter’s new EP, you’re transported into the sweatiest, most exclusive nightclub you can imagine. Thumping beats are the order of the day, and if you’re a lover of basslines, you’ll be in heaven (one that is downright debaucherous). I <3 Girls is a celebration of the trans girls and queer girls in Robert’s life and is begging to be played at countless pre-drinks. In Nameless, they embracing anonymity while partying on the other side of the globe, a canonical event for many Australian 20-somethings.



It would be easy to write off PARTYANIMAL as the latest in a long line of Australian pop projects that has wholeheartedly embraced clubbier sounds. However, at the heart of the EP lies a sincerity, with their lyricism revealing a more vulnerable side. BRB is a response to a music industry figure trying to undermine them, while closer Sky City pays tribute to the community they’ve built around themself, far from their origins growing up in rural Victorian town Shepparton. PARTYANIMAL is the type of project begging to be played at Berghain. It’s best listened to with the lights off and well after a typical bedtime has passed. World.title: That NFL match actually cost double previous estimates. But the jubilation made it worth it
World.content:
NationalVictoriaOpinion That NFL match actually cost double previous estimates. But the jubilation made it worth it Stephen Brook September 19, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Winter in Melbourne was awful. The weather unremitting: cost of living, deadly potholes, local shops firebombed, local gyms firebombed, teenagers stabbing each other. But unexpectedly, a burst of joy. The three-hour, 10.35am Friday NFL match at the Melbourne Cricket Ground between the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers last week had it all. Grand spectacle, folly (courtesy of the LA Rams attempts to defy jet lag) and something we have been missing for a while – jubilance. I didn’t attend the match nor understand what was going on. And for me, the real pleasure was not the onfield clash of titans but in the stuff that surrounded it. Fans show their support at the NFL game at the MCG. Ruby Alexander I owe thanks to a bunch of US sports writers (plus at least $30 million of taxpayer money) to blast away my jadedness about Melbourne and appreciate its pleasures anew.



I know that genuflecting to foreign arrivals is uncool, verging on pathetic. We Australian journalists have been doing this shamelessly ever since 1961 Hollywood star Vivien Leigh, fresh off the plane at Sydney Airport, was asked by the press corp what she thought about Australia. Before she had even left the terminal. Her famously arch response was: “I don’t know. You are standing in the way.” Last week it was San Francisco 49ers chief executive Al Guido smoothly telling me how “starstruck” he was arriving at the MCG. Yes, this made me happy. And I wouldn’t be the only one who looked upon their city anew after a crack squad of US football reporters arrived a week early alongside the 49ers and got among it, listing the CBD cafes they loved, posting snaps of their big brekkies. David Lombardi, of The San Francisco Standard, even taught a few Melburnians a thing or two as he looked out at the MCG from Princes Bridge, noting the City of Melbourne motto was “We gather strength as we go”. Who knew that? We all do now.



Even the highest powers were not immune. “Prayer the winning strategy as NFL makes its Australian debut,” proclaimed the newsletter of the Catholic Archdiocese of Melbourne. “Ahead of their Friday morning clash, a group of players from the San Francisco 49ers joined Melbourne’s Archbishop Peter A Comensoli for a pre-game celebration of the Eucharist. The Mass was organised through the team’s coaching staff and allowed players like star running back Christian McCaffrey, a Catholic, to partake in a different kind of preparation before the big game,” the newsletter reported. And you thought queues of 200 people outside the NFL pop-up shop on Bourke Street was the real story. NFL fans queuing up for official merchandise on Bourke Street on September 10. Eddie Jim All appropriate deference to Him, but the real star of the show was Grant Cohn, who covers the 49ers on SI.com. He posted on every aspect of his Melbourne visit. His lunchtime sausage roll and an iced coffee at 7-11. How to eat Vegemite on toast (a little bit of spread and a lot of butter). His honest assessment? “Pungent, definitely not Nutella.”



Fans include Victoria’s newish Major Events Minister Anthony Carbines, who took over from Steve Dimopoulos. And the AFL, which promptly hired him. There are lessons here for local journalists, about energy, intensity, but also in the foregrounding of daily pleasures that we treat nonchalantly. For Craig Hutchison and Eddie McGuire, ceaseless impresarios of sport and major events through their various media companies, the NFL match was nothing less than an exclamation point marking the end point of Victoria’s listless COVID-19 years. “It was a demonstration of love of sport, our passion for big events and why our city stands above all others in the world per capita in the want, willingness and enthusiasm to do that at 10.35am on a Friday morning (for) a sport that is not played here,” Hutchison enthused on his SEN podcast The Sounding Board. McGuire, unofficial ambassador for exuberance on Triple M’s Mick in the Morning radio program, said he was proud of the city.



“This is the end of the COVID era … this is the end of all the dramas, we can lift our head and be proud of Melbourne again. Back in town in a big way. “Let the politicians fight it out I don’t care about any of the stuff like that … fill a pothole in, throw a machete in a bin, we don’t care. It was tough on the Broadmeadows line in the 1970s.” Another perspective Opinion

Victoria After 37 years, I finally visited Melbourne. Here’s my verdict Paul Marshall Travel writer This was a lot, even for FM breakfast shows that are noted for exuberance – and we should note that one of McGuire’s very many hats is as a board member of Visit Victoria, which funded a large chunk of the NFL visit. Which brings us very neatly to the question of cost. The normally forthright Hutchison was uncharacteristically coy when asked directly how much the game had cost the state. “More than $15 million and a lot less than it was worth.”



While the “ballpark” figure of about $15 million per game was broadly quoted in the media, what was largely ignored was the other cost – staging the event. Simply put, that doubles the cost to at least $30 million. Extra transport, security, fan zones, the exclusion perimeter around the MCG, replacing the turf at the MCG, the MCG underground carpark becoming a vast player dressing room with players’ cabinets. And don’t think that all that media attention from NFL journalists just happened without some input from Visit Victoria. Then there was grand dinner at Government House for more than 230 guests featuring a trio of chefs – Andrew McConnell, Karen Martini and Dan Hunter, organised by The Big Group and Food + Drink Victoria. But the industry is very confident of a handsome return on investment. Hoteliers were ecstatic. Crown’s hotels had its second-biggest Thursday ever, while the Accor group, which has 53 hotels across Melbourne, including the Sofitel, Pullman and Novotel, was 25 per cent up on standard occupancy compared with the same time last year. What a waste of money better spent of schools, hospitals and potholes, I hear you say. Yes, critics might well complain such major events are a sugar hit, but there is no doubting the importance of the visitor economy for us, worth a record $48.6 billion (in the year to March 2026), creating 320,100 filled jobs, the government says.



Tourism is the state’s second most valuable export sector – bringing in overseas dollars – after education, which is undergoing a reset as the federal government bans family visas and visa hopping for international students. So the visitor economy is a long-term sustainable one. NAB put out a press release predicting that about $300 million would flow through Melbourne businesses thanks to the NFL. Which was quickly adopted as gospel. But it didn’t say what would be ordinarily spent over that period anyway. The real economic impact assessment will come later, if it is ever released. Carbines would not talk costs, either the NFL fees or staging costs, but said government investment in major events cemented the city as “Australia’s sporting, creative and cultural capital” that would “showcase Melbourne to millions around the world”. “A packed major events calendar … generated $3.64 billion in economic impact in 2025,” he said.



Major events must be bought at sensible price and have an ongoing benefit, as one-off events are a waste of money, says former premier Jeff Kennett, who took the grand prix off Adelaide in the 1990s in what was regarded a signature move indicating Victoria’s revival, giving the state a sign of hope amid painful restructure and large job losses. “Other states are envious of what we deliver. We must be forever on our toes,” Kennett says. In reference to the state’s poor balance sheet, he doesn’t suggest crimping on major events. “Here are a few other things we are wasting money on,” he says, nominating government waste, the Suburban Rail Loop, Big Build corruption, and interest payments on government debt, which could rise steeply if the state suffered a credit downgrade. Major events and sport such as the AFL were a “regular contributor to people’s happiness” he concludes. And NFL will be back again as part of its three-match commitment over four years (with an option for a fourth). But is there any Visit Victoria money left to spend on anything else?



Visit Victoria, which is on the cusp of releasing its latest annual report, must demonstrate a 10 to one economic benefit, which is in its constitution. The proof will be in whether the state can continue to attract other major events. The undoubted jewel in the crown of global musicals, Paddington, is rumoured to be going to Sydney. Can Visit Victoria win it for Melbourne? Watch and see. The strategy of bread and circuses, panem et circenses, literally as old as the Roman Empire, means subsidising the cost of grain and staging mass public spectacles to keep the masses happy, and – crucially – distracted from their rotten status in life. But it worked, here and in the US, where the game averaged 18.5 million viewers, ranking it among the top three most streamed games for its time slot. Related Article Analysis

NFL 2026 Singing, cheering and an American takeover: Why the NFL’s MCG experiment was a smash hit



David Lombardi, of The San Francisco Standard, says the popularity of his videos from Australia were an “explosion even bigger than Super Bowl coverage”. “Melbourne, you made this exponentially more massive than Americans expected. The 49ers certainly benefited from their time in the sporting capital of the world.” The fact is, we need this. As one damning assessment I came across put it:“Melbourne has to buy its visitors, Sydney, London and New York do not.” Now the days are warmer. I no longer wake at 3am. The ACO is playing Mozart’s Last Symphonies at Hamer Hall next week. The grand final is a week away. A ringtail possum is camping out in my barbecue, nesting in some local shrubbery. My niece has named it Nicholas Jr after her dad. Even Southern Cross Station seems cleaner. Meanwhile, Grant Cohn is still going. Back home, he has watched Two Hands and is trying to source a copy of The Castle.



And he announced a return visit to Australia in April when he will go wine tasting with his dad and cover the AFL. But in Adelaide, for Gather Round. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Trump says he is banning CNN and other news outlets from the White House
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump says he is banning CNN and other news outlets from the White House Michael Koziol September 19, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump said he was banning cable news channel CNN and two other prominent US media outlets from the White House because of what he referred to as their “constant ‘reporting’ fake news”. The US president made the declaration on his social media platform Truth Social on Friday afternoon, local time (Saturday morning AEST). He said MS-NOW, formerly known as MSNBC, was also banned, along with politics-focused news outlet Politico – which has just launched an Australian division. Donald Trump in the Rose Garden of the White House on Thursday night. AP Photo/Alex Brandon “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” Trump said. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.” He said the ban on the three outlets was effective immediately.



The announcement is an extraordinary escalation of Trump’s long-standing animosity towards the media and outlets that report factual stories he does not like. There was no immediate indication that Trump’s threat was being implemented. CNN reporters were still present at the White House in the hour following his social media post. CNN’s Kaitlan Collins in the White House press briefing room. AP The White House Correspondents’ Association, which traditionally manages the media presence in the White House press pool, was contacted for comment. Founded in 1980, CNN provides close coverage of US politics, with several prominent reporters ordinarily based at the White House. Owned by Warner Bros Discovery, it is set to be sold to David Ellison’s Paramount Skydance as part of a $US110 billion merger, though Paramount recently said selling the channel was an option to resolve market concentration issues in the deal.



Trump has frequently targeted CNN for its coverage of his war against Iran and other matters. He has directed many attacks at high-profile anchor Kaitlan Collins, whom he called “very dumb and unhappy” last week. He regularly accuses her of failing to smile sufficiently. Politico’s inclusion on the banned list was surprising given it is not a regular Trump target. In his Truth Social post, he dredged up an old complaint about the outlet receiving $US8 million from the Biden administration, suggesting it was “corruption”. In fact, the money was for subscriptions to Politico’s premium products. More to come Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: How this team of experts guide 80-metre turbine blades down our roads with just millimetres to spare
World.content:
It is just after midnight on a winter morning when we gather at the Port of Newcastle.

In the background coal ships slink by, in the foreground an almost inconceivably vast wind turbine blade lies along the spine of a truck bed like some sort of alien life form strapped to a gurney in a sci-fi film.

It’s so big that it’s hard to fit it all into the frame of your eye from any reasonable perspective. At its tip it tapers to the length of schoolkid’s ruler. Towards that tapered end it has a jagged edge like a cartoon dragon’s teeth, a shape designed to reduce noise as it slices through the air. Peering up at its midsection, you could be looking at a warship’s prow from the ocean’s surface.

A team of transport specialists are making last-minute preparations to move this beast through the sleeping streets of suburban Newcastle and the coal villages of the Hunter Valley, along the Golden Highway to a hillside outside Wellington on the NSW Central Slopes, where it is to be raised upon a tower as part of a Squadron Energy wind farm that will soon be generating enough electricity for about 220,000 homes.

It seems absurd that this thing can be moved at all, let alone along busy roads, but the man in charge of this circus, Steve Spiller, seems impossibly calm. Jovial, even.

The police and pilots gather before the start of the turbine blade’s trip from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW Photo: Janie Barrett

Form and function

Wind turbine blades, explains engineer Dr Rosemary Barnes, are the largest single-component objects that humans regularly either build or seek to move. Artefacts of the modern world tend to shrink as technology advances, but wind turbines, shaped by both economic and physical forces, keep growing.

Longer turbine blades scoop up more wind and generate more electricity with each rotation, says Barnes, who has spent a career designing, building and repairing turbines and blades around the world and now runs a renewable energy consultancy. A dozen huge turbines need fewer gearboxes, less cable and wiring, less maintenance, less concrete and steel to generate as much electricity as dozens of small ones.

As the turbines grow in length, so do the forces exerted upon them. In extreme conditions, a large blade might bend 10 to 15 metres from a straight line. Imagine, says Barnes, a diving board wilting under the weight of a herd of elephants.

“They have to survive that transfer of force hundreds of millions of times over a life of about 30 years. Every time the blade is in the three o’clock position, gravity is bending it one way, and then when it goes into the nine o’clock position, it’s bending the exact opposite way, and it keeps repeating like that as it spins. It’s just like if you bend a paperclip back and forth repeatedly, you know that small load is not going to break it, but you do it enough times, and you get fatigue loading, it is going to break.”

All this means that not only must a blade be handmade from tough, light composite materials, they are stronger when they are crafted in a single piece, rather than disassembled for transport, which brings us back to Spiller and his crew in Newcastle.

The monster they are about to move is 82 metres long and weighs just over 20 tonnes.

The port

The crew is doing last-minute checks on vehicles and equipment. Craig Carpenter is inspecting the Kenworth truck and the purpose-built trailer he is about to drive. The trailer has a long spine that can be extended to suit its load, and six sets of axles at the rear.

The steerer, Freddie Scheepers, checks the truck prior to the start of the turbine blade’s trip from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

Tonight Carpenter’s load from front grille to blade tip will be 92 metres long. Carpenter picked up the nickname Blade Runner One for his smooth driving while moving blades in Western Australia last year, but just as crucial is Freddie Scheepers, who is “steerer” and will pursue Carpenter in a van close behind the truck.

Scheepers must not only keep his own vehicle on the road, but when necessary will use a remote control to steer the rear axles of the trailer. He keeps in constant contact with Carpenter so at any given moment the two know exactly where the blade tip is in relation to the road and the rest of the rig.

“Those two are very, very close, and they’ve got a really good bond. They know what the other bloke is going to do before he does it.” Steve Spiller, Project Manager

When the front of the rig moves upwards and is forcing the tip towards the ground, Scheepers will also be able to raise and lower the blade itself, the last metres of which rest in a hydraulic jack that sits over the axle sets.

“Those two are very, very close, and they’ve got a really good bond,” says Spiller, watching Carpenter and Scheepers make final preparations. “They know what the other bloke is going to do before he does it.”

Mayfield Macca’s

The convoy pulls out at about 1am. There are two police cars, as required by law when moving a load of this size in NSW. There are four pilot vehicles which help manage traffic around the truck and trailer. Scheepers’ steering van hunts along behind the blade like a sheepdog, and we follow in a four-wheel drive with Spiller, the project manager.

The turbine blade starts its journey from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

Also in tow is a Transport NSW vehicle with a couple of observers, there to see if anything can be learnt or improved for future runs. After this, there are still another 195 blades to go, let alone the turbine hubs, tower sections and generators.

“When you pull back the curtain, this is what building a wind farm looks like – thousands of individual movements, decisions and people are needed to get every component to site,” Squadron Energy’s chief executive Rob Wheals later observes.

Steve Spiller, Ares Group project manager, accompanies the turbine blade on its journey from Newcastle to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

“At 80 metres long and shaped like a banana, each blade is one of the most challenging pieces of infrastructure to ever move.”

From Spiller’s radio we can hear occasional chatter from the pilot vehicles, but he leaves the “Bladerunners” to their own quiet comms channel so they can concentrate. Before we’ve even left the Port precinct the blade tip sweeps out over a cyclone fence, clearing it by what seems like centimetres.

Spiller doesn’t flinch. Every move is rehearsed, every distance measured.

The turbine blade crosses the highway from the wrong side on its journey from the Port of Newcastle to the wind farm. Photo: Janie Barrett

At a McDonald’s on a roundabout on Industrial Drive in the neighbouring suburb of Mayfield, the cop cars and pilot vehicles splay out to halt traffic coming from three directions, and Scheepers climbs out of his van to flick a switch on the rig to remote control. He adjusts the height of the suspension, and then he steers the rear of the rig around the turn.

The turbine blade crosses the highway from the wrong side at the intersection of Industrial Drive and Maitland Road, Mayfield. Photo: Janie Barrett

Speed picks up, at least until the caravan reaches the Hunter Expressway. To make it onto that section, the pilots block traffic on the expressway in both directions while the Bladerunners navigate the rig 80 metres down an off-ramp into what would otherwise be oncoming traffic, then drive a kilometre down the wrong side of the road before crossing back. Spiller seems pleased by how smoothly this dance of traffic and truck is performed.

The remote used for steering the rear of the truck that carried the enormous turbine blade. Photo: Janie Barrett

As we head northwest towards the Golden Highway, Spiller relaxes enough to tell his story. He became an expert in moving big stuff almost by accident. At 19, he took a job with a logistics firm and began moving shipping containers. Half a decade later he was moving wind turbine parts, and the work took him around the world with the global giant GE. He has moved bits and pieces of wind farms by sea and land and even air, at one point chartering the world’s biggest aircraft, an Antonov, to move a wind turbine hub and six generators from Leipzig to Adelaide.

In Germany, near the Polish border, he recalls coaxing blades through tiny villages on a truck that could raise them to near vertical from the base to navigate tight spaces.

Freddie Scheepers changes the steering of the rear of the truck from manual to automatic via an external switch on the truck. Photo: Janie Barrett

In Australia, it’s easier because we have so much space. “I moved 300 blades through Toowoomba without complaint,” he boasts. Today he works for the Ares Group, which was contracted by GE, who built the blade at a factory in China, to shepherd it safely off the ship in Newcastle and on to the Squadron Energy site outside Wellington.

Despite the late hour you can tell the convoy is having an impact along the way. In one hamlet we pass within metres of the old coal miners’ cottages. A man in a dressing gown watches on in the pre-dawn from his veranda. His expression is impossible to read in the revolving lights.

Craig Carpenter, the truck driver who drove the turbine blade from Newcastle to the Uungula wind farm. Photo: Janie Barrett

From the sections of widened road you can see along the way the years of preparation that went into this operation. EnergyCo, the NSW government authority responsible for delivering the state’s five renewable energy zones, has spent $130 million preparing this route.



Inland

There are rules about moving oversized loads in the dark on the Golden Highway, so the convoy pulls over before dawn. A quiet pall descends across the still convoy, except for cheerful noises from Carpenter’s cabin. He hums and sings to himself and taps out a rhythm before drifting into silence.

In bright early light, against the country homes in Denman, the enormity of the blade begins to become more clear. It is longer than whole blocks of the little town. Along the Golden Highway, the convoy at times creeps up to something approaching normal traffic speed, and time passes quickly until we reach the site of the wind farm, headquartered on a sheep and cattle operation on rolling green hills east of Wellington.

As the truck prepares to tackle the narrow dirt roads built for the project we are taken into a sprawling site office for a safety induction. Whiteboards on the walls show the progress in the construction of each of the 69 turbines that will soon be operational here. There are posters boosting the “core values” of Squadron Energy, which is owned by Tattarang, the investment company that in turn owned by Andrew Forrest and Nicola Forrest. The values include “Humility” and “Frugality”.

It is midafternoon on a hilltop I had last seen two years earlier when Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Forrest attended a sod-turning ceremony. Bladerunner One finally steps out of his cabin and offers up a great two-armed stretch to the sky. By now Spiller has left the site on his way back to his head office in Melbourne. Workers on-site scramble over the blade, breaking it free of its harnesses and lowering it into a cradle by a half-built tower. By the time it is operational it will stand 148 metres from base to blade tip.

There’s no getting around the impact the project is having on a beautiful landscape. Construction pads are scraped into the ground by each tower and the new roads hum with the sort of traffic flow you’d expect in a prosperous town.

The turbine blade arrives ar the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW Photo: Janie Barrett

Later I ask farmer John Holland, owner of Uungula, for which the wind farm is named, what he makes of it all. He speaks with a careful, precise manner, aware of the controversy that wind projects attract. Squadron, he says, will clean up after the construction is complete, leaving him with new roads, giving even better access to the property’s ridge lines.

He says he has no fear about the impact of the turbines on his stock. Visiting other wind farms, he has seen sheep “camping” under the towers for shade. He reckons the turbines look majestic, but admits that when he saw renders of what they would look like spread across the land he loves he found it “a little confronting.”

He thinks renewable energy is a part of the solution for Australia’s growing energy demand, but not the only one. Like many farmers, he opposes grid-scale solar plants taking up agricultural land. But he has practical considerations too. The rent Squadron will pay for each turbine will let the family retire a fair chunk of debt, though he won’t say how much. Nor will he say how many turbines his farm will host. “That’s a bit like asking how much money I’ve got in the bank. It’s a bit rude.”

But he is happy to say the income has helped settle the questions of succession that can cause such grief to farming families, and to update equipment and improve fences and dams.

“It’s the confidence to be able to run the property the way it should be run.”

I ask him what Uungula means.

“It’s an Aboriginal word,” he says. “It means wind in the hills.”

Workers unload the turbine blade after its long journey. Photo: Janie Barrett

World.content:

Accountant to the stars Anthony Bell has put his Rose Bay apartment on the market in an expression of interest campaign. Bell, whose clients have included Karl Stefanovic and Michael Clarke, said that while he initially intended to make the Rose Bay unit his principal place of residence, he enjoyed renting at Barangaroo’s Crown Residences so much that he decided to buy there. Money manager Anthony Bell has decided to offload his harbourside Rose Bay apartment in Sydney that he renovated. Records show Bell, chief executive officer and principal of accounting and advisory firm Bell Partners, bought the five-bedroom, four-bathroom Rose Bay apartment for $9,657,000 in 2024 from architect Andre Heyko-Porebski and his wife, Louise. Bell intended to make the unit his principal place of residence.



While renovating the interiors, Bell rented at Crown Residences in Barangaroo, a complex now home to a smorgasbord of corporate heavyweights and rich-listers such as Alex Birkenstock, heir of German cult sandal brand Birkenstock, Luna Park co-owner Bill Gravanis, and Lawrence Myers, chief executive officer of James Packer’s family office Consolidated Press Holdings. Anthony Bell and Annika Martyn For a short time, there was also a tenant at the Rose Bay pad. Bell said that he enjoyed Crown’s proximity to his office at King Street Wharf, a short walk away, so much that he decided to purchase there. Records show Bell bought a four-bedroom apartment at Crown for $26,588,000 in December 2024 that settled in July the following year.



Also in 2024, Bell sold his Dover Heights home for $20.78 million after he bought it for $11.5 million in 2017 from his mate, Channel Seven star Larry Emdur and his wife, Sylvie. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Fruit and veg supplier drops about $9.5m in 24 hours on Crown unit Bell also owns two Queensland properties – a Surfers Paradise home bought with wife Annika Martyn, the founder of wellness brand GG Vitality, for $5.3 million in 2024, and a Noosaville abode purchased with then-wife, former model and TV presenter Kelly Landry, for $10,301,000 in 2017. The Rose Bay harbourside pad features a neutral palette with refined marble finishes, a custom bar, private gym/Pilates studio, jacuzzi and a north-east facing terrace. Bill Malouf and David Malouf of Highland Double Bay are the listing agents.

After about two bids, Cooper secured sole ownership of the luxury property for $3,871,000. Wayne and his ex-wife Sarah Marsh Scott Barbour The three-level abode has wraparound balconies, covered entertaining areas, a tennis court that awaits a refresh, and views across the coast to Julian Rocks and Mount Warning. World.title: What the cameras missed after Lloyd Meek copped a spray from his coach
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sam Mitchell charged into Hawthorn’s change rooms at half-time of his team’s round seven clash with Gold Coast, ruckman Lloyd Meek firmly in his sights. An errant backwards handball by Meek in the dying stages of the second quarter had led to a crucial turnover, allowing the Suns to score a goal with four seconds left on the clock. Mitchell, fuming, delivered an animated spray – which amateur lip-readers discerned contained a lot of f---s – that quickly went viral on social media, largely due to the wide-eyed expressions of Meek’s shocked teammates. View post on X “I know that when he’s aggressive and he’s fired up, it’s because of how much he cares, and I’m the same,” Meek told this masthead. “I’m exactly the same. So like, we’re all competitive people. We wouldn’t be here if we weren’t. We all want to win. And sometimes those conversations are just what it takes to get the message across. “At the time, obviously no one likes being yelled out. But I was still so stoked with how we were able to respond and come out of that.”



Hawthorn went on to win the game by 49 points, holding Gold Coast goalless in the final term. Meek points out there’s a lot the broadcast cameras don’t see or show. The ruckman said Mitchell checked in with him before running out for the third quarter, and again after the game, to check he was OK. “He came up to me and said ‘well done, you responded really well’, and we had a good chat, no one sees that,” Meek said. Lloyd Meek says his coach Sam Mitchell embodies the values Hawthorn want to be known for. Eddie JIm “You just see one 30-second snippet and think ‘geez, he’s copped a spray’. But it’s like no, we’ve actually had conversations all day.” Growing up in Mininera in regional Victoria – Meek hails from a prestigious rowing family, with his dad and his siblings all winning Head of the Lake titles. He was selected by Fremantle with pick 69 in the 2017 draft, but did not debut in the AFL until his fourth season at the Dockers. He later moved to Hawthorn during the 2022 trade period to seek more opportunities in the ruck. As an example of Mitchell’s close connection to his players, Meek revealed the coach delivered handwritten letters to each of them before their qualifying final win, on the road, against Fremantle.



“[In the letter] he mentioned that he was glad that I picked Hawthorn and had faith in me, and how we’ve both, I guess, grown over that four-year period,” Meek said. Meek said he found it difficult to fully articulate what Mitchell meant to the playing group, heralding the head coach as someone who “makes every single person feels valuable”. A kiss on the head from Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell to Nick Watson after the qualifying final win over Fremantle. AFL Photos “He [Mitchell] is Hawthorn,” he said. “He’s so pivotal and so important to what we’ve built … not discrediting the[other] people; the board and the football club and the other coaches and staff, but he has built so much of the environment that we get to come in and enjoy every day, and that’s probably been something that I have valued and appreciated since coming to Hawthorn. ” “Everything he spoke about and his vision for us and the club was so aligned with what I wanted in my career.” Meek has endless praise for Mitchell’s coaching abilities, but has some doubts about the coach’s prowess at chess. Mitchell and a few other Hawthorn players regularly play chess online, with the head coach known to have a solid winning streak.



“I don’t know if I’ve ever played [against] him, but I reckon I’d be able to beat him,” Meek joked. “I think he likes to play on chess.com, so I think he’s pretty handy. He probably uses AI to cheat.” Hawthorn’s preliminary final clash with Brisbane on Saturday comes six weeks after the back-to-back reigning premiers took them to the cleaners in round 22, the Lions storming to a 67-point win at the Gabba. Related Article Analysis

Brownlow Medal The big intrigue that’s looming for Brownlow night After the thumping loss Mitchell remarked, “we’re better than that, and we’re going to have to prove it”. When he spoke to this masthead this week, Meek was yet to watch footage of the Lions’ semi-final victory over Adelaide because the game clashed with his 10-year-high school reunion in Ballarat; an event the 28-year-old attended alongside his childhood sweetheart, now wife, Elonie, who he met in Year Nine. Ahead of the prelim, Meek intended to keep things simple.

World.title: Powerhouse Parramatta’s $4.5 million opening festival revealed
World.content:
Breaking CultureArt & designCity life Powerhouse Parramatta’s $4.5 million opening festival revealed Linda Morris September 19, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 23-day festival program featuring 179 events heralding the opening of the billion-dollar Parramatta Powerhouse will be unveiled on Saturday, as the government attempts to look past executive turmoil and build public momentum for western Sydney’s first state-significant cultural institution. The launch will proceed minus the museum’s driving force, Lisa Havilah, who was stood down two weeks ago pending the outcome of a formal misconduct investigation into what Parliament was told were “serious” allegations involving two executives of the Powerhouse Museum. The construction fence has come down on the new Powerhouse Museum. Steven Siewert Havilah is said to be strongly defending her conduct. NSW Government Architect Abbie Galvin is serving as acting chief executive until an inquiry by Sydney-based law firm Lander and Rogers concludes. Despite the leadership crisis, the $4.5 million opening festival, funded by the Department of Creative Industries, runs from November 7 to 29 at the new riverside venue.



The line-up is short on high-cost spectacle such as outdoor concerts or drone shows, focusing instead on immersive works, talks and community events. The state government confirmed 65 per cent of the launch program would be free. Ticketed events will cost from $15 to $50 and will go on sale from midday Saturday September 19. “It’s a great way to ease pressure on the budget as the majority of events are free,” Arts Minister John Graham said. The festival kicks off on opening day, November 7, following a ribbon-cutting ceremony, a plaque unveiling and the previous day’s donor preview and media tour. To manage crowd capacity over the November 7-8 launch weekend, patrons will be required to book timed hourly arrival slots through the Powerhouse website from midday this Saturday. Related Article City life Too big to fund, too big to fail: The pitfalls lying in wait for the Powerhouse Seven weeks out from ribbon cutting, general admission pricing for post-opening visits remains unconfirmed, though the biggest show, Task Eternal, will require paid tickets for visitors over the age of 16 years.



At the same time as it is launching its festival, the Powerhouse is advertising itself as Sydney’s newest event destination on socials. It is also advertising rental of its “flexible, large-scale spaces for events from 20 to 1,000 guests”. During the three weeks and four weekends of the festival, operating hours will run from 10am to 5pm Monday through Wednesday, and 10am to 9pm Thursday through Sunday. Post-festival operating schedules have also not been finalised and, as the Herald has disclosed, they are expected to be wound back to 10am to 5pm permanently as Treasury searches for belated cost savings. Former NASA administrator Charles F. Bolden Jr, who flew on four space shuttle missions, leads the space and technology roster alongside science fiction author Ted Chiang (both November 8), whose short story Tower of Babylon inspired the design of the museum’s Task Eternal. Chiang will discuss the pursuit of immortality. Additional talk panels focus on bio-manufacturing, space technology and AI diagnostics. On the opening weekend, Locomotive 3265 – a 124-year-old steam train from the Powerhouse Collection originally commissioned in 1902 – will run passenger trips between Parramatta and Riverstone stations, accompanied by performances from the NSW Railway Band. Related Article Analysis

City life The inside story of the day that shook Sydney’s museum world



On the Powerhouse terrace, British artist Es Devlin presents Come Home Again, an 11-night installation featuring 244 hand-drawn depictions of endangered NSW species created alongside the Botanic Gardens of Sydney, accompanied by live choral performances from River City Voices, Barayagal and Noqu Vanua. Industrial designer Marc Newson (November 7) reflects on four decades of work, while artist Bharti Kher unveils her public sculpture Tree of Life. Sydney Chamber Opera will perform two newly commissioned works responding to Anton Bruckner’s 1869 Locus Iste and an 1879 Sydney International Exhibition cantata held in the museum’s collection. Opening ceremonies begin with a Welcome to Country by the Jannawi Dance Clan and the presentation of a kahu kuri (dog skin) cloak by artist Keren Ruki, featuring a hand-woven kaupapa base that took 3000 hours to complete. Related Article Exclusive

City life Night opening hours set to be cut at new Powerhouse museum Pacific community collective Matavai Pacific Cultural Arts will launch the hand-carved Maori watercraft Te Waka Whakakotahi alongside traditional weaving displays. Forty-four male dancers and eight musicians from Badu Island will perform Eseli’s Story, based on memories of World War II fighter planes and bombers taking off from Horn Island, marking the Torres Strait Islander story-dance’s first staging in its entirety outside its home region.

World.title: What will happen to your most cherished possessions when you die? You don’t want to know
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsParenting Opinion What will happen to your most cherished possessions when you die? You don’t want to know Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist September 19, 2026 — 5:30am

September 19, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The younger generation doesn’t want our stuff. Sorry, correction. Upon our demise, the children are happy to accept the house, the clapped-out car and the bank account (should there be anything in it) – they are less keen on the furniture, the crockery and the table linen. This is according to a recent report which, while British, rings uncomfortably true. An auctioneer is quoted in the report: “A lot of the things baby boomers collected and treasured aren’t really worth a huge amount at the moment, and [they are] flooding the market at the same time.” That vintage train set’s got a one-way ticket to the tip. Getty Images Jocasta and I are hardly “collectors”. We don’t have a lazy Jackson Pollock in the second bedroom. Jocasta lacks a Louis Vuitton handbag lurking in her top drawer. But surely our stuff is worth something? The bookshelf we inherited from Jocasta’s father is beautiful, all dark wood and skilful inlays. As is the silver bowl we picked up two decades ago on a holiday in Mexico – probably fake silver, but it looks lovely, sitting there atop Max’s bookshelf. Plus, there are our dining table and chairs, built from Sydney blue gum by some bloke in Kempsey, the timbers so big you risk a hernia whenever you offer someone a seat.



Where will these things go when we die? According to the report: to the tip, to charity or sold off cheap. Younger people don’t like old stuff. They like new things, usually with a Swedish name from IKEA. The old stuff is too big and too dark for the smaller spaces they are now required to occupy. They need a sofa called a Spjütlägä, a chair called a Färklängër, and a table made entirely of lingonberries. Perhaps, also, this generation has less interest in the past. I cheer on this idea, then remember my own lack of interest in my mother’s treasures. After her death, it fell to me to empty her home. The stuff was well-made, but not my taste. A sideboard of dark carved wood, topped with white marble. A grandfather clock, ticking away. A giant oil painting, featuring an outback scene of cattle and ringers. Younger people don’t like old stuff. They like new things, usually with a Swedish name from IKEA. I discovered that she’d taken out hefty insurance, as if every item was destined for the Louvre. Well, maybe not the Louvre. But the grandfather clock was, according to her, worth tens of thousands, as was the collection of British model cars collected by her husband. (Not my father. My English teacher. Long story.) As it turned out, the most useful things proved to be her rusty old fridge and her dented washing machine. I dispatched them to my oldest son, then setting up a household in Victoria’s Wimmera. He wringed another 10 years out of them. The rest of the stuff was sold at auction, for amounts that would have reduced my mother to tears. The couch: $100. The treasured painting: not much more. And $300 for the fancy sideboard with the white marble top.



Even worse, from my mother’s point of view, was the complete lack of interest in the British toy car collection – insured, as I remember it, for $10,000. In the absence of an offer, I became the owner. They are now in my home. Being destroyed by my grandchildren. Please yell if you are interested in a 1960s Matchbox car with two missing wheels. Related Article Opinion

Pets Lying in defence of a puppy? I think I’ve made a new friend for life Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist Will this be the fate of my own stuff? I’ve hatched a plan to create a list of all the important items in the house. I’ll take a photo of each item, explain its significance, and then send the file to my offspring. Item: An abnormally large wax penis, which we’ve kept for over 45-years. It was a prop for the Joe Orton play What the Butler Saw, an amateur production of which was produced by Jocasta at the Australian National University. I walked past the theatre one day, popped my head in the door and offered to paint her sets. (Not a euphemism.) Anyway, that’s how the parents of these two children met, and so, when they throw the wax penis on the tip, as they inevitably will, at least they’ll know why we kept it. Item: My dad’s Free French Medal. My father had some imperfections, but he was a gregarious and creative man. As a British Navy guy, he worked with the Free French, helped run a Navy newspaper in the Pacific, then visited Hiroshima just months after the bomb. Just because his ungrateful son wrote a misery memoir about his parents’ faults, doesn’t mean his achievements should be forgotten.



Item: A watercolour of a Papua New Guinean woman, drawn by a friend of my father’s, probably in the early 1950s. It has a wooden frame, and the mount – the area between the frame and the image – consists of reeds, beautifully woven. Here’s the thing: the reeds were woven by her, the woman in the picture. The wooden frame was made from the timbers of a WWII warship sunk in Port Moresby Harbour. My father told me these things, and I’ve told my sons, but it was a long time ago. I’m sure they won’t remember. We all need to make a list. I’ve started mine. If you are of my vintage, maybe you should start yours. Need more Richard Glover in your life? World.title: Once pop’s wiliest genius, Beck sounds in need of a proper sea change
World.content:
CultureMusicReview Once pop’s wiliest genius, Beck sounds in need of a proper sea change Ben Madden Barry Divola and September 19, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beck’s Ride Lonesome: a case of diminishing returns. Beck, Ride Lonesome ★★ Beck has always been at his best when taking sharp turns, veering from warped lo-fi to hip-hop-influenced indie rock to slinky funk. So when the US singer-songwriter released 2002’s Sea Change, a sincere song cycle of genuine heartbreak, it was a revelation from a guy who had previously been pretty wry. He’s returned to that mode since then, on 2014’s less convincing Morning Phase, and now he’s gone there again on his first album in seven years. And, sadly, it’s a case of diminishing returns.



The title track is a pale facsimile of 2002’s The Golden Age, from the reverb-soaked melancholia to the high-plains drifter lyrics. The low-hanging strings of In the Night repeat his past Nick Drake obsessions, while It Ends Right Here, with sugar-sweet strumming and give-me-a-hug lines such as “All these people that you knew, all these cities you walk through, all this time it took to find you” could be from the Coldplay songbook. Beck, pictured with the Sydney Symphony Orchestra in May, retreads old ground on his new album. Daniel Boud He’s assembled the same band from back in the day and worked with a similar musical template, but too many of the songs remain stagnant, replicating the sonics but lacking the soul. “I don’t know where I’m going, but it feels like I’ve been here before,” Beck sings on Bleed. He sure has – and he’s done it better. Barry Divola



Robert Baxter’s PARTYANIMAL: the sweatiest nightclub you can imagine. Robert Baxter, PARTYANIMAL ★★★ From the opening seconds of Robert Baxter’s new EP, you’re transported into the sweatiest, most exclusive nightclub you can imagine. Thumping beats are the order of the day, and if you’re a lover of basslines, you’ll be in heaven (one that is downright debaucherous). I <3 Girls is a celebration of the trans girls and queer girls in Robert’s life and is begging to be played at countless pre-drinks. In Nameless, they embracing anonymity while partying on the other side of the globe, a canonical event for many Australian 20-somethings.



It would be easy to write off PARTYANIMAL as the latest in a long line of Australian pop projects that has wholeheartedly embraced clubbier sounds. However, at the heart of the EP lies a sincerity, with their lyricism revealing a more vulnerable side. BRB is a response to a music industry figure trying to undermine them, while closer Sky City pays tribute to the community they’ve built around themself, far from their origins growing up in rural Victorian town Shepparton. PARTYANIMAL is the type of project begging to be played at Berghain. It’s best listened to with the lights off and well after a typical bedtime has passed.
