Tech.title: Sweeping EU Child Safety Proposal Would Transform Social Media, Online Gaming and AI Chatbots
Tech.content:
A new proposal this week from the European Commission, if enacted, would set some of the tightest restrictions yet on technology products, from social media to games to AI chatbots.

The EU Kids Act would follow, and in some ways surpass, similar measures that have been imposed in Australia, the UK, China and India, and would require tech companies such as Meta, Google, YouTube and Roblox to change the way they do business. But first, the legislation will need to be vetted, debated and voted on.

Its pillars include a social media ban for kids under 13, age verification for online accounts and requirements for tech companies to provide proof that their online services are safely designed. The proposal is the formal version of what’s been discussed for months and is a result of mounting public pressure for governments to get a handle on easily accessible technologies that have been shown across research and in court judgments to cause harm to children, such as internet addiction and vulnerability to contact from predators.

“Our Kids Act is reversing the burden of proof — it is for platforms to show they are safe by design,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement Thursday. “And we put parents back in the driving seat, giving them the tools to help their children navigate a safer online world.”

Megan Jenkins, an analyst at Assembly Research who studies AI and online safety, said the Kids Act “goes further than other legislation proposed so far, and represents a big shift from the blanket social media bans we’ve seen in countries such as Australia.”

Jenkins said the biggest change from some of those laws is creating a burden of proof for tech companies to demonstrate that their products are safe, which would be the first law of its kind. “If tech companies can’t prove this, they would be unable to provide services to minors,” she said.

What’s in the EU Kids Act

Discussion of what would and wouldn’t be in the Kids Act began days earlier when drafts of the proposal were leaked. Ultimately, what ended up in the Kids Act is broader than what was expected — in addition to a tiered age system for when teens can access social media, it would require companies that make online games, AI chatbots or companions, and social networks to prove that they’re safe and free from features like infinite scrolling that could be considered manipulative or addictive to children.

The biggest component is the social media ban for those under 13 years of age. For teens under 15, parents could create a mini account accessible through their own account on age-appropriate social media or video-sharing platforms. Screen time would be limited to an hour per day. Teens aged 16 to 18 could create anonymous accounts without parental consent.

Two other major pillars of the proposal are aimed at tech companies. They would be required to include no addictive design features and would need to provide easy-to-use parental controls, recommendation algorithms that are safe for kids and no options for minors to livestream. They would also be required to verify ages for new accounts or anyone logging in to an existing account.

The last part of the proposal covers enforcement: The EU would speed up the time it takes to investigate violations, with the goal of concluding them within 90 days. Companies with 45 million or more active users would need to submit a compliance plan for any new services or features and face a review of up to 30 days. New features, services or functionalities that don’t meet a “positive opinion” from the European Commission would not be allowed.

The age verification ‘sticking point’

Even if the EU proposal is passed without too many changes, enforcing it will be a challenge. It would likely face legal challenges from some of the world’s biggest tech companies and, as countries such as Australia have found, it’s hard to impose constraints that teens can’t find ways to get around.

“These restrictions are also not likely to be successful, as seen with other age verification and social media bans that have been consistently circumvented by tech-savvy kids,” said David Inserra, a fellow for free expression and technology at the Cato Institute.

Inserra added that the age verification technologies themselves pose privacy issues, “creating massive amounts of sensitive identification data that will be subject to hacks and data breaches” for teens as well as adults.

Jenkins agreed that age verification has remained a “bit of a sticking point” for online safety regulation due to privacy concerns, but said she believes the Kids Act is a positive step in moving away from blanket social media bans for kids.

Tech.title: AI Firms Knew Chatbots Were an ‘Existential Threat’ to Journalists, Court Docs Show
Tech.content:
AI companies used vast troves of published text to train their large language models, and executives at those firms were aware that doing so constituted a theft of copyrighted materials, according to comments cited by news publishers in a court filing that was unredacted this week.

The brief was initially filed earlier this month in a court proceeding that brings together several related copyright infringement cases against ChatGPT maker OpenAI and its partner Microsoft, including lawsuits brought by The New York Times and by Ziff Davis, which owns CNET.

Microsoft’s director of applied science, Brent Hecht, called it “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions” and maybe the “largest theft of labor in human history,” according to the publishers’ filing. The full exhibits showing the context of the quotes in the filing remain under seal.

The comments cited by publishers appear to undercut the argument by AI companies that the use of copyrighted material was legally protected as fair use. Under this legal doctrine, use of copyrighted material is protected depending on how it’s used, the nature of the work, how much of it was used and the effect of the use on the market for that work.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said under oath that conversations with chatbots gave information “right there on the website on the AI platform versus needing to go to the underlying source,” like the website of a publisher that reported the information, according to the filing. Similarly, an OpenAI executive wrote that publishers faced an “existential threat” from products like the company’s chatbot.

The publishers’ brief also describes steps AI developers took to evade paywalls, like that for The New York Times. It describes how an OpenAI employee told the company’s president, Greg Brockman, about “a hack to get around nytimes paywall,” to which Brockman replied, “ah nice.”

At the same time, the filing says Nadella testified that anything behind a paywall “should be licensed by anyone who wants to use it” for AI development and that if he had been aware OpenAI had trained on paywalled content, he would have required OpenAI to retrain its models.

In a statement provided to CNET, a Microsoft spokesperson said that Hecht’s comments “reflect one employee’s perspectives” and that the company’s position is in its court filings, which “explain why these transformative uses are consistent with copyright law and why Copilot is not a substitute for publishers’ journalism.”

Nadella’s comments addressed changes in how people consume information and are “perfectly consistent” with the company’s legal position, the spokesperson said. “Those observations should not be confused with conclusions about copyright questions before the Court, which Microsoft addresses in its filings.”

In its own brief in the case, Microsoft said the use of published content to train LLMs was significantly transformative. “Copyright law does not permit rightsholders to block transformative technologies like LLMs; it encourages such uses on the expectation that rightsholders will adapt and the public will be better off for it,” the company argued.

Representatives for OpenAI and Ziff Davis did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

LLMs are trained on as much published content as developers can get their hands on, and the litigation over copyright — including related cases from book authors — could have a significant impact on both AI companies and media outlets. Publishers argue AI companies should have to pay to license the content they use, while the tech companies say doing so is unnecessary and burdensome to the development of more capable AI. The Trump administration weighed in on the case earlier this month with a statement arguing a licensing requirement would impede American AI development in a race with China.

OpenAI and Microsoft employees were also aware that their chatbots’ ability to find, copy, summarize and sometimes regurgitate content from publishers was keeping readers from visiting the sites of news organizations, the publishers argue.

“Defendants’ own experts acknowledge that grounded LLMs exploit their sources rather than promote them like search uses that have been deemed fair use,” the publishers’ filing states.

Tech.title: I Toured the Company Mapping Space Debris. Then I Polled Worried and Hopeful Scientists
Tech.content:
Walking inside LeoLabs’ new space radar nestled in the Maui hills felt like entering a computer. Wires dangled overhead, servers whined, and the temperature climbed in the metal box as the air conditioning leaked out when we entered.

“You don’t want to be in there when the whole thing’s running,” said Matthew Adelman, LeoLabs’ senior manager of radar systems. “Not just for the safety, but also for the noise.”

LeoLabs’ Scout-S radar is designed to be transported and setup within hours anywhere in the world. Allyza Umali/CNET

Called Scout-S, this radar designed to track space objects is the size of a 20-foot shipping container and can be transported anywhere in the world. You can hook it up to an electrical grid and fiber internet, but its real calling card is portability. You could drop the Scout-S off-grid and have it running in a couple of hours. All you need is a generator and a Starlink dish to feed the radar’s data back to a computer.

I couldn’t help but appreciate the irony at the mention of the Starlink dish: The satellite internet service revolutionized the space industry, but it also jump-started a race to space that created the need for transportable radars like the Scout-S.

The Soviet Union launched the world’s first satellite in 1957; it would take another 53 years for the population to pass 1,000. When Starlink launched its first satellite in 2019, there were still only around 2,000 orbiting Earth. Today, we’re at 16,810, and nearly 2 out of every 3 belong to Starlink.

Each one of them is zooming above us at 17,000 mph. A collision between two of them could range from extremely troubling to catastrophic. Worst-case scenario, satellites colliding with each other or a piece of space debris could set off a feedback loop known as Kessler syndrome, in which one collision creates thousands of new pieces of debris that cause yet more collisions. It could ultimately make low Earth orbit, or LEO, the sweet spot where Starlink beams down fast, low-latency internet from 342 miles over our heads, so filled with space junk that it’s no longer usable.

“We worry a lot about it because we have seen that in the last few years, the number of spacecraft has increased exponentially, and we are not stopping it,” said Lorenzo Olivieri, a professor at the University of Padova. I spoke with him this week at the Advanced Maui Optical and Space Surveillance Technologies Conference, where he was presenting a paper on space debris populations from break-up events.

“The worrisome idea of the Kessler syndrome could be a real close future,” Olivieri said.

Exactly how worried you should be about a Kessler syndrome-like scenario depends on who you ask. When I polled scientists at AMOS, their answers ran the gamut. Some said it’s only a matter of time if we stay on our current trajectory, while others waved it off as the domain of science fiction. (See the 2013 movie Gravity for a particularly vivid dramatization.)

But you don’t have to be a Kessler syndrome pessimist to take crowded orbits seriously. Whether you’re a satellite operator looking to avoid collisions or the US military deploying space weapons, everyone at AMOS wants to know what’s going on in the skies. The industry, referred to as space situational awareness, is estimated to reach $1.9 billion this year.

Aside from dodging millions of pieces of satellite-killing debris, operators also have to communicate with each other about where and when they’ll be moving. It’s an enormous challenge: How do you get adversarial nations and competing companies to agree on appropriate behavior in space?

“Driving on the highway would be terrifying if everyone had their eyes closed,” Gabriel Swiney, the director of policy at the US Department of Commerce’s Office of Space Commerce, told me. “The problem is communication and knowledge.”

The issues circulating the AMOS conference were as terrifying as space lasers and as mundane as standardizing space data for easier sharing.

I was almost ready to write off these topics as niche industry concerns when I pulled my phone out to get directions back to my hotel. A GPS satellite zooming 12,550 miles over my head instantly showed me where I was and needed to go.

Key takeaways

Orbital congestion: Nearly 17,000 active satellites raise serious concerns about potential orbital collisions and Kessler syndrome.

Nearly 17,000 active satellites raise serious concerns about potential orbital collisions and Kessler syndrome. Tracking technology: Ground-based portable radars and in-orbit cameras monitor space debris, though tracking objects under 10 centimeters remains difficult.

Ground-based portable radars and in-orbit cameras monitor space debris, though tracking objects under 10 centimeters remains difficult. Communication barriers: The main obstacle to space safety is the lack of open data sharing among competing entities and adversarial nations.

Traffic cameras for the skies

One engineer at AMOS described space awareness to me as having three stages: collection, processing and analysis. Many of the companies hawking their wares at the conference dabbled in multiple phases, but for the most part, they specialized in one of these buckets.

LeoLabs, the company that developed the transportable Scout-S radar, is primarily in the collection business. It has a dozen radar sites around the world, some of which can detect debris as small as 10 centimeters – a dangerous blind spot for most trackers.

“Think about the busy part of Seattle,” says Darren McKnight, senior technical fellow at LeoLabs. “If you have two traffic cameras, you don’t really know what route to take. You want traffic cameras at all the major intersections.”

It’s not always tiny pieces of debris — sometimes companies are even trying to find their own satellites up there. SpaceX, the company that operates Starlink, landed its reusable Falcon 9 rocket for the first time in 2015, kicking off a wave of “rideshare” launches.

Some of these had as many as 140 payloads, making it a challenge for satellite operators to even determine which ones were theirs.

“Once the first rideshare launch became a thing, that just exploded the number of things in orbit pretty quickly,” said Belinda Marchand, chief scientist at Slingshot Aerospace. “It was no longer just one launch vehicle and one object. It was one launch vehicle and a hundred.”

LeoLabs’ traffic cameras are all based on the ground, but other companies use cameras in orbit to give them a more detailed account of what’s happening in space.

“We use cameras that are in space to take pictures of other satellites in space,” said Hilary Cohen, director of operations at HEO USA. “There are trackers that track the dots and you know exactly where those satellites are. But this lets us go a layer deeper.”

This photo from an HEO space camera shows a solar panel in an abnormal configuration. HEO USA

Google Maps for satellites

But even if companies and countries do a good job of gathering information about their orbital goods, sharing it with other operators is an entirely different challenge. The key piece of information that everyone needs is called “ephemeris,” which lists the position and velocity of an object in orbit.

“Ephemeris basically is like my Google Maps,” McKnight said. “You’re sending it to everybody on the road with you and saying, ‘Here’s where I’m going to be.’”

The way scientists talked about ephemeris at AMOS sounded like castaways on deserted islands pleading for water. As good as the radars and space cameras have gotten, they don’t tell you when and where a satellite is planning on moving.

“Our community has an ephemeris sharing problem,” Jonathan Herman, senior director of Starlink Constellation Engineering, said at his keynote address. “The No. 1 risk in LEO is not debris. It is instead that operators don’t know where other satellites are going.”

A visualization from COMSPOC, a company that tracks objects in space, shows a Chinese satellite crossing orbits. COMSPOC

Herman noted that Starlink satellites perform around 1,000 collision-avoidance maneuvers per day, all of which consume valuable fuel and decrease the lifespan of the satellites. That number of maneuvers was described to me as “horrendously high” in a previous interview.

It’s a double-edged sword: Starlink does an exceptional job at avoiding objects in space, but the fact that they have to move so much makes it harder for other operators to know where its satellites are going to be.

Still, almost everyone I talked to at AMOS spoke about Starlink as a responsible steward of space. If you wanted an example of reckless behavior in orbit, there were much easier targets.

The geopolitical barrier

Not all of the technical problems involving satellite maneuvering are particularly complex. Herman, the Starlink director, said they could be solved in a few hours by getting everyone in a room together. The bigger hurdle is communication.

“We may understand at an operator-to-operator level what the best practices are, and the Chinese operators may understand that, too,” Audrey Schaffer, senior VP of global policy and government strategy, said on a panel. “But the challenge that we have is that the Chinese government is uncomfortable with their operators going directly to other operators.”

Commercial and defense domains in space are deeply interwoven. (I heard some version of the sentence, “Space is a warfighting domain,” at least a dozen times at AMOS.) If there’s a space company that doesn’t rely on military money at all, I didn’t find it here.

“Within the last 18 months, we’ve seen a lot more open discussion of the importance of defense funding,” said Ian Christensen, senior director of private sector programs at the Secure World Foundation. “There’s been a real pivot towards defense funding as the most stable and largest source of funding.”

That tension between military and civilian operations was woven through many of the conversations I had at AMOS. This development hasn’t come out of nowhere – Elon Musk said over a year ago that Ukraine’s “entire front line would collapse if I turned it off” — but you could feel AMOS’ attendees on both the military and commercial sides grappling with the balance in real-time.

“Russia’s actions consider every vendor here a legitimate target based on their cooperation with the US government and governments of NATO,” Col. Jonathan Whitaker, chief of staff of NATO’s Combined Forces Space Component Command, said at a panel. “When you take that perspective, there’s really no safe harbor for a commercial company.”

The bottom line

I walked away from AMOS feeling simultaneously comforted and pessimistic. As one person put it to me, there are around 40,000 tracked objects, but the island of Maui alone has about 184,000 registered vehicles.

The reality is more complicated — there are an estimated 1.2 million objects in orbit the size of a softball or smaller that aren’t tracked – but it’s a fair point. As Elon Musk is fond of saying, “Space is really big.”

“What I worry about is not so much the number of objects, which do make easier headlines,” said Swiney, the director at the Office of Space Commerce. “The much harder problem to solve is, how do you get someone on the phone if you’re not allowed to talk to them, or if you don’t even know what their phone number is in the first place?

“The technical problems are relatively easy to solve if we can get past the policy.”

Tech.title: I Got the Inside Scoop on Apple’s New Health App, Now in Developer Beta
Tech.content:
Last week at Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event, Dr. Sumbul Desai, Apple’s VP of Health and Fitness, announced the redesigned Health app and its fresh features. Between the new Insights tab with Apple Intelligence-powered suggestions, a Longevity tab that shows your Health Age, a readiness score, movement assessments, a blood panel and curated doctor videos, my head was swimming with questions. The following day, I sat down for a video chat with Desai for deeper insight into Apple’s reimagined health platform.

On Wednesday, the new Health app debuted in the first developer beta of iOS 27.2. Some announced features will be available in later betas, including personalized summaries under the Insights tab, personalized recommendations and the ability to order a blood panel from Quest Diagnostics.

“Features will roll out progressively,” Apple said in an email. “Feedback during the beta period will help us continue refining it ahead of the public release in late 2026.”

Here’s everything you can expect to uncover in the Health app and the features you shouldn’t sleep on.

From data spreadsheet to intelligent experience

Launched in 2014, the Health app was initially intended to be like a spreadsheet, with data flowing in, Desai explained. However, the team realized they wanted more from the app, so it evolved over the past 12 years into what Desai now calls “an experience.”

Those at the helm of the Health app’s 2026 makeover considered how to leverage Apple’s machine learning and AI to help people live healthier, while also personalizing the app’s recommendations and turning it into an intelligent hub, not unlike the iPhone itself. For instance, as you open the app and move through your day, different screens appear to reflect your health status.

Movement assessments have also been added to provide an even more complete picture of a user’s health and track progress or decline. Desai described them as a “mini physical” you can complete at home.

All assessments under the app’s Longevity tab are science-based and contribute to a rainbow-petal visual that illuminates your state of health. Some assessments rely on vision-based AI models that integrate the phone’s camera, marking the first time Apple has used the camera for health.

The current iteration of the Health app is just the beginning and was designed to set in motion the next era of the team’s work in health and fitness, as Desai said those working on the app still feel they have more to do.

The Longevity tab’s rainbow visual. Apple

Health Age: Biological vs. birthday

One standout feature from Apple’s event was the Health app’s Longevity tab, which will include a feature called Health Age that uses health metrics such as your VO2 max (the maximum amount of oxygen your body consumes during exercise), resting heart rate, sleep and heart rate variability, along with lab data such as LDL cholesterol and A1c for your average blood sugar level, to provide your biological age, which represents how your body is aging on a cellular level when compared to your actual age.

Apple’s own Heart and Movement Study, which it applies across all its health products, informs both Health Age and Readiness, which uses your activity data, daytime and overnight vitals and sleep data to tell you about your capacity for the day ahead.

The five-year Heart and Movement Study was conducted in collaboration with the American Heart Association and Brigham and Women’s Hospital to explore the connection between heart health and physical activity. Apple used that data to create the normative ranges for the insights it provides in the app.

While Desai acknowledged the Health Age assessment is more of a “fun way to look at your health habits” and that no one can tell you your actual biological age, it’s another way to provide insight and suggest healthy habits users can integrate into their lives.

I’m also hoping my Health Age is lower than my actual age. Apple

Apple’s secret sauce

Apple isn’t the first company to offer features such as a readiness score or biological age, but Desai said that it stands out from competitors because of its unique perspectives, experiences and the science behind its work.

“When we first started our work in health, when we announced our irregular heart rhythm notifications and ECG, those were clinically validated scientific features,” she said. Desai likened those early days to building a muscle that lets the team create impactful products the medical community will appreciate, and users can easily understand.

That muscle Apple first built has been exercised with all the Health app’s new features, as Desai said that everything is rooted in science. On her team, for instance, physical therapists graded each movement in the app’s mobility assessments to ensure that when a movement is picked up and a result is given, it’s graded the way an actual physical therapist would grade it.

Uniting science and expertise, Desai said that’s what Apple brings to the table, and its Health app experience.

The new Health app’s ‘sleeper hit’

Much of the discourse following Apple’s event has been about the new readiness score and Health Age. I was curious what Desai felt was the “sleeper hit” feature that didn’t get as much attention.

“It’s actually the assessments,” Desai said. “You’re going to be able to, on a regular basis, do a push-up test and a core test and see if you’re improving. Then we give you insights and things that you can do to improve, and then you can test again. It’s almost like having a physical therapist or a trainer.”

The VO2 max test, in particular, marks the first time Apple’s doing an on-demand, in-the-moment VO2 max test.

You can then take all your assessment results, and the Health app will put them into a report you can share with your doctor.

A person performing a movement assessment using their iPhone. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Homing in on your body’s big players

Based on its new assessments, the Longevity tab’s visualization has seven tabs: heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement health, metabolic health, hearing and nutrition. But how did Apple narrow it down to those seven?

“We picked areas where we felt like we had the appropriate data to comment on,” Desai explained. “For example, we do a cardiovascular risk score through some of the questions. It’s based on traditional risk scores and cardiovascular risk scores that are done.”

The team prioritized information they believe people will use and assessments they’ll complete, while ensuring the chosen health areas feel holistic and will help people concerned about long-term quality of life.

“There’s still more that we think we can do, but this is where we’re starting,” Desai stated. In other words, Longevity’s rainbow visual could gain more colors in the future.

Keeping privacy at Apple’s core

When it comes to its Health app, Desai said privacy is where they start and end.

“Candidly, we may not always be the first to market, but when we release something, we can stand behind it from a privacy standpoint,” Desai stated. “All the features you saw [announced] are no different. … It’s part of the conversation every day, and up till the day that the products are launched.”

Apple will hold off on releasing a product if it hasn’t met its privacy bar. The team behind the Health app also uses a checks-and-balances system, having other teams review their work to ensure they are nailing their privacy approach.

“In this world where more things happen in the cloud, we want to make sure that’s all encrypted and private, which is why we have Private Cloud Compute,” said Desai. Private Cloud Compute is Apple’s cloud intelligence system designed for private AI processing.

The team’s approach is end-to-end because privacy matters for all your data, not just health data.

Apple Intelligence has suggestions

The Health app’s new Insights tab uses Apple Intelligence to analyze your health metrics and provide a timely summary that updates throughout the day.

“We also make suggestions,” said Desai. “For example, if you have an injury or you’re trying to work on your mobility, we’ll give you suggestions on the types of exercises you might be doing.”

It’s another example of how the app is evolving from a database to something that more closely resembles a personalized health advisor.

The daily insights are meant to be bite-size pieces of information that are one small thing you can do for your health each day. Some days these insights may be interesting; other days, you might be given information you already know.

Under Insights, the For You section will use your data to offer personalized recommendations and relevant articles. Apple

Health on a cellular level, explained

For $119, the new Health app will let you purchase a blood panel with over 50 biomarkers through Quest Diagnostics. You can also get your blood pressure, height, weight and waist and hip circumferences measured. All this helps provide a more complete picture of metabolic health.

The revamped app will include videos from doctors that help people better understand what they see in the app.

“When you get your assessment results, you’ll actually see your own data in the videos where they’re explained by clinicians,” said Desai. “We have a physician, a physical therapist, a sleep expert, a mental health expert. The reason we did that is, for certain things, gamification works, but for certain things, you just want to know the information in an easy-to-understand way from an authoritative resource.”

While an expert explains the subject at hand, your health data, whether from your labs or your Apple Watch, will be overlaid on the video so you can see it as you learn more.

Ultimately, Desai doesn’t see the future of the Health app as one size fits all. Depending on the feature, the team always chooses what makes health as accessible and understandable as possible. In a world with an abundance of health data, perhaps that’s what matters most: ensuring people understand the numbers they see on their devices, and knowing what to do with them once the screen goes black.

Tech.title: iOS 27.2’s First Developer Beta Brings These Features to Some iPhones
Tech.content:
Just two days after Apple released iOS 27 to the general public, the tech giant released the first developer beta for iOS 27.2. While iOS 27 brought Siri AI and more to your device, this early look at iOS 27.2 shows Siri AI expanding to other languages and a few upgrades in other apps, like Facetime.

If you’re wondering what happened to iOS 27.1, Apple has said the foldable iPhone Duo will launch on 27.1 next month, and all devices will be able to update to 27.2 sometime later.

Since this is a beta, I recommend downloading it only on something other than your primary device. This isn’t the final version of iOS 27.2, so the update might be buggy and battery life may be short — it’s best to keep those troubles on a secondary device.

Also, since this isn’t the final version, more features could end up landing on your iPhone when Apple releases iOS 27.2.

Here are some features developers can try now in the first iOS 27.2 developer beta.

Siri AI in more languages

In iOS 27, Siri AI is only available in English. But the first developer beta of iOS 27.2 expands Siri AI to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish.

Apple previously said Siri AI would expand to these additional languages, so this shows the company moving quickly on that promise.

Use front and rear cameras simultaneously in Facetime

In the first developer beta of iOS 27.2, you can use your front and rear facing cameras at the same time in Facetime calls. This allows you to Facetime call with a larger group of people — you don’t have to squeeze everyone into a single frame in order to see the person on the other end of the call. However, everyone on the call needs to be on iOS 27 or later for this feature to work.

Refreshed Podcasts options

The Podcasts app also gets an update in the first iOS 27.2 developer beta. The beta introduces two rows to the top of the Home tab within the app: New Episodes and Continue Playing. This can help you keep track of what podcasts are new and what podcasts you still have to finish.

It’s a small, pleasant addition to the interface, and I appreciate how it helps keep my podcasts organized.

Apple TV profile expansion

In the first developer beta of iOS 27.2, you can create TV Profiles in your Apple TV app. You can assign a profile to your child or someone else and ensure your preferences aren’t messed with.

So if you’re tired of being recommended kids shows after letting your child watch the series Shape Island, you can create a profile for your child and let them watch those quirky little shapes all they want. (But also, it’s possible that I like Shape Island more than my son does, so you should check it out.)

Apple TV multiview on iOS

Another Apple TV update in the iOS 27.2 developer beta is Multiview. Developers who subscribe to Apple TV can watch up to four live sports streams, including streams from Major League Soccer and Formula 1, at once. That way, you don’t miss an important game, or you can look at a map of the racecourse while watching feeds from driver-view cameras.

Updated Health app

Developers can see a redesigned Health app in the first developer beta of iOS 27.2. However, the redesign is expected to launch sometime later this year, despite being featured in this beta.

Those are a few of the new features developers can try now with the first developer beta of iOS 27.2. There will likely be more betas before the OS is released to the public. Apple has not said when exactly it will release iOS 27.2 to the general public, but we expect it to land on devices in October.

For more, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and why your battery might be draining faster after updating. You can also check out why the iPhone Duo will launch with iOS 27.1.

Tech.title: Breville’s Wild New Toaster Swaps the Timer for Optic Sensors to Tell When Toast Is Done
Tech.content:
It may not seem like much, but a slice of toast is often the subtle touch a meal needs — one reason toasters remain a mainstay in many kitchens, even in the age of air fryers and toaster ovens. While it’s certainly a more convenient option than making toast in a pan, it’s not always easy to lock in your preferred doneness. Toasters typically monitor doneness in two ways: time and temperature.

That said, most people use one method, but few toasters use a third: visual doneness. Enter the recently launched Breville Eye Q 850 Auto Toaster. It uses a pulsing internal sensor to watch the color of the bread as it toasts, only finishing when it hits the perfect result, at least in theory. I put the theory to the test over the last month with a sample from Breville to see if this $300 high-tech toaster lives up to its promise. While I generally think it does, I noticed a few things that are worth considering. Let’s dig in.

What makes the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster different?

An optic sensor seems like a good way to ensure your toast always reaches the right doneness without tweaking settings between batches. John Carlsen/CNET

At first glance, the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster looks like any other high-end toaster — my test sample featured a matte black brushed stainless steel case and a ceramic top portion. But the real magic happens when you start the toast cycle. The Eye Q lowers the bread, and a green light inside the toaster begins to flash. This Eye Q Optic Sensor reminds me of something you’d see on fitness trackers, but instead of tracking a pulse, it monitors the bread’s visual doneness.

The sensor is only in the left-side slot, so you can toast a single slice, which I think is very helpful. Importantly, the toaster won’t run without something inside, which is a great safety feature. Like most premium toasters, this Breville unit uses a motorized lift to lower and raise your bread. It won’t pop up with a spring-loaded mechanism as on a typical toaster. It will, however, play a little chime at the beginning and end of each toasting cycle — the volume is adjustable, so you can turn it off or up depending on your needs.

I found the controls fairly intuitive once I figured out how to activate each mode, like timer mode. John Carlsen/CNET

Five buttons on the unit start/stop the toasting process, adjust the doneness, toggle bagel and English muffin modes, and trigger a feature called A Bit More. Most notably, the start button selects the operation: One press toasts normal bread, a long press does the same for sourdough, and two presses switch on the timer mode for things like Pop-Tarts.

I’m a huge fan of the power cord storage slot on the bottom of the unit, which holds the cord when you need to put the toaster away. This saves you from having to wrangle the cord another way. The crumb tray is completely removable, making the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster fairly easy to clean out. However, the tray isn’t dishwasher safe, so you’ll need to wipe off the old crumbs with a cloth instead. I doubt there’s much else to say about the tech in this toaster without digging into its performance, so let’s jump into my tests.

My time with the Breville Eye Q

Hitting the A Bit More button is an excellent way to finish toasting if it’s not quite perfect. It’s also a good option for folks who want to reheat forgotten toast that sat in the toaster too long, though you should expect it to get even more done. John Carlsen/CNET

Unlike an air fryer, a toaster isn’t a particularly versatile kitchen appliance. It makes toast, more toast, and the occasional Pop-Tart or frozen waffle. So this simplifies my testing, allowing me to focus on a few different types of bread — white, brown and sourdough — in addition to Pop-Tarts and frozen French toast (something I’ve long used my toaster to reheat).

I had a few problems with most of what I toasted. Aside from the darkest setting being a bit much for my usual preference, both white bread and sourdough turned out well across all of the doneness settings. I really liked the results for the sourdough using the corresponding setting, which was nice and crisp, despite not showing as much visual browning. I’m confident that the Eye Q Auto Toaster is perfectly suited for light-colored breads.

I can’t say that the surface of the toast always browns evenly—one side generally sees less toasting than the other, but I’m happy with the results. John Carlsen/CNET

However, dark brown bread threw a curveball. The lowest setting was way too crispy, and I had to cancel the toasting on the second-lowest after smoke appeared. I’d previously tested some of the same dark bread in the toaster without issues, so it’s possible my continuous toasting session somehow threw off the accuracy for darker bread. I can’t say whether this would be a long-term issue, but it’s something to watch out for.

Beyond my tests with sliced bread, Pop-Tarts showed that the Timer Mode requires a little more attention and experimentation to get the results you want. At one point, I accidentally used the Auto Mode on Pop-Tarts, and they came out overdone, but not burned, so it’s probably best to stick to the timer or a low setting for toaster pastries. Reheating frozen French Toast went fairly smoothly, but I set the timer too short and had to retoast until the center was nice and hot. I imagine the experience would be similar for frozen waffles.

Should you buy the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster?

If the choice came down to getting a toaster or an air fryer for $300, I’d choose the air fryer. John Carlsen/CNET

I’ll say it outright: the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster is a fantastic toaster, but the $300 price tag is out of reach for budget-conscious households. If you want a more affordable standalone toaster, I recommend something like the $40 Cuisinart CPT-122, which has been a reliable workhorse in my home for years.

Similarly, you might check out the Breville BTA720XL, a solid mid-range model for around $110, even though it’s Breville’s most affordable option. That said, if you use a toaster daily and can afford something in the premium category, it’s worth considering, especially compared with the disappointing $450 Revolution Cooking R180 Connect Plus Smart Toaster.

Tech.title: Projector Screen: Do You Need One for Your Home Theater?
Tech.content:
GettyImages/mgstudyo

Do you need a screen for a projector? Short answer: Technically, no. Longer answer: It depends, but probably yes. Even longer answer: A screen will dramatically improve the image quality, and often the brightness, of any projector. Even a cheap screen can improve the performance of the best projectors. More expensive screens can reduce ambient light, greatly improving image quality if there’s any light in the room. Also, while your painted wall may seem smooth, there’s still a texture, and every tiny imperfection will be visible as part of your movie, TV show or game.

Look at it this way, movie theaters have screens for a reason. Spending even a little money on a screen will improve how the projector you spent a lot of money on looks in any room. It is an added cost, though, plus the added complexity of setup and mounting. So if you’re not sure, here are all the reasons why you should get a screen, especially if you have an ultra-short-throw projector, plus a few situations where you don’t need one.

To screen or not to screen

There are three main reasons to get a screen:

Brighter image: Even simple screens are better than walls of any color.

Even simple screens are better than walls of any color. Smoother image: Walls have texture that will be visible in the projected image.

Walls have texture that will be visible in the projected image. Potentially better contrast and overall image quality: Some screens can “focus” more light toward your eyes, making the image seem brighter. Others can reject ambient light, so the image is better with any lights on.

Now, in fairness, if you have a tiny, budget projector that puts out only a handful of lumens, you won’t gain much by adding a screen. There’s very little performance to begin with, so there’s not much to improve. Full-size budget projectors and anything more expensive can definitely benefit. Many screens can “add” brightness by focusing more of the light back to where you’re sitting, instead of scattering it all over the room.

That scattering is especially problematic if you have an ultra-short-throw projector. Enough so that I’ve got a whole section below about them specifically.

You don’t need a dedicated home theater to get more from your projector — just the space for a screen. GettyImages/vostok

Regardless of the type of projector, any ambient light in the room will bounce off your wall (or screen) and negatively impact the image. It will wash it out, making it harder to see. There are ambient light-rejecting and ceiling light-rejecting screens that can help considerably if you want to use a projector but also don’t want to live in a cave. More on these below, but keep in mind no screen can magically make your projector look like a TV in the daytime.

Ultra-short-throw projectors need screens

Ultra-short-throw projectors have gotten quite popular, or at least their marketing has. These projectors sit just a few inches from the wall/screen, compared to short-throw projectors (a few feet away) and traditional projectors (many feet away). That placement ends up being a significant issue due to how light bounces off flat surfaces. Without diving too far into the physics of it, what happens is that a large amount of light ends up bouncing off the projection surface into your ceiling. This lightshow is distracting, at best, and depending on your ceiling, can reflect enough light back onto the screen to reduce image quality.

The solution is a special type of screen that helps direct light in specific ways to minimize this unwanted scattering. To test UST projectors, I bought a ceiling light-rejecting screen from Elite. The difference is huge. As you can see:

These side-by-side images were taken with the same shutter speed, aperture and UST projector. The only change is the screen. On the left, a traditional white screen. On the right, a CLR screen. Note the extreme light bounce pollution on the ceiling when using the traditional screen and how much darker the entire room is when using the CLR screen. All projectors look better with lower ambient light. The ceiling reflections would be even more pronounced without the screen’s case blocking some of the light. Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

A number of companies make CLR screens, both in fixed, motorized and manually retracting versions. Due to their more complex optical properties, CLR screens are harder to manufacture than traditional models, making them more expensive. This is something often unmentioned or waved away in the marketing for UST projectors. This is especially concerning since UST projectors are more expensive than similarly performing non-UST projectors. As a package, they’re just really expensive, so if you can fit a traditional projector, or even a regular short throw, they’ll be far cheaper, even with a screen.

ALR vs. CLR

CLR screens are a subset of ALR, or ambient light-rejecting screens. Both can minimize the impact of ambient light. As their names suggest, CLR screens work best when the light is coming from above, which is the main issue with UST projectors, but also if you have recessed lighting above the screen. ALR screens are designed for mixed lighting, aka a standard assortment of lamps, windows, etc.

The manufacturers of UST projectors specifically recommend CLR screens, so it’s best to go with that type if you’re getting one of those projectors. For other projectors, an ALR screen is better for most rooms. That said, the best option for non-UST projectors is room light control. Curtains and turning off the lights will work far better than any screen. No screen is magic, but they can help if you have the budget.

Other important factors to consider (digging deeper)

So that’s all the basics, but if we dig deeper, there’s a surprising amount of physics involved in getting an image from a tiny chip inside a projector, through the air and into your eyeballs. The same projector in two different rooms could have radically different performance. Two of the biggest reasons for this are the placement of the projector and the screen.

As mentioned above, a decent screen is crucial to any projector’s performance. This is because all projectors need to reflect off a surface to be seen at all. That surface does a combination of reflection and absorption, both of which are key in how the image appears to you.

Movie theaters use real screens for lots of reasons. GettyImages/dimitri-otis

To understand how screens work, it helps to imagine three different surfaces: a thick black curtain, a mirror and a piece of white paper. Shining onto these surfaces is the light from a projector or, if it’s easier to envision, the light from a flashlight.

Firstly, a curtain will absorb most of the light coming from the projector, and the image will appear dim. The same is true, to a lesser extent, if you’re using a wall instead of a screen. Even brighter shades of paint will absorb more light than a dedicated screen.

A mirror, on the other hand, reflects nearly all the light and in such a way that it’s impossible to see the image. The light bouncing off it travels at a specific angle in relation to how it hits the mirror. This analogy is important for screens because most projectors have an upwards throw, so they’re either mounted above the top of a screen or placed on a stand/table below the screen. If the projection surface was a mirror, most of the light would bounce toward the floor (in the case of a ceiling mount) or the ceiling (in the case of a stand/table). This is the issue I mentioned above regarding ultra-short-throw projectors, since the severe angle they are in relation to the screen means that without a special screen, a lot of light gets wasted on the ceiling.

Sony

Now imagine a piece of white paper that could, theoretically, reflect light evenly. This surface could combine the best properties of the previous two types by enabling you to: 1) see the image, and 2) get most of the light reflected back to you. However, in reality the paper would scatter the light too much, or at least more than what many screens do, so the image wouldn’t be as bright as it could be.

These extremes should give you an idea of what’s necessary with a screen. At its simplest, a screen has to reflect the light evenly so you can see the image. Beyond that, many screens have additional special coatings that can direct or focus the light. Screens with a positive “gain” can make the image appear brighter where you’re sitting, similar to how a lighthouse beacon’s lens focuses the light so boats can see it farther away.

As mentioned above, CLR and ALR screens take this one step further, not only directing light coming from a sharp angle more toward your eyes, but absorbing or redirecting light coming from different angles so the image isn’t as washed out.

A few companies make reflective paint that you can apply directly to your wall instead of using a screen. Even the smoothest of these can have visible texture, which will show up in the image. They also won’t be able to focus the light as much as a higher-gain screen.

Improving brightness

If a screen isn’t in your budget but you want to improve how your projector looks, there are a few things you can do to improve the image’s brightness. They’re not going to transform a dim projector into a bright one, but they’ll help.

Size : The first, and perhaps most obvious, is to just make the image smaller. If you don’t have a screen, either at all or yet, experiment with zoom or placement to make the image smaller. A small decrease in size can greatly increase how bright the image is.

A small decrease in size can greatly increase how bright the image is. Lamp and laser/LED settings : Most projectors have a setting to increase lamp power to increase brightness. This, unfortunately, has some side effects. A brighter lamp won’t last as long (not an issue with LED and laser-based projectors), so you’ll be replacing it more often. This usually means the projector’s fans will run more and at higher speeds, increasing noise in your room. Some projectors have a Dynamic lamp mode (or another feature with a similar name), which increases the lamp power for bright scenes and decreases it for dark scenes. Typically these extremes are the same as the projector in its brightest and darkest modes.

Many projectors will have a lamp hour counter in the menu that tells you roughly how old the lamp is. You can check online to see how close this is to the recommended replacement life. If you bought it used, it’s possible the seller reset this counter, so be skeptical if it’s a few years old with no hours on the lamp. If you’ve replaced a still-working lamp, save it in case something happens with the new lamp. That way you’ll still have something while you wait for a new replacement. Avoid third-party or knock-off replacement lamps though, as they might be dim compared to their “real” counterparts. However, modern LED and laser projectors don’t have lamps, and so aren’t susceptible to this issue.

Beyond that, it’s just about getting a brighter projector. Fortunately, we’ve got a few picks along those lines.

Tech.title: The Clicks Communicator Ships in December With More RAM and New Mobile Service
Tech.content:
At a time when nearly every phone-maker is raising prices and cutting memory, one company is bucking the trend by adding more RAM.

The $649 Blackberry-inspired Clicks Communicator phone will launch in December, but the company behind it just announced that the unreleased handset will have a larger battery and more RAM than originally expected. Clicks Technology, better known for its keyboard cases and Power Keyboard accessory, released a video on Friday sharing a number of upgrades, feature details and news about the launch.

The Clicks Communicator will ship with 12GB of RAM (up from the promised 8GB) and a 4,350-mAh battery (up from 4,000 mAh). Given this year’s trends, it is absolutely wild that the company is adding more RAM while keeping the previously announced preorder price of $499. Google, Motorola, Samsung and, most recently, Apple, have raised prices on most of their phones, including the new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, citing higher RAM and component costs driven by the increased demand for memory by AI data centers.

Clicks Technology announced the keyboard phone at CES in January. The marquee feature is a built-in physical keyboard that is similar to the one found on the company’s keyboard cases. The design was inspired in part by using a Motorola Razr’s cover screen inside a Clicks keyboard case for the phone. After receiving an unexpectedly high number of preorders, Clicks was able to upgrade the design and features, including the processor.

I took this photo in March. On the left is a dummy prototype of the Clicks Communicator, and next to it is a Motorola Razr (closed) inside a Clicks Keyboard case. Notice the Razr has the Niagara launcher on its cover screen. Patrick Holland/CNET

Turns out, plenty of people want a thoughtfully designed handset that combines old-school features — including a keyboard, dedicated notification light and headphone jack — with a modern smartphone focused on messaging, calls and efficiency. The Communicator, designed by a former BlackBerry designer, is the phone I’ve been looking forward to most this year.

People who preordered the Clicks Communicator can now configure their phone’s color, keyboard layout, charging covers and accessories on the company’s website. If you’re considering buying one, you can preorder it for $499 ($150 off) until Sept. 30.

The Communicator is sold unlocked, meaning that you can use your current carrier’s nano SIM card or eSIM with it. But you also have the option to use the company’s new voice and data service for phone called Clicks Mobile. It’ll run on AT&T in the US and Vodafone in the UK.

The video also showcases a number of Communicator features in depth. Here are a handful that stood out.

The Communicator will ship with the game Brick Breaker. Patrick Holland/CNET

Clicks Care

You can extend the warranty beyond a year and add accidental damage protection. “If something happens, even from day one, we’ll ship you a replacement,” says Jeff Gadway, Clicks Technology co-founder, in the video. Clicks Care will be available in the US and Canada for $129 for two years.

Prompt Key

While the physical keyboard is the main attraction, you can press the Prompt Key for speech-to-text input. The feature is powered by an on-device model, but Clicks Technology is exploring ways for Communicator owners to use other apps and services for voice input. The Prompt Key can also be used to bring up Gemini when you’re not in a text field.

Signal Light

An LED loop around the Prompt Key glows in different colors for calendar reminders, tasks and to indicate incoming calls and messages. You can customize the Signal Light with different colors for different contacts and priorities. The light will flash in different patterns to distinguish between a call and a message. This is what Pixel HiLight on the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro Max should have been; instead, that sits mostly dormant on the back of the phone and only glows during calls or when Gemini is “listening” to a prompt.

Quick replies

You can read and respond to message previews straight from the home screen, without opening the app. Gadway explains that the company is working to make it possible to reply and dismiss message previews using just keyboard shortcuts: No need to touch the screen.

Message Hub is a quick way to reply to messages without having to open apps. Patrick Holland/CNET

Message Hub

A curated pop-up on the home screen, the hub prioritizes incoming message notifications according to your Signal Light preferences. You can hop into the Message Hub at any time by pressing the Prompt Key or the Clicks Key on the keyboard.

Customizable hardware keyboard

The physical keyboard has a red Clicks Key that can be used to trigger shortcuts, similar to Click’s keyboard cases and the Power Keyboard. You can also reassign the bottom-row keys to take screenshots, switch between apps and perform other tasks.

Locking your phone

You can lock the Click Communicator by double-tapping the app list on the home screen. The phone uses a special version of Niagara Launcher, which displays apps in a list that you can navigate by sliding your finger along the right side of the screen.

The Saffiano leather charging covers will cost $79. Patrick Holland/CNET

MagSafe charging covers

The phone supports 15W Qi2 wireless charging and has a swappable backplate available in a variety of colors. There will be two Saffiano leather charging covers.

Case, bumper and screen protector

Accessory maker Dbrand is creating a $39 case for the new phone called MNML (pronounced “minimal”) and a $35 screen protector. Clicks is selling its own bumper case for $49 — it gives off a strong iPhone 4 bumper vibe.
